You were taught "to do all things in the name of the Lord," to act in the name of God; and yet you say, "May I not name the name of the Lord"? But what sort of name are you about to name? "The name of other gods you shall not call to remembrance in your hearts," and you say, "I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name"? He speaks then having suffered something human, which we too are often in danger of having suffered. And especially if anyone is conscious that, on account of teaching and the word, he once was miserable and suffered and was hated, he often says: I withdraw; what have I to do with troubles? If from this I am even involved in troubles—from teaching, from putting forth the word—why do I not rather withdraw to the desert and to quiet? Something of this sort the prophet also suffered, saying, "And I said: I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name."

But herein the Lord is good, who prevents such sins in men of such stature. He did not permit the prophet to speak truly in saying what lies before us, but in this too he made Jeremiah call upon faithlessness and break what had been said. For he said, "I will not name [any longer in his name] the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name." But he says, "It became in my heart as a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am utterly enfeebled and cannot bear it." The word of the Lord became a fire burning his heart. "And it became in my heart as a blazing fire, burning in my bones." He cast off the sin which he had committed in saying, "I will not name the name of the Lord, and I will no longer speak in his name," and Jeremiah cast off the sin at the very moment of speaking. Would that I too, at the very moment of sinning and speaking a sinful word, might perceive that "a fire has come to be in my heart, burning and blazing, so that I cannot bear it."

The word is about to venture something, but I do not know whether it is expedient for such an audience and such a one: it has said that there is a kind of fire, a fire not perceptible to the senses, that chastises the one chastised with pain to the point of his not bearing it. For he said, "It became in my heart as a blazing fire" and "burning" not in my heart only but also "in my bones, and I am utterly enfeebled and cannot bear it." I fear lest such be what is laid up for us, becoming a fire, as it came to be in the heart of Jeremiah. But we have not suffered it. If we had suffered this, and the two fires were set before us—this fire and the outer fire which we see upon those burned by the rulers of the nations—we would choose that fire rather than this. For that fire burns the surface, but this burns the heart, and beginning from the heart it penetrates to all the bones, and penetrating to the bones it comes upon the whole of the one being burned, and it comes in such a way that the one being burned cannot bear it. Who, upon this fire, can say, "and I cannot bear it"? I know that even robbers have been able to endure this fire, the pain from this fire. Another is the pain from the fire which Jeremiah described, saying, "And it became in my heart as a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am utterly enfeebled and cannot bear it." That fire the Savior kindles, who said, "I came to cast fire upon the earth." And since the Savior kindles that fire, therefore for those who are beginning to hear him he begins from the fire and first casts fire upon their heart; which Simon and Cleopas confess, saying concerning his words, "Was not our heart burning within us on the way, as he opened to us the Scriptures?" Here the heart is burned with fire, both Simon's and Cleopas's. Hear them saying, "Was not our heart burning?"

Who is now worthy to receive that fire in the heart, so that he may not receive it there? I wish to describe who it is that has this fire in the heart. Describe for me two who have committed the same kind of sin, the foul and unclean fornication, and of these two who have fornicated, the one not grieving nor pained nor stung, but suffering what is said in Proverbs concerning the harlot woman, "who, whenever she has acted, washes herself and says she has done nothing amiss." But look for me at the other, who after the fall cannot contain himself, but is chastised in his conscience, tormented in his heart, unable to eat and drink, fasting not by decision but by the anguish of repentance. Describe for me such a one "the whole day going about downcast and worn down, roaring from the groaning of his heart, seeing his sin before him" continually, convicting him in his presence. And behold such a one chastised not for one day nor for one night, but for a long time. Which of the two do you prefer? Which do you say has hopes with God? Is it that one who fornicated and was not concerned, but "grew callous, having given himself over to licentiousness," or this one who after the single sin mourns and laments? This one is † of hopes. The more he is burned by the fire of grief, so much the more is he pitied, and there is for him a sufficient time of chastisement, as much as the time of chastisement given to that one who fornicated and grieved. And since there is for this one a profitable time of chastisement here, therefore he contrived to chastise the one who has fornicated, and when he had chastised him with grief and saw the grief was sufficient, he says, "Lest such a one be swallowed up with too much grief, confirm your love toward him." Let each of us examine his own conscience, and let him see what he has sinned; for he must be chastised. Let him pray to God that this fire that was in Jeremiah may come upon him, and then the one that came upon Simon and Cleopas, so that he may not be reserved for the other fire; for if he has not received the fire here but has both sinned and been unconcerned, he will be reserved for that fire.

Now a fire such as this laid hold of Jeremiah the prophet, when the word was in him as a fire, and he said, ‘I pass away from every place, and am not able to endure it.’ And our Lord Jesus Christ, being good and a lover of men, came that He might cast this upon earth, and said, ‘And what? would that it were already kindled!’ For He desired, as He testified in Ezekiel, the repentance of a man rather than his death; so that evil should be entirely consumed in all men, that the soul, being purified, might be able to bring forth fruit; for the word which is sown by Him will be productive, some thirty, some sixty, some an hundred. Thus, for instance, those who were with Cleopas, although infirm at first from lack of knowledge, yet afterwards were inflamed with the words of the Saviour, and brought forth the fruits of the knowledge of Him. The blessed Paul also, when seized by this fire, revealed it not to flesh and blood, but having experienced the grace, he became a preacher of the Word.

Or possibly there are some who advise you to hide, because you have given your word upon oath not to accept the office if elected. For I hear that they are buzzing in your ears to this effect, and consider that they are thus acting conscientiously. But if they were truly conscientious, they would above all have feared God, Who imposed this ministry upon you. Or if they had read the divine Scriptures, they would not have advised you contrary to them. For it is time for them to blame Jeremiah also, and to impeach the great Moses, in that they did not listen to their advice, but fearing God fulfilled their ministry, and prophesying were made perfect. For they also when they had received their mission and the grace of Prophecy, refused. But afterwards they feared, and did not set at nought Him that sent them. Whether then you be of stammering utterance, and slow of tongue, yet fear God that made you, or if you call yourself too young to preach, yet reverence Him Who knew you before you were made. Or if you have given your word (now their word was to the saints as an oath), yet read Jeremiah, how he too had said, ‘I will not name the Name of the Lord,’ yet afterwards he feared the fire kindled within him, and did not do as he had said, nor hid himself as if bound by an oath, but reverenced Him that had entrusted to him his office, and fulfilled the prophetic call. Or are you not aware, beloved, that Jonah also fled, but met with the fate that befel him, after which he returned and prophesied?

I think, too, we cannot leave out of sight that fire when we read that the Lord Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire, as John said in his Gospel. Rightly was the sacrifice consumed, for it was for sin. But that fire was a type of the Holy Spirit Who was to come down after the Lord's ascension, and forgive the sins of all, and Who like fire inflames the mind and faithful heart. Wherefore Jeremiah, after receiving the Spirit, says: "It became in my heart as a burning fire flaming in my bones, and I am vile and cannot bear it." In the Acts of the Apostles, also, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and those others who were waiting for the Promise of the Father, we read that tongues as of fire were distributed among them. The soul of each one was so uplifted by His influence that they were supposed to be full of new wine, who instead had received the gift of a diversity of tongues.
On the Duties of the Clergy 3.18.102

Indeed, Christ, loving Moses, appeared to him in fire. And Jeremiah, having in himself the gift of divine love, said: "And there was a fire inflaming in my bones: and I was dissolved on every side, and I cannot bear it." Therefore, good charity having the wings of a burning fire, which flies through the chests and hearts of the saints, and consumes whatever is material and earthly: it tests whatever is sincere, and improves whatever it touches with its fire. This fire the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth, and faith shone forth, devotion was kindled, charity was illuminated, justice shone brightly. With this fire, he inflamed the hearts of his apostles, as Cleophas testifies, saying: Was not our heart burning within us, while he opened the Scriptures? Therefore, the flames of the Scriptures are divine. Indeed, the Scriptures were opening up, and the fire was coming forth, and it was penetrating the hearts of the listeners.

And thus with greater ardour she raises herself to the very bosom of the Father, wherein is the Only-Begotten Son of God Who declares the secrets of God, which in the time to come are to be revealed face to face. But even now He discloses them partly and in a figure to those whom He deems worthy, and at the same time sheds forth from the Spirit and from His own countenance floods of resplendent light, so that he who is illuminated thereby may say, "But it was as a fire blazing in my bones and I am melted on all sides, and cannot stay." And David says, "Let my sentence come forth from Thy presence!"

The interrogator. How is it that the service of hope is so delightful, and its labours so few and its work so easy to the soul?

The Father. This is because it excites the natural longing in the soul and gives them this cup to drink and makes them drunk. And from this moment they nevermore perceive fatigue but become apathetic against troubles. And during the whole of their course it is to them as if they were moving in the air without bodily motion, without seeing anything of the difficulty of the road or the streams and hills that are before them; but the crooked becomes to them straight and rough places plain, because they always see the bosom of their Father; and all those things which are far and invisible it makes to them clear in themselves, so that they gaze at them mysteriously with the hidden eye of faith. For all the parts of the soul become hot as by fire, on account of the expectation of those things which, though far, become as near; for towards them is tended the whole direction of their deliberations; and they hasten to know when they will reach [their aim] and when they will approach unto every single virtue by practice. They do not practice them partly, but all of them together, at the same time. For they do not take their course along the king’s way, as the generality of men, but choose short paths along which a few heroes move, who easily reach the Apartment. For hope warms them as with fire, and they cannot pause in their incessant course, on account of their joy. And to them happens as in the word of Jeremia: I said: I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones. Such is the recollection of God in the heart of those who move in the expectation of the promise. Short paths I call the concise virtues, because in them there is no winding nor the long space of many ways of discipline leading from here to there, nor place nor time nor distraction. But they stand on the way and accomplish it at once.

"And it became in my heart as a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am utterly enfeebled and cannot bear it, because I heard the blame of many gathered round about." The blameless, the blessed Jeremiah (I speak with exception of this small sin and if he committed any other slight thing) was blamed by many. But the blame from the many was for him a commendation with God. For those who blamed him said, "Conspire, and let us all conspire against him, all the men his friends; watch his design, and he will be deceived." They wished to deceive him with another deception, a destructive one, opposite to the deception concerning which he said, "You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived." And these who conspire against him say, "And we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our vengeance upon him." Those convicted for their own sins think they have been wronged, and therefore, supposing they have been wronged, they say, "We shall take our vengeance upon him." Something of this sort those also did who sawed Isaiah asunder; for as though wronged (since the prophecies turned them about and chastised them, convicted them, rebuked them) they sawed him and condemned upon him a sentence of death.

All the men who were peaceable toward me and guarding my side: if somehow he may be deceived, and we may prevail against him and take our revenge on him! But the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior. When adversaries have risen up, and those who were once friends and peaceable have turned to war and have wished to lay snares for us, let us not be greatly concerned, but let us choose to say this, which the prophet too speaks: But the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior.
But many of the teachers in the Church even today endure similar things, hearing the reproach of many gathered round about against them and who say: Persecute, and let us persecute them!

But Jeremiah says concerning these who conspire, "And the Lord is with me as a mighty warrior." If we become such as we ought to be, and receive that fire coming upon us for our sins, as upon Jeremiah and those like him, the Lord thereafter becomes with us "as a mighty warrior." And "therefore they persecuted and could not understand" [the Jews who persecuted him: "they were greatly ashamed and did not perceive their disgrace," being for so long a time disgraced they do not confess their own sins], because the Lord was with the persecuted one, and the persecuted one cannot come under their power. May it not then be, since many things of Jeremiah are referred to the Savior, that this too can be such? For "Conspire, and let us conspire against him" is said also concerning the Savior. And "the Lord" was with him "as a mighty warrior; therefore they persecuted and could not understand," the Jews who persecuted him; "they were greatly ashamed and did not perceive their disgrace," being for so long a time disgraced they do not confess their own sins, "which through the age shall not be forgotten," but they suppose that in this age their iniquities shall be forgotten. But we see that through the age their iniquities shall not be forgotten, and seeing this we remember the saying, "Be not high-minded, but fear; for if God did not spare the natural branches, how much more" the unnatural ones "will he not spare?"

Therefore those who persecute me shall fall and shall be weak — or therefore they persecuted and could not understand —, they shall be greatly confounded, because they did not understand the reproach or the everlasting ignominy, which will never be blotted out. Because they persecuted, therefore they could not understand the prophetic word, and vehement confusion followed upon their ignorance; nor did they understand the everlasting ignominy which will hold them fast and will be blotted out by no forgetting. Let them say, then, what they will, the men once peaceable and those who guarded my side, and let them desire to deceive, provided that so great a vindication and such great rewards attend the righteous man and teacher of the Church after persecution.

"They shall be greatly confounded, because they have not understood everlasting reproach." The second error concerns fatal necessity, as regarding the constellations: if a man is born under such a constellation, he will necessarily be a thief, or evil, or good. This empties free will and merit and reward of meaning: for if a man does of necessity what he does, what is the value of freedom of will? What will he merit? It also follows that God would be the origin of all evils. It is true that some disposition is left by the stars; but nevertheless God alone rules over the rational soul. Those who err thus shall have everlasting reproach.

For God does not hold out against his children when they beg his pity. And for you he will pray purely, held in high honor as an angel of God, and grieved not by you but for you. This is sincere repentance. "God is not mocked," nor does he give heed to vain words. For he alone searches the innermost recesses of the heart, and hears those that are in the fire, and listens to those who supplicate in the whale's belly and is near to all who believe, and far from the ungodly if they do not repent.
Who is the Rich Man that Shall Be Saved?

"The Lord," then, "of hosts" is with us, "who tests just things, understanding reins and hearts." The Lord tests just things and rejects unjust things, and he is, so to name it, a moneychanger of just and unjust things; and this Lord is also "one who understands reins and hearts." I inquire how "to understand reins and hearts" differs, and "to examine hearts and reins" is another thing. He does not examine the hearts and reins of all, but of those who have sinned; for I attend to the meaning of "examine," which is used in this life concerning those who are tortured. In the courts some examine, others are examined, and there are those also in the heaviest pains. But the Lord alone has a new manner of examinations, for he is one who examines hearts, and to the Lord alone belongs the examining of hearts and reins. Robbers here are examined in their sides at the command of a ruler, but there it is not by command of God, but by the Lord himself that one is examined as to reins and hearts—unless indeed I here say that the one commanded is the Son, and the one commanding is the Father, and that the Word is the one who examines hearts and reins. And of all tortures, I think, of all pains, heavier are those from the Word, when it examines both hearts and reins. Therefore let us do all things, so that we may not be handed over to that examination. Than which examination I think those handed over to those called in the Gospel the tormentors suffer less; for they are handed over to many, perhaps to more tormentors at the beginning, not yet becoming worthy to be handed over to the one Word that examines hearts and reins. That rich man was not yet worthy to be handed over to the one who examines hearts and reins; therefore he was tormented by more. But later, whether that one too suffers this or not, let him who is able examine. Nevertheless, what awaits us are tormentors and one who examines the hearts and reins for our sins; from which sins, if we are not more quickly delivered, in these we shall be. Therefore, having risen up, let us ask for the help that comes from God, that we may be blessed in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory unto the ages. Amen.

And you, Lord of hosts, tester of the righteous — or who test righteous things —, who see the reins and the heart, let me see, I pray, your vengeance on them! for to you I have revealed my cause. The Lord alone is the one who knows how to test righteousness, just as he alone is the one who beholds the inward parts of the heart; hence Jesus too, knowing the thoughts of men, is God not by advancement, as some think, but by nature. Something of the kind sounds in the Psalms as well: no one living shall be justified in your sight. If one who lives in virtues is not justified, how much more one who is dead in sins! And though the righteous man knows that he has God as his champion, yet through the impatience of human frailty he desires to see even now what he knows is to come. And he revealed his cause to him who says in another place: vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. Happy, then, the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord, as the Apostle says: everything that is made manifest is light.

Sing to the Lord, praise the Lord, for he has delivered the soul of the poor man from the hand of the most wicked! He who is poor in spirit and has not the riches which have received their consolation in this world, and of which Paul speaks: only that we should be mindful of the poor, when he has obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises the Lord in spirit and glories that he has been rescued from the hand of the most wicked. Yet all this comes about not by our merit, but by the grace of him who delivered the poor man; and he has not the riches of a pride that falls to ruin, but the humility of a poor man set free.

For neither would so great and such a prophet — I mean Jeremiah, who was "sanctified in the womb" of his mother and "consecrated a prophet unto the nations" — have set down anything emptily in books that were to remain forever, unless it contained something secret and full of vast mysteries, when he says: "Cursed be the day in which I was born, and the night in which they said: Behold a male. Cursed be he that told my father, saying: A male is born to thee. Let that man be glad like the cities which the Lord overthrew in fury, and repented not." Does it seem to you that the prophet could have imprecated things so grave and so burdensome, unless he knew there was something in that bodily nativity which both seemed worthy of curses of this kind, and on account of which the lawgiver would arraign so many uncleannesses, upon which he would consequently impose fitting purifications?

How much dissatisfaction do we see that even the brief stages of our lives bring on us! The boy longs to be a young man. The young man counts the years when he will be older. The mature man, ungrateful for the blessing of being in the prime of life, eagerly desires the honor associated with old age. Thus, to all there comes naturally a desire for change, simply because we become dissatisfied with what we are now. Therefore, even the very things that we have wished for become wearisome to us on their enjoyment, and what we have desired to obtain we reject on its attainment. Consequently, holy people have not without reason lamented their prolonged sojourning here: David lamented it, Jeremiah lamented it, Elijah lamented it. If we can believe wise people, even those in whom the divine Spirit spoke were hastening to better things.

Cursed be the day on which I was born; the day on which my mother bore me, let it not be blessed! Cursed be the man — or the person —, who brought the news to my father, saying: A son, a male child, is born to you, and as it were made him glad with joy! Let that person be as the cities are which the Lord overthrew and did not repent! Let him hear a cry in the morning and wailing at the time of noon, who — or because he — did not kill me from the womb, so that my mother might become my grave, and her womb an everlasting conception! Why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and that my days should be consumed in confusion? Those who think that souls were in the heavenly places and were cast down from a better state into a worse use this and testimonies of this kind, namely that it would have been better to dwell in the heavenly places than to dwell in the earthly ones and take on the body of humiliation, seeking certain new, nay rather already old, arguments for their heresy. We, however, reading that saying of blessed Job: cursed be the day on which I was born, and that night in which they said: behold, a male, and: cursed be the person who brought the news to my father, saying: a boy is born to you, fit them to this testimony, namely that it is better not to be than to live in torments, according to what is written: death is rest to a man for whom God has shut his way, and again: why is light given to the wretched, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul? And in the Gospel we read it said simply: it would have been better for him if he had not been born, not that one who has not been born exists, but that it is better not to be than to exist wretchedly; for it is one thing not to be at all, another, while one exists, to be tormented without any intermission, just as we prefer a quiet death to a miserable life. Hence Amos too calls the day a day of darkness, a day of affliction; and Jacob, because he lived in toil and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil; and the apostle Paul says: that he might rescue us from the present evil age, and again: redeeming the time, because the days are evil. The Hebrews reckon the fifth month, in which Jerusalem was taken and the temple overthrown, as that of Jeremiah's birth, by certain inextricable and incredible arguments. But if they were able to prove this, how they could interpret the testimony of Job I do not know; unless perhaps they claim that that day too, by a certain prefiguration and prophecy of things to come, belonged to the overthrow of the temple.

The apostle says, "God commends his charity toward us, because when as yet we were sinners, Christ died for us. Much more now that we are justified in his blood shall we be saved through him from the wrath." Of this wrath he says, "We were by nature children of wrath even as the rest." Of this wrath Jeremiah says, "Cursed be the day when I was born." Of this wrath holy Job says, "Let the day perish wherein I was born." Of this wrath the same Job says again, "Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries."

And as for his imprecating the likeness of the overthrown cities, I think it is said of Sodom and Gomorrah; and all time in mourning, so that in the morning there should be a cry and at noon wailing. And as for what he adds: who did not kill me in the womb, they think that God is meant. 'That there might be for me,' he says, 'an everlasting conception'; all of which is said hyperbolically. Finally he sets out the reasons why he prefers death to life, and not being at all to existing wretchedly, adding: why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and that my days should be consumed in confusion?
21: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah, and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying: Inquire of the Lord for us, for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us; if perhaps the Lord will do for us according to all his wonders, and he will withdraw from us. Above, the high priest Phassur or Phaschor, who struck Jeremiah, had Immer as his father, but this Phassur is the son of Malchiah; this is said so that no one may think him the same man. Now King Zedekiah sends to the prophet without wishing either the people or the princes to know, so that by a secret message through envoys he may learn what sentence the Lord holds concerning the city of Jerusalem and the people of the Jews. And what he adds: for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us, shows that Zedekiah asks this of the prophet when Jerusalem was already besieged. And it must be noted that in the prophets, and above all in Ezekiel and Jeremiah, the order of kings and of times is by no means kept, but, in reverse order, what according to the history happened later is related first, and what was done first is related later; for it is one thing to write history, another to write prophecy. Thus in the present place Zedekiah, who was captured with the city of Jerusalem, is written of as sending to Jeremiah, and that at the time when Jerusalem was being besieged; and afterward is narrated the history of Jehoiakim his brother, who was king before him, and of Jehoiachin, that is, Jeconiah, who was the son of Jehoiakim, concerning whom we shall speak in what follows.

And Jeremiah said to them: Thus shall you say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the vessels of war — or the weapons of war —, which are in your hands and with which you fight against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans, who besiege you round about the walls, and I will gather those things — or those men — into the midst of this city, and I will vanquish you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm — or a lofty one — and in fury and in indignation and in great wrath, and I will strike the inhabitants of this city; men and beasts shall die of a great pestilence. 'In vain', he says, 'do you wish to resist the besieging Chaldeans and prepare weapons of war, of which you will have the use only in the midst of the city, so that you may seem to be armed. For the rest, while they besiege you, I will vanquish you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm and will strike you with my fury and indignation, so that both you and everything that breathes may die of famine and pestilence in the midst of the city.' And this indeed we read was done; for without any ring of assault or din of combatants the city was taken by siege alone, so that they had none to conquer, but only those to capture; better off, he says, were those wounded by the sword than those slain by famine.

And after this, says the Lord, I will give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his servants and his people, and those who have been left in this city from the plague and the sword and the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their life; and he shall strike them with the edge of the sword, and he shall not be moved, nor spare, nor have mercy. This, which we translated: into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, is not found in the Seventy; and for what we said: he shall not be moved, nor spare, nor have mercy, the Seventy translated: I will not spare, nor have mercy. And it is better according to the Hebrew, so that the cruel and inflexible sentence may seem to belong to the Babylonian king rather than to the Lord. First, then, prophecy was made concerning the whole city; now it is foretold particularly to Zedekiah and to his people, those who would be left after the plague, the sword and the famine, that he is to be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, and to be slain with his friends by the sword, and that he should hope for no mercy from him whose covenant and bond he had abandoned by perjury.

Through your works you have revealed the everlasting structure of the world. You, Lord, created the earth. You are faithful throughout all generations, righteous in your judgments, marvelous in strength and majesty, wise in creating and prudent in establishing what exists. You are good in all that is observed and faithful to those who trust in you. You are merciful and compassionate. You forgive us our sins and our injustices, our transgressions and our shortcomings. Do not take into account every sin of your servants and slave girls, but cleanse us with the cleansing of your truth and "direct our steps to walk in holiness and righteousness and purity of heart," and "to do what is good and pleasing in your sight" and in the sight of our rulers. Yes, Lord, "let your face shine on us" in peace "for our good," that we may be sheltered "by your mighty hand" and delivered from every sin "by your uplifted arm"; deliver us as well from those who hate us unjustly. Give harmony and peace to us and to all who dwell on the earth, just as you did to our ancestors when they reverently "called on you in faith and truth," that we may be saved, while we render obedience to your almighty and most excellent name, and to our rulers and governors on earth.

There are two ways, one of life and one of death; but a great difference between the two ways. The way of life, then, is this: First, thou shalt love God who made thee; second, thy neighbour as thyself; and all things whatsoever thou wouldst should not occur to thee, thou also to another do not do. And of these sayings the teaching is this: Bless them that curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for them that persecute you. For what thank is there, if ye love them that love you? Do not also the Gentiles do the same? But do ye love them that hate you; and ye shall not have an enemy. Abstain thou from fleshly and worldly lusts. If one give thee a blow upon thy right cheek, turn to him the other also; and thou shalt be perfect. If one impress thee for one mile, go with him two. If one take away thy cloak, give him also thy coat. If one take from thee thine own, ask it not back for indeed thou art not able. Give to every one that asketh thee, and ask it not back; for the Father willeth that to all should be given of our own blessings (free gifts). Happy is he that giveth according to the commandment; for he is guiltless. Woe to him that receiveth; for if one having need receiveth, he is guiltless; but he that receiveth not having need, shall pay the penalty, why he received and for what, and, coming into straits (confinement), he shall be examined concerning the things which he hath done, and he shall not escape thence until he pay back the last farthing. But also now concerning this, it hath been said, Let thine alms sweat in thy hands, until thou know to whom thou shouldst give.

And the way of death is this: First of all it is evil and full of curse: murders, adulteries, lusts, fornications, thefts, idolatries, magic arts, witchcrafts, rapines, false witnessings, hypocrisies, double-heartedness, deceit, haughtiness, depravity, self-will, greediness, filthy talking, jealousy, over-confidence, loftiness, boastfulness; persecutors of the good, hating truth, loving a lie, not knowing a reward for righteousness, not cleaving to good nor to righteous judgment, watching not for that which is good, but for that which is evil; from whom meekness and endurance are far, loving vanities, pursuing requital, not pitying a poor man, not labouring for the afflicted, not knowing Him that made them, murderers of children, destroyers of the handiwork of God, turning away from him that is in want afflicting him that is distressed, advocates of the rich, lawless judges of the poor, utter sinners. Be delivered, children, from all these.

See that no one cause thee to err from this way of the Teaching, since apart from God it teacheth thee. For if thou art able to bear all the yoke of the Lord, thou wilt be perfect; but if thou art not able, what thou art able that do. And concerning food, bear what thou art able; but against that which is sacrificed to idols be exceedingly on thy guard; for it is the service of dead gods.

It was not God's law that became the cause of my being brought into subjection to corruption, but the devil, that he might be made manifest. He wrought evil through that which is good. The inventor of evil became and was proved to be the greatest of all sinners. "For we know that the law is spiritual." So the law cannot injure anyone in any way. Spiritual things are far removed from irrational lust and sin. "But I am carnal, sold under sin." This means, "I am carnal and placed between good and evil as a voluntary agent, so that I have it in my power to choose what I wish." For "behold, I set before you life and death." This means, "Death would result from disobedience of the spiritual law, that is, of the commandment, and from obedience to the carnal law, that is, the counsel of the serpent." By such a choice I am sold to the devil, fallen under sin. Hence evil, as though besieging me, clings to me and dwells in me. Justice gives me up to be sold to the evil one, as a result of having violated the law.

And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. He who dwells in this city shall die by the sword and by famine and by plague; but he who goes out and deserts to the Chaldeans, who besiege you, shall live, and his soul shall be to him as a spoil; for I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good, says the Lord; into the hand of the king of Babylon it shall be given, and he shall burn it with fire. To those who had been sent by the king and had come to beseech the prophet to inquire of the Lord for them, he had given the answer above, and what they should report to King Zedekiah; now he urges them to answer the people, and gives counsel that they desert to the Chaldeans against the royal will; and no one is unaware that this was dangerous for the prophet. Hence he even calls down death upon himself and says: cursed be the day on which I was born, and: why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow?; not that it is a light thing to counsel those not yet captured to hand themselves over to captivity of their own accord — as if men about to suffer shipwreck were ordered, before the shipwreck and the breaking up of the ship, to seize oars and planks and commit themselves to the waves — but that it is more tolerable to live as captives in whatever way than to be consumed by the sword, famine and plague. There are those who expound this passage according to tropology thus: that it is better to give oneself to secular studies, and above all to philosophy, than to remain in that church in which there is a famine of the word of God and the whole people dies by the sword of the heretics, by the dearth of doctrine and by the heretical plague.

And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, house of David! Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the one falsely accusing, lest perhaps my indignation go forth — or so that my indignation may not go forth — like fire, and be kindled, and there be none to quench it; and what follows: because of the wickedness of your pursuits, is not found in the Seventy. Because he had said above: and to this people you shall say: thus says the Lord, he now accordingly adds: and to the house of the king of Judah, so that there is understood: 'you shall say: thus says the Lord'; for by apo koinou [in common, i.e. shared by both clauses] both what precedes and what follows are joined, so that the sense is: 'and to this people you shall say: thus says the Lord, and to the house of the king of Judah you shall say: thus says the Lord'.

Properly, however, the word is addressed to the royal house, chiefly on account of whose guilt the city is besieged, so that it may amend its error by repentance and obtain the mercy of the Lord. 'Judge', he says, 'judgment in the morning' — not in the darkness of iniquity, but in the light of righteousness — 'and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the false accuser, so that you do not respect persons in judgment, but, when the rich oppress the poor, the command of God may prevail more with you than the power of the persecutor! And if', he says, 'you do this, the fire of my fury will by no means be kindled among you, nor will it find material to consume.' And in this place an incredible mercy of God is shown: those of whom he had said above: for I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good; into the hand of the king of Babylon it shall be handed over, and fire shall burn it, he now, while the Lord's sentence is already bearing down upon them, calls to salvation; not that he does not know that the city of Jerusalem is to be captured, but so that free will may be preserved for man, and they may be seen to perish not through ignorance of the future but by their own will; just as the Savior too knew that the people would deny him and that he was to be crucified, inasmuch as he had often foretold this to the apostles, and nevertheless he admonished them, wishing to correct them toward repentance, so that whatever they afterward suffered befell them by their own fault, not by the harshness of the one who threatened.

Behold, I am against you, inhabitant of the solid and level valley, says the Lord, you who say: Who shall strike — or terrify — us, and who shall enter our houses? And I will visit upon you; and what follows: according to the fruit of your pursuits, says the Lord, is not found in the Seventy. And I will kindle, he says, a fire in its forest, and it shall devour everything round about it. For 'inhabitant of the solid and level valley' the Seventy translated: behold, I am against you who dwell in the level valley of Sor, for which Symmachus translated 'rock', Theodotion 'besieged', Aquila's first edition 'solid', the second 'Tyre'; for 'Sor' or 'Sur' in the Hebrew language means 'Tyre' and 'flint' and 'narrowed'. Now he speaks against Jerusalem, which was walled in by siege; or which, in the likeness of Tyre, is so surrounded by the Babylonian army, as by a great sea, that it cannot escape; or else which, like the hardest rock, thinks itself impregnable and strong because of the solidity and size of its walls, and says: 'who will be able to terrify us and who shall enter our houses?', whereas God, on the contrary, says: 'I will visit you; you will not be able to escape my eye. And I will visit you unto destruction and render to you the fruit of your wickedness, and I will kindle a fire in your forest: not the Babylonian, as you think, not the king of the Chaldeans, but my wrath will accomplish all these things.' And he calls Jerusalem and all the region around it a 'forest', because, having no fruit-bearing trees of good works, it has been made ready for burning. And fittingly he calls the 'valley' 'level', because it lies open to the enemies, and not a 'lofty mountain', which can be climbed only with difficulty; in accordance with which it is also said in Isaiah: the vision of the valley of Zion. Whatever is prophesied concerning the royal house and the mother city, let us refer to the ecclesiastical order and to the princes of the churches, those only, that is, who have given themselves over to pride and riches and wantonness. Nor will it be delivered from destruction at once simply because it is the royal house; just as among those who were of the stock of David very few were found who pleased the Lord, such as David himself, Hezekiah and Josiah, and a great part of the princes and of the royal stock provoked the wrath of the Lord against the whole people.
22: Thus says the Lord: Go down into the house of the king of Judah, and there you shall speak this word and say: Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, who sit upon the royal seat of David, you and your servants and your people, who enter through these gates! Thus says the Lord: Do judgment and righteousness, and deliver him who is oppressed by force from the hand of the slanderer, and do not grieve the stranger and the orphan and the widow, nor oppress them unjustly — or impiously — and do not shed innocent blood in this place! For if you indeed do this word, there shall enter through the gates of this house kings of the race of David sitting upon his throne, and mounting chariots and horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you do not hear these words, by my own self I have sworn, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation. This vision, nay rather this word of the Lord, comes to the prophet either before Zedekiah sent messengers to him, or certainly after he had instructed the messengers what they should report to the king; Jeremiah is commanded not to speak to the king through messengers at all, but to go himself to the palace and speak to him there. And at the same time let us note the divine wisdom, in that through the messengers he orders sad tidings to be announced, mixed with prosperous ones too, should the king be willing to do repentance. Here, however, because he himself is commanded to go, he does not announce sad tidings and a captivity now on the very point of coming, but he advises what the king ought to do in order to escape the impending sentence of God.

Whatever was said to the royal house, let the bishops and their associates, the presbyters and deacons, and the whole ecclesiastical order understand: that if they do what has been commanded, and among other things do not shed innocent blood by causing even the least to stumble and by wounding the consciences of individuals, they will retain the dignity handed down to them by the Lord; but if they are unwilling to do it and despise it, they themselves will reduce the Church to desolation. Now those of the race of David enter through the gates of Jerusalem and sit upon the throne of him whose name means 'strong of hand', and they mount chariots and horses, when they rein in both their own disturbances and those of the people, and walk in the Church with composed step and with a choir of many virtues singing in harmony with them on every side. And that we may believe this to be true, he swears by himself, who, according to the Apostle, has no other greater by whom he could swear.

Now it is the proper work of kings to do judgment and righteousness, and to deliver from the hand of slanderers those oppressed by force, and to give help to the stranger and the orphan and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. And to instill in them a greater care for the precepts of God, he added: 'Do not grieve, so that you not only rescue them, but do not even allow them, through your connivance, to be grieved by others, and do not shed innocent blood in this place!' For to punish murderers and the sacrilegious and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the ministry of the laws.

'If', he says, 'you do these things, O kings of Judah, you will hold your former power and will enter the gates of Jerusalem with pomp; but if you are unwilling to do them, O royal house, it will be not so much the Lord's cruelty as your own will that the whole city is reduced to desolation.'

He threatens, therefore, the royal house and the city of Jerusalem and the temple, which he calls the head of Lebanon, that it is to be reduced to desolation together with all its cities, not by the power of the Babylonian king but by the command of the Lord, who says: I will sanctify against you one who slays. And Nebuchadnezzar and all his army are called 'holy' because he carries out the sentence of God. 'And they shall cut down', he says, 'your choice cedars' — all the powerful men and princes of the city — 'and cast into the fire, so that the flame devouring all things may consume them.

For thus says the Lord concerning the house — or to the house — of the king of Judah: You are Gilead to me, the head — or the beginning — of Lebanon; if I do not make you a desolation, cities uninhabitable. And I will sanctify against you a man who slays, and his weapons, and they shall cut down your choice cedars and hurl — or cast — into the fire. And many nations shall pass through this city, and each shall say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord done thus to this great city? And they shall answer: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God and worshiped strange gods and served them. Scripture records that Gilead, which the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed, lies beyond the Jordan; on this mountain Laban overtook Jacob as he fled, and the mountain, according to Genesis, received the name sōros, that is, 'mound of witness', because Jacob and Laban swore there, after stones had been gathered into a heap. Now it is the head or beginning of Lebanon, a lofty mountain which is planted all over with cedars, according to that word of David as he sings: and the Lord will shake the cedars of Lebanon, and elsewhere: I saw the wicked man exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and in Zechariah we read: Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars! Therefore in the present passage, since he was speaking to the royal house, he speaks by metaphoran [metaphor] to the temple, or to the house of the stock of Judah, because it is itself on a height, or because remedies for all sins were sought from the temple and the sanctuary; whence this same prophet also records: Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has the healing of the daughter of my people not gone up?

He calls Jerusalem "Lebanon," and he calls the royal palace in Jerusalem "Gilead." And there is a region in Lebanon that is called by that name, and there is also another Gilead in Israelite territory. But I think that the palace is being compared with the Gilead in Lebanon because of the impiety that they had dared to do in their midst. For this reason he threatens complete destruction on them.

Let the royal house of our city, too, hear this, and its princes and cedars, which lift their crown up to the clouds and say in their pride: 'Who will not see us?', that they will quickly be consumed by the flame of the Lord if they are unwilling to submit to his precepts. But the sanctification of the slayer and of his weapons is one thing, that of the priests and of those who minister to the Lord another.

And when everything has been destroyed, many nations will pass through the city and the temple, which before they were not permitted to enter, and each will say to his neighbor, why the Lord has wrought so sudden and so great an overthrow upon a city so renowned and great. And those who are asked', he says, 'will answer and set forth the causes of the ruins, saying: because they forsook the covenant of the Lord their God and venerated idols in place of God.'

Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn over him! Lament with weeping him who goes out, for he shall not return again, nor see the land of his birth! For thus says the Lord to Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, who went out from this place: He shall not return here any more, but in the place to which I have carried him away, there he shall die, and he shall not see this land any more. Josiah, a righteous king, had three sons, Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. The first of them Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, led captive into Egypt, and there he died; and he set up in his place as king his brother Eliakim, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. When he died, his son Jeconiah reigned, who was led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, the Babylonian king, together with his mother and the princes; in his place his uncle Zedekiah reigned, who, when Jerusalem was taken, was led into Babylon. And so it is asked who this is who ought not to be wept for, and who is to be led into captivity and will never return, since three were taken and carried away. The Hebrews think that this fits all of them, that is, Jehoahaz and Jeconiah and Zedekiah, and that all the sons of Josiah are called 'Sellem' or 'Sellum', which means 'consummation' or 'completion', because the kingdom of Judah came to its end in them. To me, however, this seems to be said properly of Zedekiah, about whom the prophecy of both the present and the previous chapter is, in whom the kingdom of Judah truly came to its end, under whom the city also was taken, and who, it is written, was led into Babylon and died there. He is 'Sellum', that is, 'consummation' and 'completion', son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father. Jeconiah, on the other hand, was not the son but the grandson of Josiah, the son of Jehoiakim, so that from the beginning of the vision, when there sent to Jeremiah King Zedekiah Pashhur son of Malchiah, and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, down to this chapter, we are to understand that everything is said to the king and about King Zedekiah.

Jeremiah too laments over his impenitent people, saying, "O that my head were waters and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for … my people!" And further on he gives a reason for his lamentation: "Do not weep for the dead," he writes, "or bemoan him, but weep sorely for him who goes away, for he shall return no more."

The apostle indicated the one who builds a house with righteousness when he said, "You are a field of God, a building of God." But he also says that no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds, and so on. Therefore, through the one who taught him, the believer has Christ Jesus as a foundation. And if any person builds well, it is with gold, the teachings of truth; silver, the saving word; precious stones, a structure built from virtues. And if anyone builds in an evil way by building what is bad for Jesus—I mean wood, hay and stubble—how is he not impious? It is for him that the threat comes: Woe to him who builds his house without righteousness! The one who makes a structure up high, yet not according to reason and truth of God, does not make the upper chambers in judgment. And similarly one can also view those who teach either a true or a falsely called knowledge. Paul builds the house, the church, with righteousness, he builds the upper chambers; Timothy and Luke and those such as them, in judgment.

But such a house as this sensual persons, they who dwell in cieled houses and delight in chased silver, do not build. For as they despise pure silver, so also they despise simple dwellings. They enlarge the site of their houses, they add more and more, joining house to house and farm to farm, they dig up the ground; so that the very earth itself gives way to their habitations, and like sons of the earth they are laid up within her womb, and hidden in her bowels. They surely are those of whom Jeremiah says, "Woe unto him that buildeth his house in unrighteousness." For he who builds in righteousness, builds not on earth but in heaven.

Woe to him who builds his house in unrighteousness and his upper rooms not in judgment, who oppresses his friend for nothing and does not pay him his wage; who says: I will build myself a broad house and spacious upper rooms, who opens windows for himself and makes ceilings of cedar and paints them with red ochre! Will you reign, since you compare yourself to the cedar? Did not your father eat and drink, and do judgment and righteousness then, when it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy to his own good; was it not therefore, because he knew me?, says the Lord. But your eyes and heart are for avarice, and for shedding innocent blood, and for slander, and for the course of evil work. LXX: O you who build your house not with righteousness and your upper rooms not in judgment! With him his neighbor works for nothing, and he will not pay him his wage. You have built yourself a little house, upper rooms open to the wind, set off with windows and raftered with cedar and daubed with red ochre. Will you reign, because you contend against Achaz, your father? They shall not eat and they shall not drink; it was better for you to do judgment and good righteousness. They did not know, they did not judge judgment for the lowly, nor judgment for the poor. Is not this your not knowing me?, says the Lord. Behold, your eyes are not upright nor your heart good, but they are for your avarice and for shedding innocent blood, and for iniquity and murder, to do them. I have set down both editions in full, so that both the Hebrew truth and the difficulty of the common edition may be more easily recognized. Now the word is against Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, of whom we spoke above, whom Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, set up in place of Jehoahaz his brother, whom he led bound into Egypt. And we read, and the history both of Kings and of Chronicles relates, that Jehoiakim son of Josiah reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, and reigned cruelly, and proved impious, and afterwards died; and yet his burial is not related, although holy Scripture has this custom, that it reports of all the kings both that they died and that they were buried. This one, however, it properly relates to have died and not been buried; of which we shall speak later. He laments, then, the aforesaid king, because he trusts in unrighteousness and thinks his royal dignity perpetual, and makes himself upper rooms, and oppresses his friends, and does not pay those who work for him their wage, and supposes the building of his palace to be everlasting.

We can, however, take this passage according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense] against the heretics, who build for themselves a house not great and most broad with the abundance of the Church, but a little one. And they build not with righteousness and judgment, desiring to plunder what belongs to others; whence it is said: You have built yourself a little house, upper rooms open to the wind, which are carried about by every wind of doctrine, and set off with windows; for they have no lasting building and no solid firmness. And raftered, he says, with cedar: they seem indeed to have the most beautiful rafters, but in the rains and the storm of persecutions they quickly rot and collapse. And daubed with red ochre: for they too promise the passion and the blood of the Lord, but they do not reign forever, because they contend with and provoke to anger 'araz', that is, 'cedar', their father. For every heretic is born in the Church, but is cast out of the Church, and contends and fights against his parent. And as for what he adds: They shall not eat and they shall not drink, 'the body and blood of the Savior' is understood; and the rest that is like these. And he says that all their error comes down from this, that they have not known God and do not have upright eyes, but their heart is bent on avarice, to plunder what belongs to others and to shed the blood of those they have deceived; for this is to commit murder. Obscure matters must be discussed more fully.

'Will you', says the divine word, 'be able to reign forever, since you desire to compare yourself to the lofty cedar, that is, to your father Josiah, a righteous king? Your father', he says, 'both ate and drank and enjoyed royal wealth; and yet he did not offend God in this, that he had riches, but pleased him in this, that he did judgment and righteousness, and therefore it was well with him, and will be, both in the present age and in the one to come. He judged', he says, 'the cause of the poor and needy, and to the refreshment of those whom he heard, and properly to his own good. And all these things turned out prosperously for him because he knew me, says the Lord. But your eyes, O Jehoiakim, turn aside to avarice, and, so that you may shed innocent blood, to slander and to the course of evil work.' But what sense the words have according to the Seventy I cannot understand; for while the rest agree with one another to some extent, as for what is added: Will you reign, since you contend with Achaz your father?, in place of which in the Hebrew is written 'araz', and this word means 'cedar', it is plain that it has no sense; and so too what follows: They shall not eat and they shall not drink, and the rest, which are so scattered and confused among themselves that without the truth of the Hebrew reading they have no intelligible meaning.

Therefore thus says the Lord to Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: They shall not lament for him: Woe, brother, and woe, sister! They shall not cry out together for him: Woe, lord, and woe, renowned one! But with the burial of an ass he shall be buried, rotted and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: They shall not lament for him: Woe, brother, and woe, sister, is not found in the Seventy. And it is said properly against Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the riddle which before seemed hidden is opened, and the ambiguity among the three brothers is resolved, so that the word is not about Jehoahaz nor about Zedekiah, but properly about Jehoiakim, who, the Hebrew history relates, was killed by raiding bands of the Chaldeans, of Syria, of the Ammonites and of the Moabites; whence also in Malachim [Kings] it is written that he died, and his burial is passed over in silence. In the book of Days we read that he was bound with chains and led into Babylon, and nothing further is reported of him. And finely he says that he is to be buried with 'the burial of an ass', so as to signify in other words that he would be unburied, that is, torn apart by beasts and birds. For this is the burial of an ass.

Go up to Lebanon and cry out, and in Bashan give your voice, and cry to those passing by, for all your lovers are crushed! I spoke to you; in your abundance you said: I will not hear! This is your way from your youth, that you have not heard my voice. The wind shall feed all your shepherds — or lovers — and your lovers — or friends — shall go into captivity; and then you shall be confounded and shall blush for all your wickedness. You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars, how you groaned when pains came upon you like the pains of a woman in labor! By metaphoran of Lebanon and Bashan, regions and mountains beyond the Jordan, the word is directed to Jerusalem, because she trusted in Egypt in vain; or to Jehoiakim himself, who at that time was reigning in Jerusalem and had been set up as king by the Egyptians, because he hopes in vain for the help of the Egyptians, and because they too are to be overcome by the Babylonian king and led into captivity.

And where we said: cry to those passing by, and in the Hebrew is written 'meabarim', the Seventy and Theodotion translated 'across the sea', Symmachus 'from opposite', to signify that the voice of the prophet must reach from Jerusalem as far as Mount Lebanon and Bashan.

And in saying: 'I spoke to you' — that is, God himself through the prophets — or: 'They spoke to you' — so that 'my prophets' is understood — 'and you in your abundance said: I will not hear', he convicts her of pride, and of having abused the greatness of her riches to despise God, and he relates that not only at this time but from the beginning, when she was led out of Egypt, she did not hear the voice of God; whence all her shepherds and princes too have been scattered hither and thither and have bowed their necks to the Babylonian captivity. And in adding: You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars, he taunts her arrogance, which had grown out of the abundance of all things, and says that like a woman in childbirth sudden pain and an unexpected captivity will come upon her.

In commentaries and expositions, whose custom it is to set down the differing opinions of interpreters, I am accustomed to insert language of this kind: 'Some say this, others assert that, certain ones think thus.' For this both wretched Grunnius himself and, many years later, the disciple of Jovinian and of him have slandered and still slander me, saying that I set down my own opinions under others' names, which I do for the sake of kindness, so as not to seem to tear anyone apart by name. Since, then, kindness has been turned into slander, I now say both to him who is dead and to this one who lives and tries to restore his heresy, that their master Origen refers this passage to Christ: that he was torn like a ring from the hand of God the Father and sent into the land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and handed over to the cross; and that his mother too — no doubt the synagogue — was taken and cast out. And in recalling these things he is not afraid to understand what follows also: Land, land, land, hear the word of the Lord! Thus says the Lord: write this man abominated or barren, and the rest, of the Lord of majesty. And he writes this, lest his disciples dare deny it, in the fifth book of the Stromateis.

As I live, says the Lord: though Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a ring on my right hand, I will tear him — or you — from there, and I will give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whose face you dread, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, — which is not found in the Seventy — and into the hand of the Chaldeans. And I will send you — or I will cast you — and your mother who bore you into a strange land, in which you were not born, and there you shall die; but to the land to which they lift up their soul, to return, there they shall not return. He had said above: 'To the house of the king of Judah you shall speak these things', and then: Go down into the house of the king of Judah, and again: Thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah; and in reversed order, after he has spoken about Zedekiah, who was the last of the kings in Jerusalem, he returns to Jehoiakim his brother, who reigned before him. This prophecy completed, he now speaks to the son of Jehoiakim, the grandson of Josiah, the king of Jerusalem, Jeconiah, who is also called by another name Jehoiachin, who was taken by Nebuchadnezzar and led into Chaldea with his mother and the princes and the craftsmen and many nobles, and died there. This, then, is what is said: 'If, as a ring does not leave the hand of the one who wears it and slips from the finger only with difficulty, Jeconiah were on my hand, yet I will tear him away and hand him over to the Babylonian king, and there he will die with his mother and all his companions, and he will no more see the land of Judea, which he longs for.'

Wretched Grunnius, who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue a lie, translated into Latin one book of Sextus the Pythagorean, a thoroughly pagan man, and divided it into two volumes, and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome; in these volumes there is no mention of Christ, none of the Holy Spirit, none of God the Father, none of the patriarchs and prophets and apostles; and with his usual rashness and madness he named this book 'The Ring', and it is read through many provinces, and above all by those who preach apatheian [freedom from passion] and sinlessness. As, then, the Lord threatens that he will cast Jeconiah from his hand and finger like a ring, so I beseech the reader to throw away this wicked book, and, if he wishes, to read it as he reads the other books of the philosophers, not as a church volume.

Since they did not imitate the piety of their ancestors though taking pride in their kinship with them—making much of Abraham, Isaac, Israel, David, Hezekiah and Josiah, men conspicuous for their virtue—for this reason the God of all rejects the arrogance of Jeconiah in these words: Even if he were a ring and were placed on my right hand, I would pull it off and hand it over to the enemy. Thus, let him not trust in his forebears' virtue without emulating their virtue.

As to Jeconias, whom the prophet Jeremiah declares in these words to have been rejected from the land of Judah, “Jeconias was dishonoured like a vessel for which there is no more use; and because he was cast out he and his seed; and none shall rise from his seed sitting upon the throne of David and ruling in Judah,” the matter is plain and clear. On the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, the kingdom had been destroyed, and there was no longer an hereditary succession of reigns as before. Nevertheless, at that time, the deposed descendants of David were living in captivity. On the return of Salathiel and Zerubbabel the supreme government rested to a greater degree with the people, and the sovereignty was afterwards transferred to the priesthood, on account of the intermingling of the priestly and royal tribes; whence the Lord, in things pertaining to God, is both King and High Priest. Moreover, the royal tribe did not fail until the coming of the Christ; nevertheless, the seed of Jeconias sat no longer upon the throne of David. Plainly it is the royal dignity which is described by the term “throne.” You remember the history, how all Judæa, Idumæa, Moab, both the neighbouring regions of Syria and the further countries up to Mesopotamia, and the country on the other side as far as the river of Egypt, were all tributary to David. If then none of his descendants appeared with a sovereignty so wide, how is not the word of the prophet true that no one of the seed of Jeconias should any longer sit upon the throne of David, for none of his descendants appears to have attained this dignity. Nevertheless, the tribe of Judah did not fail, until He for whom it was destined came. But even He did not sit upon the material throne. The kingdom of Judæa was transferred to Herod, the son of Antipater the Ascalonite, and his sons who divided Judæa into four principalities, when Pilate was Procurator and Tiberius was Master of the Roman Empire. It is the indestructible kingdom which he calls the throne of David on which the Lord sat. He is the expectation of the Gentiles and not of the smallest division of the world, for it is written, “In that day there shall be a root of Jesse which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek.” “I have called thee…for a covenant of the people for a light of the Gentiles”; and thus then God remained a priest although He did not receive the sceptre of Judah, and King of all the earth; so the blessing of Jacob was fulfilled, and in Him “shall all the nations of the earth be blessed,” and all the nations shall call the Christ blessed.

Is this man Coniah an earthen vessel, and broken? Is he a vessel without any pleasure — or usefulness —? Why are he and his seed cast away and cast forth into a land which they did not know? For what we said: Is he an earthen vessel, and broken, Symmachus translated: Is he refuse or worthless sweepings, and cast away?; in place of which there is nothing in the Seventy, but they translated only this: Jeconiah has been dishonored like a vessel in which there is no usefulness. And when this is said of Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, does anyone dare to refer it to the type of Christ, and, from the fact that the Apostle says that the Lord Savior is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, that is, wisdom, word, truth, life and righteousness, to say that he is called the ring which is cast off or torn away from the hand of the Lord and handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar? They are cast away, he says, he and his seed, and cast forth into a land which they did not know, which no one doubts happened to Jeconiah. 'Iechonias' means 'the preparation of the Lord'; in the present passage the first syllable, that is, the name of the Lord, is taken away from him, and he is called 'Chonias', so that 'prepared for perdition and destruction' is understood.

Someone who is in a state of ignorance is sinful and considered "earth and ashes." Someone who is in a state of knowledge, being assimilated as far as possible to God, is already spiritual and thus is considered elect. Scripture calls the senseless and disobedient by the term "dirt," which is clear from what Jeremiah the prophet says in reference to Joachim and his brothers: "Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Inscribe this man as an outcast."

Land, land, land, hear the speech of the Lord! Thus says the Lord: Write this man barren, a man who shall not prosper in his days; for there shall not be of his seed a man who sits upon the royal seat of David and has power any longer in Judah. If I should wish to note, place by place, how much the Seventy have either passed over or changed, it would become long, especially since the diligent reader can consider from each edition what has been changed, what added, what taken away. For 'barren' in the Hebrew is written 'ariri', which Aquila's first edition translated 'barren', the second anauxēton, that is, 'not growing', Symmachus 'empty', the Seventy and Theodotion 'abominable' and 'disowned'. And the question arises how the prophecy can stand that no one was begotten of his stock who sat upon the throne of David or was prince any longer in Judah, when our Lord and Savior was born of his seed, about whose birth Gabriel speaks to Mary: Behold, you will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the seat of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. We can therefore say this: that what is lacking in the Seventy, namely in his days he shall not prosper or shall not grow, has created the problem for those who do not know. For the Seventy translated: Write this man a disowned man, for there shall not grow from his seed a man who sits upon the throne of David, a prince any longer in Judah, which in the Hebrew is put twice; and those who wrote from the beginning, thinking this had been added in the Greek books, took it away. Let us answer, then, that in the days of Jeconiah no man succeeded him who sat upon his throne, but long afterward there was born of his seed one who obtained his royal seat. It can also be resolved thus: there will indeed not sit upon the throne of David a man and a human being, but God will sit, and his kingdom will not be earthly and brief, as David's was, but perpetual and heavenly, as Scripture says: He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end. Of Jehoiakim, then, was born Jeconiah, of Jeconiah Shealtiel, of Shealtiel Zerubbabel, and so in order one comes to Christ. But in the days of Jehoiachin no king, his son, succeeded him, as he himself had succeeded his father; but he was in captivity, and neither Shealtiel nor Zerubbabel nor anyone down to Christ obtained royal power. And this is so because in the Hebrew is written: in his days, and in the very time in which he lived, not shall there be a man who sits upon the royal seat of David. For all were captives, and of the stock of David no one thereafter held rule in the land of Judea. Whence Josephus too reports that princes of the priestly race and of the tribe of Levi ruled, whom Herod, son of Antipater the proselyte, succeeded, and that afterwards, under Vespasian, the kingdom of this race, nay rather the semblance of rule, was utterly destroyed.
23: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear the flock of my pasture — or O shepherds, who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture —, says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, to the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, you have driven them out and have not visited them; behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your pursuits, says the Lord. And I will gather the remnant of my flock from all the lands to which I shall have driven them out there, and I will bring them back to their fields — or I will restore them to their pastures — and they shall grow and be multiplied. And I will raise up shepherds over them and they shall feed them; they shall fear no more and shall not be dismayed, and none shall be sought from the number, says the Lord. The prophetic discourse is addressed to the shepherds, or concerns the shepherds; and since we read it written of Jeconiah, the next-to-last king of Judea, who was of the stock of David: O land, land, land, hear the words of the Lord! Write this man down as rejected — or barren — and there shall not be of his seed a man who shall sit upon the throne of David, and all hope of the Jewish kingdom had been cut off, the discourse passes over to the princes of the Church, and, the synagogue with its shepherds being abandoned and condemned, it is addressed to the apostles, of whom it is said: and I will raise up shepherds over them and they shall feed them; they shall fear no more and shall not be dismayed, and none shall be sought from the number, says the Lord. For the apostles will feed the flock of the Church confidently and without any fear, and the remnant of the people of Israel will be saved from all the lands and will be brought back to their fields or to their pastures, and they will grow and be multiplied. But upon the evil shepherds, the scribes and Pharisees, the Lord will visit because of the wickedness of their pursuits. We can also understand this according to tropology of the princes of the Church who nevertheless do not rule the sheep of the Lord worthily: that, these being cast off and condemned, the people may be saved, handed over to others who have proved worthy, and the remnant may be saved. Those shepherds destroy the sheep who teach heresy; those tear and scatter them who make schisms; those drive them out who separate them from the Church against righteousness; those do not visit them who withhold their hand from the penitent. On all these the Lord will have mercy, restoring to them their former pastures and taking away the evil shepherds.

[Passages quoted, Jer. xxiii. 6-8, xxx. 8, 9.]

Jeremiah prophesies thus long after the death of David and even the time of Solomon concerning a king who is to arise from the seed of David, whom he first calls "the rising," not simply but with the adjective "just," as though he were to shine forth from the sun of righteousness, of whom I treated in my evidences about the Second Cause, where I shewed that the pre-existent Word of God besides many other names was called Sun of Righteousness, quoting the prophecy which said, "To them that fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise." Therefore the prophecy in the present passage is that God will raise up "a righteous rising" to David, in the sense of a sun of righteousness. And he calls the same Being an understanding king, and one who does judgment and justice on the earth. He gives him too the same name as David, who died very long before. For you must note carefully how at the beginning he says, "And I will raise up to David a righteous rising," and adds at the end, "And I will raise up David to be his king." Whose, but David's?—for it was to him that he said He would raise up a righteous rising.

And Zechariah prophesying of the same Being likewise calls Him "arising," saying, "Behold I will raise up my servant, the rising," and also, "Behold a man whose name is 'The Rising,' and beneath him springs righteousness."

But no one, it is certain, arose after the time of Jeremiah among the Jews who could be called "a righteous rising" and "an understanding king doing judgment and righteousness on the earth." For if it be suggested that Jesus son of Josedec is meant, it must be answered that the prophecy is inapplicable to him. For he was neither of David's seed nor did he reign as king. How could this apply to him, "And I will raise up David to be his king," when he was of the tribe of Levi, and of high-priestly rank, and of another tribe than David, and is never recorded to have been king?
