And on the contrary, of the basket that had bad figs: And as the very bad figs, he says, which cannot be eaten because they are bad, so will I give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes and those who fled over into Egypt and who remained in this city, to vexation and affliction to all the kingdoms of the earth, when they were captured in Egypt too, and Nebuchadnezzar set his throne in Tahpanhes, and the Lord sent upon them the sword, famine and pestilence, until they were consumed from the land which he gave to their fathers. But what he said of the good figs: I will give them a heart, that they may know me, that I am the Lord, is like the apostolic saying: It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, in that not only our works but our will too rests on the help of God. In this place the ever-allegorical interpreter raves, and, wishing to do violence to the truth of the history, relates that some were captured from the heavenly Jerusalem and carried over into the land of the Chaldeans and will return again to their former place, such as Jeremiah and the other holy prophets, while others, who were sinners, will die in this land and in the valley of tears. I have set out the whole perikopēn [passage] of this vision together, so as not to divide the sense in the exposition.

But let us follow the simple and true history: that he called Jeconiah the basket of good figs, who by the counsel of Jeremiah and the command of God had handed himself over to the Babylonian king, and to whom the Lord also promises prosperity; and the basket of bad figs Zedekiah, who, contradicting the sentence of God, was captured, and with his eyes blinded was led to Babylon and died there. And to such an extent did God set his eyes upon them for good, those who acquiesced in his command, and bring them back into their land, and build them and not destroy them, and plant them and not pluck them up, and give them a heart, that they might know him, that he himself was the Lord, and that they might become his people and he himself might be their God, that even in the captivity he set his eyes upon them and permitted them to work the land, to build houses and to plant orchards in the region of Babylonia; Daniel, through miracles of signs, was suddenly made a prince from a captive; the three youths were gloriously delivered from the fire of the furnace; and when the seventy years were completed, under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the great priest, and Ezra and Nehemiah, the greatest part returned to Jerusalem, whose number is contained in the volume of that same Ezra.

Christ is a builder and architect, about whom it has been said in the prophets: "He will build my city, and he will turn back the captivity of my people." Thus the Lord said, "And I will build them up, and I will not tear them down." For the God who is good takes down certain buildings. For it is necessary that the building of unclean spirits be destroyed in us, and a temple to God be built in this way from virtues and right teachings so that his glory can be seen in it.

Put away doubting from you and do not hesitate to ask of the Lord, saying to yourself, "How can I ask of the Lord and receive from Him, seeing I have sinned so much against Him?" Do not thus reason with yourself, but with all your heart turn to the Lord and ask of Him without doubting, and you will know the multitude of His tender mercies; that He will never leave you, but fulfil the request of your soul. For He is not like men, who remember evils done against them; but He Himself remembers not evils, and has compassion on His own creature.
25: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judea — or upon all the people of Judah — in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. These things are earlier than the preceding vision; for that one took place under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been carried off to Babylon, but these under Jehoiakim, the son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah. For it was not their concern, as I have already said before, to preserve the chronological order of prophecy, which the laws of history require, but to write in whatever way they knew to be useful to those who would hear and read; hence also in the Psalter some wrongly look for the order of the psalms according to the sequence of history, which is not observed in lyric song.

This is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, which is not found in the Seventy; and there follows: which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim son of Josiah, father of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar took up the rule in Babylon, and so it came about that the year which was the first of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon was the fourth of King Jehoiakim in Jerusalem. Then, in the eighth year of his reign, he led into captivity Jeconiah with his mother and the princes, who had reigned only three months after the slaying of his father Jehoiakim. Now Jehoiakim was slain in the eleventh year of his reign in Jerusalem.

From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, up to this day, this is the twenty-third year, the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising by night and speaking; and you have not listened. In the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, who reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years, Jeremiah began to prophesy, and he prophesied under him for nineteen years. His son Jehoahaz succeeded him in the kingdom; and when he was at once led into captivity by Neco, the Egyptian king, his brother Jehoiakim obtained the kingdom, in the fourth year of whose reign this word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah. And so it was the twenty-third year of Jeremiah the prophet since he began to speak to the people, and he never ceased to preach, but every day, rising at dawn and by night, he spoke to the people; and you have not, he says, listened. But if, as the new heretics sprung from the old would have it, the law was given once for all as a help, and precepts were established which we either do or do not do by the volition of our own free will, how is it that the prophet always presses himself upon them and daily repeats the commandments of God, which, once received, would surely have sufficed for those to whom they had been given, unless it is to show that we always need God's help, and that what has been given once can never suffice unless it is renewed daily by the Lord's admonition?

He mentions the great number of years in order to emphasize God's long-suffering in putting up with unbelievers for so long. I sent my servants the prophets to you, he says. I urged you to abandon the road to ruin and travel by the other road that produces life. I, in fact, promised you blessings for doing this. But you did not listen, and instead you chose the worship of idols. And to censure the purpose of this unbelief he went on, "So that you might provoke me by the works of your own hands to your own misfortune." To provoke me, you committed those things, but then you also reaped their harmful effects then as well.

When the Jews often resisted wholesome precepts and departed from the divine law, going astray to the impious worship of false gods, then God filled just and chosen men with the Holy Spirit, appointing them as prophets in the midst of the people, by whom he might rebuke with threatening words the sins of the ungrateful people and nevertheless exhort them to repent of their wickedness. Unless they did this and, laying aside their vanities, returned to their God, it would come to pass that he would change his covenant, that is, bestow the inheritance of eternal life on foreign nations and collect to himself a more faithful people out of those who were aliens by birth. But they, when rebuked by the prophets, not only rejected their words but, being offended because they were scolded for their sins, killed the prophets with calculated tortures. All these things are sealed up and preserved in the sacred writings. For the prophet Jeremiah says, "I have sent to you my servants, the prophets. I sent them before light, and you hearkened not to me nor inclined your ears to hear when I said to you, 'Return, you, every one from this evil way and from your wicked devices, and you shall dwell in that land that I have given to you and to your ancestors forever and ever. Do not go after strange gods to serve them, and do not provoke me to wrath by the works of your hands for afflicting you.' "

Nor did you incline your ears to hear, when I said: Return, each one, from his evil way and from your very wicked thoughts, and you will dwell in the land which the Lord gave to you and to your fathers from age and even unto age. So great was the hardness of the people that it would not even take on the bearing of one who listens and incline its ear, above all when the Lord was warning it that each one should turn back from his evil way and from his very wicked thoughts. And O infinite clemency: not to inflict punishment for the crime, but to call to repentance both for evil works, which the evil way signifies, and for very wicked thoughts, which even by themselves, without the deed, are reckoned as sin! And he promises a reward if they do what is commanded: that they should dwell in the land which was given to their fathers and taken away because of the vices of the sons. And his saying: from age and even unto age, or: from eternity even unto eternity, shows that God's gifts are perpetual, if those to whom they were given prove worthy.

And the Lord sent to you all his servants, the prophets, rising at dawn and sending; and you have not listened. Not through one prophet but through all of them God always admonished his people, and as though he himself were stationed on watch and on guard, he rose at dawn to warn his people. And you have not, he says, listened, so that the more frequent the admonition, the greater were the sins of those who despised it.

And do not go after strange gods, to serve them and worship them, nor provoke me to anger in the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you; and you have not listened to me. 'And these things', he says, 'I was urging together with the earlier ones: that you should not serve strange gods and worship them, and that you should not, by doing these things, provoke me to anger because of the works of your hands, so that I should do what I did not wish and afflict you; and you have not listened to me'. And what follows: says the Lord, so that you provoked me to anger in the works of your hands, to your own harm, is not found in the Seventy.

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you have not listened to my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant. 'Because you have provoked me to anger and done evil to your own destruction, and have trampled with a proud foot him who called you to repentance, I will send', he says, 'to all the families, or nations, of the north, and I will bring their prince Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant'. Now the Lord sends either angels to stir up the nations, or else he moves thoughts of such a kind that they do the will of the Lord. And as for his calling Nebuchadnezzar 'his servant', he is not called 'servant' in the way the prophets and all the saints are, who truly serve the Lord, but in that in the overthrow of Jerusalem he serves the will of the Lord, in accordance with what the Apostle too says: whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. And that the Chaldeans lie in the northern quarter with respect to the position of Jerusalem is doubtful to no one.

And I will bring them upon this land and upon its inhabitants and upon all the nations that are round about it, and I will slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations. These are the rewards of those who despise the words of God and refuse to hear them; whatever evil, therefore, is brought upon us, our sins have brought about. And just as all the nations were then brought against Jerusalem, so today they are brought against the negligent Church, that he may slay them and make them an astonishment and a hissing and everlasting desolations, so that they may be an example and a marvel to all. Now hissing is a sign of marvel and astonishment, and everlasting desolation is found in those who do not have God as their protector.

Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by the prophet; ‘I will take away from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the scent of myrrh, and the light of a lamp, and the whole land shall be destroyed.’ For the whole service of the law has been abolished from them, and henceforth and for ever they remain without a feast. And they observe not the Passover; for how can they? They have no abiding place, but they wander everywhere. And they eat unleavened bread contrary to the law, since they are unable first to sacrifice the lamb, as they were commanded to do when eating unleavened bread. But in every place they transgress the law, and as the judgments of God require, they keep days of grief instead of gladness. Now the cause of this to them was the slaying of the Lord, and that they did not reverence the Only-Begotten.

And I will destroy from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bride and the voice of the bridegroom, the voice of the mill and the light of the lamp. And all its land shall become a desolation and an astonishment. This is proved even today in the assembly of the malignant, in that their teachers do not teach the word of God but hiss like a serpent. And there perishes in them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, so that they never hear that saying of the Apostle: rejoice, again I say, rejoice!; also the voice of the bride, that is, of the Church's faith, and the voice of the bridegroom, that is, of the Lord the Savior, for he who has the bride is the bridegroom; the voice of the mill, so that grain is not ground in it and given to the peoples to eat; and the light of the lamp, namely the teaching and knowledge of the prophets. Indeed, of John the Baptist too it is said: he was a shining lamp, and another prophet says: a lamp to my feet, he says, is your word, O Lord, and a light to my paths. 'All', he says, 'the land of the heretics shall become a desolation and an astonishment, when its last end has been shown to be foolish'.

And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will visit upon the king of Babylon and upon that nation, says the Lord, their iniquities, and upon the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it everlasting desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have spoken against it, all that is written in this book, whatever Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations. Just as Jerusalem after seventy years receives back its former inhabitants and, its punishments completed, because it obeyed the sentence of God, enjoys its former happiness, so the king of Babylon, because he was lifted up into pride and judged that his reigning over the nations was the work of his own strength and not of the Lord's will, will be destroyed when the Medes and Persians come. Indeed, to this day only the remains of the city of Babylon survive, and the Lord has made it an everlasting desolation and has fulfilled all the words that are contained in the book of this very prophet. For in what follows the discourse of Jeremiah describes what evils Babylon is to suffer.

[Daniel 5:2] "Being now drunken, he therefore gave order that the golden and silver vessels be brought in which his father, Nebuchadnezzar, had taken away from the temple which was in Jerusalem, in order that the king might drink from them..." The Hebrews hand down some such story as this: that up until the seventieth year, on which Jeremiah had said (Jeremiah 25:11) that the captivity of the Jewish people would be released (a matter of which Zechariah also speaks [Zechariah 1:12] in the first part of his book), Belshazzar had esteemed God's promise to be of none effect; therefore he turned the failure of the promise into an occasion of joy and arranged a great banquet, scoffing somewhat at the expectation of the Jews and at the vessels of the Temple of God. Punishment, however, immediately ensued. And as to the fact that the author calls Nebuchadnezzar the father of Belshazzar, he does not make any mistake in the eyes of those who are acquainted with the Holy Scripture's manner of speaking, for in the Scripture all progenitors and ancestors are called fathers. This factor also should be borne in mind, that he was not sober when he did these things, but rather when he was intoxicated and forgetful of the punishment which had come upon his progenitor, Nebuchadnezzar.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

We have seen the promises that God made to Abraham—to be the father, first, of the Jewish race according to the flesh, and second, of all nations who were to embrace the faith. The development in history of the City of God will show how these promises were kept. The end of the preceding book brought us up to the reign of King David. I shall now begin with his reign and treat of what ensued in as much detail as the theme of this book requires. There is a period that begins with the prophecies of Samuel and continues through the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity (which Jeremiah had foretold) and ends with the rebuilding of the temple, after the Israelites came home. This period is known as the age of the prophets, although, of course, the patriarch Noah, in whose lifetime the whole earth was destroyed by the flood, and others before and after him up to the time of the kings were prophets also. At least, they prefigured, in some fashion, many things touching the City of God and the kingdom of heaven and sometimes actually prophesied. Consequently, it is not too much to speak of these men as prophets; some of them are explicitly in Holy Scripture, for example, Abraham and Moses.

Because they served them, though they were many nations and great kings; and I will repay them according to their works and according to the deeds of their hands. This is not found in the Seventy. And it signifies that Jeremiah prophesied not only against Babylon but also against the other nations which were in the Babylonian army and fought against the people of the Lord. Indeed, in what follows words are spoken against Egypt and the Philistines and Moab and Ammon and Idumea and Damascus and Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor and Elam, and at the last against Babylon and the land of Chaldea.

In the same way in which physicians apply remedies to the sick, in order that by careful treatment they may recover their health, God so deals toward those who have lapsed and fallen into sin, is proved by this, that the cup of God's fury is ordered, through the agency of the prophet Jeremiah, to be offered to all nations, that they may drink it, and be in a state of madness and vomit it forth. In doing which, God threatens them, saying that if anyone refuses to drink, he shall not be cleansed. By this certainly it is understood that the fury of God's vengeance is profitable for the purgation of souls.

It is clear that Jesus wished to drink the cup of the passion. For by comparison it was better that it should pass because of his drinking of it than that it should not pass because he had not drunk it. For suppose the Lord had not drunk that cup and for this reason it had not passed from him: without doubt neither would the spirits working sins have passed from the human race, and fittingly neither would the penalties have passed which were owed for the sins. Therefore it was expedient for all that the cup should pass from him, because the Savior drank it, so that all of us who believe in him who drank it may not drink that cup "of unmixed wine", which gives to drink and is going to give to drink to "all the nations", so that those drinking it "may become drunk and vomit, and cease to rage". For just as "he died for us all", so that the death hostile to Christ might pass us by, so for us all (who were "debtors", bound to drink forever) he drank that cup, so that by this very thing—that the cup passes from him—it might pass also from us who do not drink it. Concerning this cup Jeremiah says: "The Lord God of Israel said to me: Take this cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you, and they shall drink and vomit and cease to rage before the sword which I send into the midst of them". Those, therefore, who hear the Lord and live according to his word and are cleansed through faith in him, no longer have need of that cleansing which comes about through that cup of wrath. For just as those who have been washed have no need to be washed, because they are clean (because they are Christ's disciples), so those who are not clean have need of that cup, the Lord exhorting them: "Drink and be drunk and vomit". For hear how Jeremiah speaks (or rather God in Jeremiah), exhorting those who have need of such a cup, since they ought willingly to drink it who have need of such a cleansing. And since God says these things exhorting them to drink, consider what he says further below: "And it shall be", he says, "when they are unwilling to receive the cup from your hand to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Drinking you shall drink, for in the city upon which my name has been invoked, upon it I will begin to bring evils, and you shall be cleansed with cleansing".

Know that it was foretold that wars would continue frequently to prevail, death and famine accumulate anxiety, health would be shattered by raging diseases and the human race be wasted by the desolation of pestilence. It was predicted that evils should be multiplied in the last times and that misfortunes should be varied and that as the day of judgment is now drawing near, the censure of an indignant God should be more and more aroused for the scourging of the human race. For these things do not happen, as your false complaining and ignorant inexperience of the truth asserts and repeats, because your gods are not worshiped by us, but because God is not worshiped by you. For since he is Lord and Ruler of the world and all things are carried on by his will and direction, nor can anything be done save what he has done or allowed to be done, certainly when those things occur that show the anger of an offended God, they happen not on account of us by whom God is worshiped, but they are called down by your sins and by what you deserve, by whom God is neither in any way sought or feared, because your vain superstitions are not forsaken, nor is the true religion known in such a way that he who is the one God over all might alone be worshiped and petitioned. Finally, listen to himself speaking with a divine voice at once instructing and warning us: "You will worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve." And again, "You will have no other gods but me." And again, "Do not go after other gods to serve them, and do not worship them, and do not provoke me to anger with the works of your hands to destroy you."
Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 5-6

'In the ways', he says, 'of your sister Samaria you walked; therefore you must drink the cup of her whose sins you followed — and that a cup is often taken for punishments and torments, there are many examples, among which is this: A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine, mixed. And he has tilted it from this; yet its dregs are not emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink; and in Isaiah it is called 'the cup of ruin' and 'the draught of fury'; and God speaks to Jeremiah, saying: Take the cup of pure wine from my hand, and you shall give drink to all the nations to which I shall send you; and they shall drink and vomit, and go mad; for just as certain cathartics are given so that the noxious humor that is in bodies may be purged out, so the Lord too gives a most undiluted cup of torments, to take away from sinners whatever there is of gall and bitterness and restore them to their former health — ; and the cup itself will be deep and wide: deep in the magnitude of the punishments, wide in the length of the captivity; but when', he says, 'you have been made drunk and seized by sorrow, and have drunk the cup to the dregs and drained it to such a degree that you devour even the fragments of the cup itself, then you will be weary of your former fornication and will tear the breasts which had been broken in Egypt and which were subdued and crushed by your lovers — or I will take away all your feasts and new moons, so that in place of solemnity and gladness you may have eternal lamentation and grief —.

For thus says the Lord God of Israel to me: Take this cup of the wine of fury — or of pure wine — from my hand, and you shall give drink from it to all the nations to whom I shall send you; and they shall drink and be drunk — or vomit — and go mad before the sword which I shall send among them. And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord and gave drink to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me. The giving to drink of the cup, and of the cup 'of pure wine' or 'unmixed', which in Greek is called akratou, is a sign of the Lord's fury, so that all the nations which made war on the people of God drink of the cup of the Lord's fury, of which Isaiah too writes against Jerusalem: the bowl of fury, the cup of ruin you have drunk up and emptied; therefore arise! And this cup is drunk by all the nations for this reason: that they may vomit and go mad. This, indeed, a perverse interpreter takes in a good sense, as though, like a cathartic potion, it forces out whatever bile and phlegm and harmful humor there is in the breast, and restores former health. He also takes the Savior in place of Jeremiah, because he himself gave drink to all the nations, to whom he was also sent, so that, casting off idolatry, they might dedicate themselves to the worship of God. That this is contrary to holy Scripture what follows will show; for not as a remedy, as he would have it, but as a punishment are they given to drink from the undiluted cup.

And he calls God's punishment the "cup of unmixed wine." … By "drinking" and "vomiting" Jeremiah implies they have had enough, and in their "raving," he alludes to the terrible nature of their punishment. Then the prophet further relates how Jerusalem and the cities that paid tribute to it, along with their kings and rulers, were made to drink this cup.

He gives the name drinking cup to punishment, as also in another psalm, "In the hand of the Lord there is a cup of wine, full of a strong mixture," and a little later, "all the sinners of the earth will drink it." This drinking cup blessed Jeremiah was ordered to offer to the nations.

To Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah and to its kings and to its princes, to make them a desolation and an astonishment and a hissing and a curse, as it is this day. 'I thought', he says, 'that I was giving drink to the nations alone, and therefore I had gladly offered myself for this ministry; but among the other nations, nay rather before the other nations, I gave drink to Jerusalem and to the cities of Judah and to its kings and princes, to make them an astonishment and a desolation and a hissing and a curse, as is also proved by the present example'. Hence he also says above: You have deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you were stronger, and you prevailed!

To Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and to his servants and to his princes and to all his people and to all in general. After Jerusalem, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, drinks, and his allies; the princes drank, and the whole people, and everyone who is indeed not an Egyptian but dwells in its regions, whom the Seventy translated symmiktous, that is, 'people of mixed stock', a populace not of the Egyptian region but foreign and immigrant.

To all the kings of the land of Ausitis. It is called 'Vs' in Hebrew, and the history relates that Job too was from it: there was a certain man in the region of Ausitis, named Job. And yet it should be known that this short verse is not found in the Seventy, and that Theodotion translated 'island' for 'Vs'.

And to all the kings of the land of the Philistines and of Ashkelon and of Gaza and of Ekron and to the remnants of Ashdod. In general he set down the Philistines, that is, the land of the Palestinians, and in particular their cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, Ashdod; Gath alone he passed over in silence, which is contained in the 'remnants'. For this is what is written: and to the remnants of Ashdod; for the region of the city of Gath is neighboring and bordering on Ashdod, which in Hebrew is called Esdod. And Isaiah too writes that the Palestinians were captured and laid waste by the Babylonians.

To Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon and to all the kings of Tyre and to all the kings of Sidon. Idumea is the land in which are the mountains of Seir, and which in Hebrew is called Edom; Moab and Ammon are themselves the sons of Lot, neighbors of the Dead Sea. Tyre and Sidon are the chief cities on the coast of Phoenicia, which themselves too were overcome when the Babylonian came; Carthage is their colony, whence also the Poeni are so called, by a corruption of the word, as though Phoeni, and their language is to a great extent akin to the Hebrew language.
And to the kings of the islands which are beyond the sea. He passes over to Cyprus and Rhodes and the islands which are called Kyklades [the Cyclades]; for these too were occupied by the Babylonians.

And Dedan and Teman and Buz and all who are shorn round the hair. These nations are in the wilderness, neighboring on and intermingled with the regions of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, and of whom it is said: who are shorn round the hair.
And to all the kings of the west, who dwell in the desert, and to all the kings of Zimri. This too is not found in the Seventy.
And to all the kings of Arabia. This is not found in the Seventy. After Dedan, then, and Teman and Buz and the Ishmaelites, the order of the regions follows.

And to all the kings of Elam and to all the kings of the Medes. From the fact that Elam and the kings of the Medes follow Zimri, we judge that Zimri too is a region of Persia, unless perhaps, from the fact that Arabia came before, these too are to be understood as kings of the desert. Now Elam is a region of Persia beyond Babylon; hence also the Elamites, and the Medes too and the Persians, by whom Babylon was captured and destroyed; and they themselves also drank the undiluted cup when Alexander, king of the Macedonians, gave it them to drink.

And to all the kings of the north, near and far. Because he had enumerated the regions of Persia and Babylon, of Elam and of the Medes, he now sets down in general all the kings of the north, who are near and far. For 'north', which in Hebrew is called 'safun', the Seventy translated aphēliōtēn, which we can call 'the east wind'.

Each one against his brother, and to all the kingdoms of the earth which are upon its face. So that it should not become lengthy to enumerate one by one all the regions of the eastern province, he set down in general all the kingdoms of the earth which dwell on the earth. And as for his saying: against his brother, there is understood 'I gave the undiluted drink', so that all should rage, vomit, go mad and fight one another in mutual battles. And what he added:

King Sheshach shall drink after them, and is not found in the Seventy, has this sense: 'All the nations round about', he says, 'will be subject to the Babylonian empire, and he will subject all things to his power, so that all the nations which the preceding discourse has recounted serve him and drink of his cup'; hence also in the vision against Babylon it is written: Babylon is a golden cup that makes all the earth drunk. But last of all the king of Babylon will drink this potion, given him to drink by the rider of the chariot, of the camel and of the ass, Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians. But how Babylon, which in Hebrew is called 'Babel', is to be understood as 'Sesach' will not greatly trouble anyone who has even a little knowledge of the Hebrew language. Just as among us the Greek alphabet is read in order up to the last letter, that is, 'alpha, beta' and so on up to 'omega', and again, for the sake of children's memory, we are accustomed to reverse the order of reading and mix the last letters with the first, so that we say 'alpha omega, beta psi', so too among the Hebrews the first letter is 'aleph', the second 'beth', the third 'gimel', up to the twenty-second and last letter 'thau', of which the next-to-last is 'sin'. And so we read 'aleph thau, beth sin', and when we come to the middle, the letter 'lamed' meets 'chaph'; and just as, if it is read straight, we read 'Babel', so with the order reversed we read 'Sesach'. But the vowel letters between 'beth and beth and lamed' and 'sin and sin and chaph' are not set down in this name, according to the idiōma [idiom] of the Hebrew language; and I think it was prudently concealed by the holy prophet, so that he should not openly stir up against himself the madness of those who were besieging Jerusalem and were on the very point of taking it. We read that the Apostle too did this with regard to the Roman Empire, when he wrote of Antichrist: do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains, that he may be revealed in his own time, Antichrist being understood. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only he who holds now, until he be taken out of the midst. And then the wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the spirit of his mouth and destroy with the illumination of his coming. By 'he who holds' he indicates the Roman Empire; for unless it has been destroyed and taken out of the midst, according to the prophecy of Daniel, Antichrist will not come before. If he had chosen to say this openly, he would foolishly have stirred up the rage of persecution against the Christians and the Church then coming to birth. We have spoken of this passage at greater length than the brevity of commentaries allows, which the Greeks and Latins will perhaps disdain, because it is not found in their codices. But what will that profit them, when in what follows this same prophet says: how Sheshach has been taken, and the renowned one of the whole earth seized; how Babylon has become an astonishment among the nations? Allegorical interpreters refer this whole passage to all the nations which the devil has made drunk with the most undiluted cup of sins; for he himself too, they say, will at the last drink punishments and torments, he of whom the Apostle writes: whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the spirit of his mouth, whence also in another place he says: but the last enemy will be destroyed, death. It requires great powers to be able to carry the names of different nations over into their etymologiais [etymologies] and to fit individual vices to individual names.

And when he says that he gave it to drink to the other nations and to Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, he adds: Thus says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk, and vomit, and fall before the face of the sword which I shall send among you (Jer 25:27). And it is to be noted that this cup of the Lord's fury is his sword, which is sent into the midst of sinners. Here a question arises: how, after the drinking, the drunkenness and vomiting and the fall, it is said in Jeremiah that Jerusalem cannot arise, and now he speaks to her through Isaiah: Lift yourself up, lift yourself up, arise, Jerusalem. It is resolved thus: as long as someone drinks the cup, and is drunk, and raves, and vomits, and falls, he cannot arise; for he has not yet drained the cup of the Lord, nor come to the dregs, so as to have drunk it to the bottom. But now he speaks to Jerusalem in the past tense: who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury, and not, who are drinking.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and be drunk and vomit and fall and do not rise, before the sword which I will send upon you! 'After', he says, 'you have given drink to all the nations and fulfilled the command of the Lord, you will again command these things with the words of the Lord and say: Drink and be drunk and vomit and fall and do not rise!' If 'to drink, to be drunk, to vomit and to fall' is a sign of salvation, so that, like a cathartic potion, everything harmful is expelled, how does there follow: and do not rise? And what the drink is that makes them fall forever he sets down more plainly, that is: before the sword which I will send among you.

In the same way in which physicians apply remedies to the sick, in order that by careful treatment they may recover their health, God so deals toward those who have lapsed and fallen into sin, is proved by this, that the cup of God's fury is ordered, through the agency of the prophet Jeremiah, to be offered to all nations, that they may drink it, and be in a state of madness and vomit it forth. In doing which, God threatens them, saying that if anyone refuses to drink, he shall not be cleansed. By this certainly it is understood that the fury of God's vengeance is profitable for the purgation of souls.

And when they refuse to take the cup from the hand, to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Drinking you shall drink; for behold, in the city in which my name has been invoked, I am beginning to afflict; and will you, as though innocent, be exempt — or and will you be clean with cleanness — ? you shall not be exempt, or you shall not be clean. He covertly shows that those who have refused to do the command of God willingly will undergo it by necessity, and will hear: drinking you shall drink. 'Whether you will it', he says, 'or not, the sentence of God must be fulfilled. For if the city of Jerusalem, in which the name of God was known, as the prophet says: God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel, drank the undiluted cup, the cup of fury, how much more will you not be clean, who worship idols in place of the name of God!'

For I am calling a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord of hosts. This is the most undiluted drink, this the cup of the Lord's fury, which is called not upon Jerusalem alone but upon the whole earth and all the nations round about; of which he had said above: 'and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them upon this land and upon its inhabitants and upon all the nations that are round about it.'

And you shall prophesy to them all these words and say to them: The Lord will roar from on high — or will give answer — and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; roaring he will roar over its beauty — or he will answer over his place —, a chant as of those who tread will be sung together against all the inhabitants of the earth. The sound — or destruction — has come to the ends — or upon a part — of the earth, for the Lord has judgment with the nations; he himself is judged with all flesh; the wicked he has given over to the sword, says the Lord. First let us say how the truth of the translation stands. 'To all the nations', he says, 'you shall prophesy and say that the Lord roars from on high, that is, gives a sign of his fury, according to what is written: the lion will roar, and who will not fear? the Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?' and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice, so as to terrify all who hear. And he will roar over its beauty, that is, over the temple. And when he has roared, a chant will be sung like that of those who tread in the winepresses, and at the shedding of one another's blood a mournful song will be sung together, which Symmachus calls katalegma, Aquila iasmon; and the sound of this chant and song will reach to the ends of the earth, for the judgment of the Lord is with the nations. But if the judgment of the Lord is with the nations, the merits of the nations too are diverse. This serves to expound that passage, as some would have it: he who does not believe is already judged. He is judged indeed in that he did not believe; but those very ones who do not believe will be afflicted with punishments that differ among themselves. He himself is judged with all flesh, so that no one goes away unjudged. But the wicked — that is, those who do not believe in the Lord — he gives over to the everlasting sword. Allegorical interpreters expound this passage according to the Seventy in such a way as to refer the Lord's open threat to a good sense. 'The Lord', they say, 'will give answer from on high, namely to those whom he is going to save, and from his holy place he will utter his voice, and he will answer a word in his place. But they, like vintagers, full of the fruits of that sentence, will answer. Upon all the inhabitants of the earth destruction will come, not upon the whole earth, but upon a part of the earth, namely, of those who do not believe; for the Lord will have judgment among the nations, and he himself will be judged with all flesh, but the wicked will be given over to the sword'.

Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, affliction — or evil — shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind — or tempest — shall go forth from the heights — or the ends — of the earth. And the slain of the Lord — or those wounded by the Lord — shall be on that day from the height of the earth to its height; they shall not be lamented, and they shall not be gathered up nor buried; they shall lie as dung upon the face of the earth. Let them blush who try to do violence to holy Scripture by expounding in a good sense things that are full of threatening. Now of this passage I think the Lord too spoke: nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and the rest that is contained in that same saying of the Gospel. And let us understand that these things were done according to the history, when all the nations round about were subjugated by the Babylonian king and felt his cruel rule, or according to prophecy, as things that are to come long afterward at the consummation of the world. And they are called slain by the Lord, not because the Lord himself strikes them, but in that in the destruction of the most wicked the will and command of the Lord is fulfilled.

Howl — or shout for joy —, you shepherds, and cry out, and sprinkle yourselves with ashes, you nobles of the flock — or lament, you rams of the sheep —, for your days are fulfilled, that you should be slain, and your scatterings, and you shall fall like precious vessels — or like choice rams —. And flight shall perish from the shepherds, and deliverance from the nobles — or rams — of the flock. It should be noted that only in this place have the Seventy put 'jubilation' in a bad sense, for which the other translators rendered 'howling', as it is written in the Hebrew. Between the shepherds and the rams, or nobles, of the flock there is this difference: the shepherds pertain to rational beings, while the rams and nobles refer to the rich, who themselves too are called part of the flock. And as for what he adds: your days are fulfilled, that you should be slain, their days will be fulfilled then, when their sins have been fulfilled, and they will be scattered and will fall like precious vessels, so that once broken they cannot be restored, and the more precious they were before, the greater the loss in their breaking; or like choice rams, so that they may be a fat victim for those eager to devour them. Flight, he says, shall perish from the shepherds, when they have not shown repentance. Indeed, it is said to the Pharisees: brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? And in the Psalms we read: flight has perished from me. And deliverance, he says, from the nobles of the flock, or rams; apo koinou [in common, i.e. shared by both clauses] 'shall perish' is understood.

The voice of the cry of the shepherds and the howling of the nobles of the flock — or the jubilation of the rams —, for the Lord has laid waste their pastures. And the fields — or the beautiful things — of peace have fallen silent before the wrath of the fury of the Lord. Here too it should be noted that in the Seventy 'jubilation' is put for 'howling'. Now between the shepherds and the rams there is this difference: the shepherds are taken to be those in the Church who preside over the flock with wisdom and learning and teaching, but the rams those who seem indeed to be leaders among the people, but have in themselves nothing of teaching and wisdom, and through excessive simplicity are almost neighbors of folly. But when we have peace and do not understand either the good things or the beautiful things of peace, but give ourselves over to luxury and idleness and pleasures, then the good things of peace will grow quiet, or fall silent, and will be taken away from us because of the wrath of the Lord's fury, and that which is written will be fulfilled: when they say: peace and security, then sudden destruction will come upon them, at whose coming all things will fall silent.

He has forsaken, like a lion, the shade — or the lair — that is his — and, as is more correct, the tabernacle; for this is what the Hebrew 'soccho' means —, for their land has become a desolation — or trackless — before the wrath of the dove — or before the great sword — and before the wrath of the fury of the Lord. The Lord, of whom he had said above: from on high he will roar, and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice; roaring he will roar over its beauty, will himself forsake his tabernacle, of which it is written: his place has been made in peace — or in Salem — and his dwelling in Zion; he himself will desert his seat and will fulfill what he spoke through this same prophet: I have left my house, I have forsaken my inheritance. And he has left, like a lion, his lair, so that all the beasts have power to lay waste his land. For while the lion is its guardian and protector, no one dares to approach it. Their land, he says, has become — without doubt either that of the people of the Jews, or else that of all the nations — a desolation and trackless before the wrath of the dove. He who has read above that Nebuchadnezzar is called the Lord's 'servant' will not be surprised that he is understood as the Lord's 'dove' — for which the Seventy translated 'great sword' —, although we can also take the 'dove' in the person of Jerusalem, because she is angry and sad that she has lost the guardianship of her lion and that her land has come into desolation.
26: In the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and you shall speak to all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them; do not withhold a word! If perhaps they will hear and turn, each one from his evil way, and I may repent of the evil — or I may rest from the evil —, which I am thinking to do to them because of the wickedness of their pursuits. This prophecy is earlier than the former one, although it was made under the same king. For that one was made in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, but this one in the beginning of the same king, as Scripture says: in the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying. Therefore, as we have often said already, the order of history is not to be woven together in the prophets, since in the present case, under the same king, earlier things are spoken afterwards and later things before.

The Novatians bring up a question from the words of the apostle Peter. Because he said, "if perhaps," they think that he did not imply that forgiveness would be granted on repentance. But let them consider concerning to whom the words were spoken—of Simon, who did not believe through faith but was contemplating trickery. So, too, the Lord, to him who said, "Lord, I will follow you wherever you go," replied, "Foxes have holes." For he knew that the man was not being fully sincere. If, then, the Lord refused to him who was not baptized permission to follow him, because he saw that he was not sincere, do you wonder that the apostle did not absolve him who after baptism was guilty of deceit and whom he declared to be still in the bond of iniquity? But let this be my answer to them. As to myself, I say that Peter did not doubt, and I do not think that so great a question can be so easily disposed of by the questionable interpretation of a single word. For if they think that Peter doubted, did God doubt, who said to the prophet Jeremiah, "Stand in the court of the Lord's house, and you shall give an answer to all Judah, to those who have come to worship in the Lord's house, even all the words that I have appointed for you to answer to them. Do not omit a word, perhaps they will listen and be converted." Let them say, then, that God also did not know what would happen. But ignorance is not implied in that word, but the common custom of Holy Scripture is observed to be taken in its simplest sense. Inasmuch as the Lord says also to Ezekiel, "Son of man, I will send you to the house of Israel, to those who have angered me, both themselves and their ancestors, this very day, and you shall say to them, Thus says the Lord, if perhaps they will hear and be afraid." Did God not know that they could or could not be converted? So, then, that expression is not always a proof of doubt.

But he who is about to speak the word of the Lord ought to stand with Moses and to hear with the psalmist: you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. And he is commanded to speak to all the cities of Judah, although the Seventy did not translate 'cities', lest perhaps it should seem unfitting to speak, in the court of the house of the Lord, to cities which were not present; but when he speaks to the peoples and to the citizens, he speaks to the cities themselves. And he fittingly stands in the court and vestibule of the temple of the Lord, so that, on the occasion of prayer to the Lord and of worshiping him, they may be compelled to hear the words of the prophet. 'Do not', he says, 'withhold a word; although it be sad, although the rage of those who hear be stirred up against you, nevertheless say what has been commanded you, fearing not the persecutions of those who are to be stirred up against you, but the command of the Lord who orders it!'

And that we may not fancy that the Lord granted this specially to the Ninevites, He continually affirms by Jeremiah that He will do the same in general towards all, and promises that without delay He will change His sentence in accordance with our deserts; saying: "I will suddenly speak against a nation and against a kingdom to root out and to pull down and to destroy it. If that nation repent of the evil, which I have spoken against it, I also will repent of the evil which I thought to do to them. And I will suddenly speak of a nation and a kingdom, to build up and to plant it. If it shall do evil in My sight, that it obey not My voice: I will repent of the good that I thought to do to it." To Ezekiel also: "Leave out nota word, if so be they will hearken and be converted every one from his evil way: that I may repent Me of the evil that I thought to do to them for the wickedness of their doings." And by these passages it is declared that we ought not obstinately to stick to our decisions, but to modify them with reason and judgment, and that better courses should always be adopted and preferred, and that we should turn without any delay to that course which is considered the more profitable. For this above all that invaluable sentence teaches us, because though each man's end is known beforehand to Him before his birth, yet somehow He so orders all things by a plan and method for all, and with regard to man's disposition, that He decides on everything not by the mere exercise of His power, nor according to the ineffable knowledge which His Prescience possesses, but according to the present actions of men, and rejects or draws to Himself each one, and daily either grants or withholds His grace.
The Second Conference of Abbot Joseph, Chapter 25

He did not use the word perhaps out of ignorance, aware as he was of their disobedience. Instead, he expressed such uncertainty to avoid their taking note of the divine sentence and despairing of salvation. It resembles also what was said by Ezekiel, "If then they hear, if then they see." In other words, it was not a result of ignorance. It was, rather, to prevent their saying, He foretold our disobedience, and he is trustworthy, so how is it possible for us to be changed? Thus, in the present words he emphasizes that it is possible to undergo a change in behavior, if they are willing.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God; if perhaps even they will hear, and if perhaps they will be quiet. Something similar is written in Jeremiah too: If perhaps they will hear and repent, and in the Gospel: Perhaps they will respect my son. Now God speaks these words with the disposition of one who is in doubt, so that they may show the free choice of man, lest the foreknowledge of future things make immutable, whether for evil or for good, what God knew would come to be: for it is not because he knows what is to come that we must necessarily do what he foreknew; rather, what we are going to do by our own will, he, as God, knows will come to be.

Perhaps, he says, they will hear and turn. The ambiguous word 'perhaps' cannot befit the majesty of the Lord, but he speaks according to our feeling, so that free will may be preserved for man, lest by his foreknowledge man be compelled, as if by necessity, either to do something or not to do it; for it is not because God knows that something is going to be that it is therefore going to be, but because it is going to be, God knows it, as one who foreknows things to come. And yet it must be known, according to this same Jeremiah, that if the Lord has foretold evils and the people has repented, he himself too will repent over the things which he threatened to do; and if he has promised prosperity and the people has acted negligently, God changes his sentence and brings evils instead of good things. Something of this kind is also that saying in the Gospel: I will send my son; perhaps they will reverence him; which is surely said in the person of almighty God. Finally, in the present passage too he says: 'if perhaps they will hear and turn, each one from his evil way, so that, when they have turned, I too may repent of my sentence and not do what I am thinking to do to them. But I am thinking to do it because of the wickedness of their pursuits; and if these have been changed, my sentence too will be changed.' Let us read the history of Jonah and Nineveh.

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If you will not hear me, to walk in my law which I gave you, to hear the words of my servants, the prophets, whom I sent to you, rising up by night and sending, and you did not hear, I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city I will make a curse to all the nations of the earth. It is therefore placed in our power either to do something or not to do it, only in such a way that whatever good work we will, seek and accomplish, we refer to the grace of God, who, according to the Apostle, has given us both to will and to accomplish. But if it suffices to walk once in the law which was given to us through Moses, as the foolish heresy supposes, how is it that he added: to hear the words of my servants, the prophets? who surely were sent after the law, and not once but frequently, nor idly and as from one at ease, but always and as from one who is anxious.

'I sent', he says, 'to you my servants daily and rising up by night; and if you will not hear them, I will make this house' — that is, the temple of God — 'like Shiloh', where the tabernacle was. And when the temple has been destroyed, consequently the city too will be a curse to all the nations of the earth. And just as, when the temple had been built on the threshing floor of Ornan and on Mount 'Moria', that is, 'of vision', on which Abraham is related to have offered his son Isaac, the worship of Shiloh ceased and no sacrifices were afterwards celebrated there, so, when the Church had been built and spiritual victims had been offered in it, the ceremonies of the law ceased, and the city of the Jews was made a curse to all the nations of the earth, from which the Lord has freed us, as the Apostle says: Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having been made a curse for us.

And the priests and the prophets — or false prophets — and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets — or false prophets — and all the people seized him, saying: Let him die the death, because he has prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying: This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be made desolate, so that there is no inhabitant. The priests and the prophets, whom the Seventy more plainly translated as 'false prophets', are angry with Jeremiah because he preaches true things, and because, with the temple overthrown and the city deserted, their religion would perish, and the profits coming from religion; therefore they seize him and, with the people consenting with them, destine him for death, because he had said in the name of the Lord: This house shall be like Shiloh, and the city shall be made desolate, so that there is no inhabitant. If, then, at any time, because of the commandments of the Lord and the truth of the faith, either priests or false prophets or a deceived people are angry with us, let us not greatly care, but let us carry out the sentence of God, pondering in our mind by no means present evils, but future goods.

And all the people was gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. And the princes of Judah heard these words, and they went up from the king's house to the house of the Lord and sat in the entrance of the new gate of the Lord. Jeremiah was prophesying the words of the Lord in the temple and had said: I will make this house like Shiloh, and this city a curse to all the nations of the earth, and at once, a riot having been stirred up by the priests and prophets and people, the whole crowd is gathered against the prophet into the temple, where the prophet was and was being held by the hands of the priests and prophets and crowd.

When the princes of the city, who were staying in the royal house, had heard this, they crossed over, or went up from the king's house to the house of the Lord. And it is to be noted that to go to the house of the Lord is always an ascent. And they sat in the entrance of the new gate of the Lord. For it was the duty of the princes to sit in the gate of the house of the Lord and there to learn the truth of the business and of the riot. But the gate is called 'new' because those who sat in it and presided over the judgment resisted the slanders of the priests and false prophets.

And the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes and to all the people, saying: There is a judgment of death for this man, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears. While the princes of the city, who had run from the king's palace to the temple so that the riot of the people might be calmed, were sitting in the gate of the temple and in the new gate, and an assembly of the people had been gathered, the priests and false prophets accuse him; and the prophet would have perished, as far as it lay with the priests and prophets, if the accusers themselves had had the power of judgment. From this we understand that those who seemed devoted to religion were crueler toward the prophet, through envy of his holiness, than those who presided over public needs.

And Jeremiah said to all the princes and to all the people, saying: The Lord sent me to prophesy to this house — or upon this house — and to this city — or upon this city — all the words which you have heard. Now therefore make good your ways and your pursuits, and hear the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil which he has spoken against you — or and the Lord will rest from the evils which he has spoken against you —. As for me, behold, I am in your hands; do to me as is good and right in your eyes — or as is expedient for you — ! Nevertheless, know and understand that, if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood against your very selves and against this city and its inhabitants; for in truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak in your ears all these words. When, with the people present, the princes of the city were sitting in the gate, and the priests and prophets were accusing Jeremiah the prophet and pressing a capital charge, Jeremiah speaks to the princes and to all the people, whom the faction of the priests and false prophets had stirred up, prudently and at the same time humbly and steadfastly. Prudently, in that he said he had been sent by the Lord to speak against the temple and the city, and gave the counsel that, if they were willing to hear his counsel and to repent, the Lord too would change his sentence. Humbly, in what he says: behold, I am in your hands; do to me as is good and right in your eyes! And steadfastly: in truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak in your ears all these words. And in other words he says: 'If you are angry because I have spoken against the temple and the city of the Lord, and the safety of the city and of the temple is your concern, why do you add sins to sins and make both the city and its inhabitants guilty of my blood?' If, then, at any time we too have need of humility because of the straits of necessity, let us so take it up that we do not desert truth and steadfastness; for it is one thing proudly to insult the one who judges, which is a sign of folly, another so to avoid the impending danger that you subtract nothing from the truth.

And the princes and all the people said to the priests and the prophets: There is no judgment of death for this man, because he has spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God. The people, which had earlier been tripped up by the priests and false prophets, joins the princes of the city and speaks for Jeremiah, saying that he is by no means guilty of death, but has prophesied in the name of the Lord and from his mouth; for the untaught crowd, once it has received a reason, quickly changes its opinion. But the resentment of the accusers, especially of the priests and false prophets, cannot be changed; and therefore, while they accuse and persevere in the accusation, the people is changed, because he had given them hope of the Lord's pardon, if they made their ways good and heard the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord too would bend his sentence.

And there rose up men of the elders of the land and said to the whole assembly of the people, speaking: Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house the heights of the forests. Did Hezekiah, king of Judah, and all Judah condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord, and the Lord repented of the evil which he had spoken against them? So we are doing a great evil against our own souls. The princes of the city and the people understand the truth of the judgment; but the elders, whose proper task it was to know old things, unfold the history and prophecy of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied under King Hezekiah, compare it with the prophecy of Jeremiah, for which a capital charge is being pressed against him, and show that Micah had said graver things and yet had suffered nothing from the righteous king Hezekiah, but that they, converted to repentance, had turned the sentence of the Lord in a good direction. For Micah said: Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house the heights of the forests; and Jeremiah: I will make, he says, this house like Shiloh, and this city I will make a curse to all the nations of the earth. And they give counsel, thinking that what Micah had foretold would by no means come to pass, because for a long time it had not been done on account of the repentance of the people, and that this too, which Jeremiah spoke, would by no means come to be, if, according to his counsel, they made good their ways and their pursuits and heard the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord would not bring the evil with which he had threatened them. And at the same time they break the rage of the accusers and mingle themselves with them, saying: So we are doing a great evil against our own souls, not that they ought to do it, but because, if they did it, they would by no means harm the accused, but their own souls, which they could have freed by a change of their sentence.

There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah, son of Shemaiah of Kiriath-jearim, and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and his princes heard these words, and the king sought to kill him; and Uriah heard and was afraid and fled and entered Egypt. And what follows: and King Jehoiakim sent men into Egypt, Elnathan, son of Achbor, and men with him into Egypt, is not found in the Seventy. Then is joined: and they brought Uriah out of Egypt and led him to King Jehoiakim; and he struck him with the sword and cast his corpse into the graves of the ignoble common people. Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, was with Jeremiah, so that he should not be delivered into the hand of the people and they kill him. It is asked why, when Uriah, son of Shemaiah, from the town of Kiriath-jearim, had prophesied the same things as Jeremiah, and, struck with fear, fled to Egypt and, dragged back from there, was killed, Jeremiah was able to escape, who certainly had not fled, but, boldly persevering in his former statement, was freed both by the judgment of the crowd and of the princes and by the counsel of the elders against the accusers, the priests and false prophets. To this one must briefly answer that the judgment of God can by no means be known, when, in the same cause and for the same statement, one is punished and another is freed; unless perhaps we can answer this, that Uriah was slaughtered to the condemnation of both the accusers and the people, while Jeremiah was preserved by the judgment of God, so that he might preach to the remnant of the unhappy people and draw them back to repentance. This indeed we also read in the Acts of the Apostles: that the apostle James at once suffered the sentence of Herod and was crowned with martyrdom, but Peter and the other apostles were preserved for the teaching of the Lord. And the prophetic steadfastness is to be noticed, in that not even when dragged back from Egypt did Uriah change his statement, but, seeing death threatened against him, nonetheless spoke what the Lord had commanded. And that he feared and fled and entered Egypt is a sign not of unbelief but of prudence, lest we offer ourselves to dangers in vain. Otherwise we read that the Lord and Savior too slipped out of the hands of his persecutors, and that he commanded the apostles: when they persecute you in this city, flee to another!

It is also asked how Jehoiakim, king of Judah, a king of small dominion, weakened, and about to perish at any moment, had the power of sending into Egypt and of bringing Uriah out from there. This is easily solved if we consider that he had been appointed prince by Neco, king of Egypt, and that this prophecy was made in the beginning of his reign.
Jeremiah needed the help of Ahikam. How much more do we need that of God.

But although Jeremiah was freed by the help of the Lord, yet it is reckoned as a reward to him also through whom the Lord freed his prophet, namely to Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as we shall read later, when Jeremiah is freed from the danger of death out of the cistern of mud by the counsel and protection of Ebed-melech the eunuch.
27: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying. This is not found in the edition of the Seventy, and many think it is the beginning of the following chapter, which is by no means so; rather, it is to be joined to the preceding one, so that whatever is reported as said and done we should believe to have been done in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim; whence too he had the power of sending into Egypt, as to a friendly king. But the Seventy seem to me to have passed over this title in silence for this reason, lest they should seem to say it a second time; for they had already set down at the beginning: in the beginning of King Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying.

Thus says the Lord to me: Make for yourself bonds and chains — or kloious [collars], which in Hebrew are called 'mutoth', and in common speech they call them 'boias' [neck-shackles] — and you shall put them on your neck and you shall send to the king of Edom and to the king of Moab and to the king of the sons of Ammon and to the king of Tyre and to the king of Sidon by the hand of the messengers who have come to Jerusalem to Zedekiah, king of Judah. And you shall command them to speak to their masters: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Thus shall you say to your masters. The previous vision came to the prophet in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, but this one under Zedekiah, who reigned last in Jerusalem and under whom the city was taken and overthrown. And Jeremiah is commanded to put chains, or wooden forks, which, as we have said, are called 'mutoth' in Hebrew, on his neck, and to send them to the kings of Edom, Moab, the sons of Ammon, Tyre and Sidon by the envoys who had come to Zedekiah, and to command them to announce to their masters that they must serve King Nebuchadnezzar and hear the things which the prophet's following discourse goes on to set out. And lest perhaps the envoys and the kings of these nations should answer: 'Why do you not command this to your own people?', he speaks similar things to King Zedekiah too, and to the priests and prophets. This passage the ever-allegorical interpreter, who flees from the truth of history, interprets of the heavenly Jerusalem: that its inhabitants must voluntarily take on bodies and descend into 'Babylon', that is, into the 'confusion' of this world, which is set in the evil one, and serve the Babylonian king, without doubt the devil; and that, if they will not do this, they will by no means bear heavy bodies, but will perish by sword and famine and pestilence, and will by no means become men, but demons. Let this stand as what he said, lest his defenders bring a false charge against us. But as for us, let us follow the simple and true history, lest we be wrapped in certain clouds and illusions.

I made the earth and man and the beasts that are upon the face of the earth, by my great strength and by my outstretched arm, and I gave it to him who pleased in my eyes. Although this scripture speaks anthrōpopathōs [in human terms], in the way that we men can speak and understand, yet the 'strength' of God and his 'arm' is he of whom the Apostle also speaks: 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God', and Isaiah: Lord, who has believed our hearing, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? John the evangelist also writes: all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. David too speaks in his song: by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth. And as for his saying: I gave it to him who pleased in my eyes, this signifies that all things have been granted to the human race through the grace of God. I, he says, made the earth and man and the beasts. The order is reversed; for in Genesis the living creatures are made first and man last, but here he names man first and afterwards the things that are subject to man.

We have long felt that God is angry, yet we do not try to appease him. It is our sins that make the barbarians strong. It is our vices that vanquish Rome's soldiers. As if there were here too little material for carnage, civil wars have made almost greater havoc among us than the swords of foreign foes. Miserable must those Israelites have been compared with whom Nebuchadnezzar was called God's servant. Unhappy too are we who are so displeasing to God that he uses the fury of the barbarians to execute his wrath against us. Still, when Hezekiah repented, 185,000 Assyrians were destroyed in one night by a single angel. When Jehosaphat sang the praises of the Lord, the Lord gave his worshiper the victory. Again, when Moses fought against Amalek, it was not with the sword but with prayer that he prevailed. Therefore, if we wish to be lifted up, we must first prostrate ourselves.

Now therefore I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant; and moreover I have also given him the beasts of the field, that they may serve him. And all the nations shall serve him and his son and his son's son. Of what great unhappiness is Israel, when in comparison with it Nebuchadnezzar is called 'servant of God'! It is written in the Gospel: the world was made through him, and the world did not know him; he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. Rightly therefore does the Creator hand over his creation to whom he will. Finally the devil too, as whose type Nebuchadnezzar went before, confesses: all these things have been handed over to me. And as for what he added: moreover I have also given him the beasts of the field, that they may serve him, either we ought simply to understand every kind of living creature — for together with man the things subject to him are also handed over — or certainly let us take the 'beasts' as the savage nations, because even those serve which before had not known how to serve.
And his 'son' and 'son's son' — according to the Hebrew — he calls Belshazzar and Evil-merodach, of whom Daniel writes.

Until the time of his land and of himself comes. Fittingly, lest the empire of Nebuchadnezzar be thought perpetual, he says that he himself too is to be taken by the Medes and Persians; for this is what it signifies: until the time of his land and of himself comes. But this too is not found in the Seventy.

And many nations and great kings shall serve him. He did not say 'all' — for this is properly due to the empire of Christ —, although according to Symmachus one does not read: many nations and great kings shall serve him, but: many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude, so that he himself too, whom all the nations had served before, serves the Medes and Persians. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: I have given him, that they may serve him, and all the nations shall serve him and his son and his son's son, until the time of his land and of himself comes and many nations and great kings subject him to servitude, is not read, as we have already said, in the edition of the Seventy.

The great and honourable name of Godhead He withheld not from His righteous ones; even as, though He is the great King, without grudging He applied the great and honourable name of Kingship to men who are His creatures.

For by the mouth of His prophet God called the heathen King Nebuchadnezzar, King of Kings. For Jeremiah said:—Every people and kingdom that shall not put his neck into the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Kings, My servant, with famine and with sword and with pestilence will I visit that people. Though He is the great King, He grudges not the name of Kingship to men. And (so), though He is the great God, yet He grudged not the name of Godhead to the sons of flesh.
Demonstration 17 (Of Christ the Son of God), Sections 5-6

But the nation and kingdom which will not serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and whoever will not bend his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, with sword and famine and pestilence I will visit upon that nation, says the Lord, until I consume them by his hand. Not only does the Lord subject sinful nations to Nebuchadnezzar, but the Apostle too speaks of sinners: whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme; and in another place: I have handed over such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. He also warns that the powers must be obeyed not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience, lest we be condemned by them.

For Jeremiah also prophesied that the Lord commanded them to go into Babylon. He reproved as false prophets any of the other prophets who told the people not to go to Babylon. Let those who read the Scriptures remember this as we do. Let those who do not, give us credit. Jeremiah, then, on the part of God, threatened those who would not go to Babylon, whereas he promised rest to those who would go and even a kind of contentment in the cultivation of their vines, and planting of their gardens and the abundance of their fruits.

You therefore, do not listen to your prophets and diviners and dreamers and augurs and sorcerers, who say to you: You shall not serve the king of Babylon; for they prophesy a lie to you, to remove you far from your land and to drive you out, and you perish. But the nation that puts its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, I will leave it in its own land, says the Lord, and it shall till it and dwell in it. In this place too the allegorical interpreter raves, and exhorts those set in the heavenly Jerusalem not to hear their prophets and diviners, dreamers and augurs and sorcerers, but rather to serve Nebuchadnezzar and take on the body of humility, infancy, the wailing and the cradles of little ones; for if they do this, when their servitude and the condition of human mortality have been fulfilled, they will return to their land and dwell in it and work the works which they worked before. And he says that he suspects that those who have despised the commands of God to be weighed down with human bodies will become demons and unclean spirits and will by no means regain their former seat.
