But let us expound simply: that there are among the nations prophets, who pretend that they foretell things to come by a divine spirit; and diviners, of whom there is also the common proverb: 'the wise, they say, divine'; and dreamers, who imitate Joseph and Daniel; and augurs, who by the flight of birds and the voices of omen-birds announce what is to be done or not to be done; and sorcerers, whom we can call either poisoners or those who serve the phantasms of demons, who in Hebrew are called 'chassane'. 'All these', he says, 'deceive you and trip you up, so that you may not serve the king of Babylon'. For it is much better to take up servitude voluntarily and to have as a friend the one you serve, and to till your native land, than to serve as captives by force and necessity.

And to Zedekiah, king of Judah, I spoke according to all these words, saying: Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why will you die, you and your people, by sword, famine and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken to the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you: Do not serve the king of Babylon; for they themselves speak a lie to you, for I did not send them, says the Lord, and they prophesy in my name falsely, so that I may drive you out and you perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. After all the nations he passes to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and speaks with the same words with which he threatened the nations; for he who has sinned sins either like or greater than the other nations does not merit the privilege of the Israelite nation. Finally, because the rebellious people disdained to hear, it was consumed by sword, famine and pestilence. And it is to be observed in holy Scripture that instead of 'false prophets' it calls 'prophets' those who prophesy falsely in the name of the Lord. 'And they do this, so that I', he says, 'may drive you out and you perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you'; therefore the destruction both of those who are deceived and of those who deceive is alike. This, which we have set down from the Hebrew: under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why will you die, you and your people, by sword, famine and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken to the nation that will not serve the king of Babylon? do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you, is not found in the Seventy; and therefore I admonish the prudent reader to understand how much is lacking, point by point, in the Greek and Latin codices.

And to the priests and to this people I spoke, saying: Thus says the Lord: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying: Behold, the vessels of the Lord will return from Babylon now quickly; for they prophesy a lie to you. — This, which we have set down, 'now quickly', is not found in the Seventy, and likewise that which follows: — Do not listen to them, but serve the king of Babylon, that you may live! Why is this city given over to desolation? And after the nations and the king he speaks to the priests and to the people, because he had already announced destruction to the prophets above, saying: so that I may drive you out and you perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. And he speaks the same things which he had spoken to the king and to the nations: that they should not hear the words of their prophets and say that the vessels which had been carried away with Jeconiah and the princes and his mother were to be brought back to the temple of the Lord right now; and he warns them to serve the king of Babylon and live, and that the city, voluntarily subjected, should by no means be handed over to burning. And in this is the clemency of the Lord: to hand them over to a lighter punishment, lest they endure a heavier one.

And if they are prophets and the word of the Lord is in them, let them meet — and what follows, which we are about to subjoin up to the end of this chapter, is not found in the Seventy — the Lord of hosts, that the vessels which had been left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem may not come into Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts to the pillars and to the sea and to the bases — for which in the Hebrew is written 'mechonoth' — and to the rest of the vessels which remained in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, did not take when he carried Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem into Babylon, and all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to the vessels which have been left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried into Babylon and shall be there until the day of their visitation, says the Lord, and I will cause them to be brought and restored to this place. These words, as we have said, are not found in the Seventy, but have been translated from the Hebrew truth; in place of which they set down something else, which was not written, saying: to me, because thus said the Lord: and the rest of the vessels which the king of Babylon did not take, when he carried Jeconiah from Jerusalem, shall enter Babylon, says the Lord, setting down the sense rather than the words, perhaps thinking it irrational that God should speak to the pillars and to the sea and to the bases and to the rest of the vessels which had remained in Jerusalem — as if we did not read both that the Lord rebuked the morning worm and that he spoke to the sea: be silent and be still! And what he says: let them meet me or the Lord of hosts, shows that a true prophet can withstand the Lord with prayers, in accordance with which Moses too stood in the smiting against the Lord, to turn away the wrath of his fury; Samuel also did the same. And the Lord to Moses: let me alone, he says, I will strike this people! But when he says: let me alone, he shows that he can be held back by the prayers of the saints. 'Let the prophets meet', he says, 'and let them show whatever they foretell fulfilled in deed, and then the prophecy will be proved by its truth'. Now the pillars and the sea and the bases and the rest of the vessels we read of in Malachim [Kings] and at the end of this prophet's volume; and there are enumerated the vessels that were carried into Babylon when Zedekiah was taken and the city burned and the temple overthrown.
28: And it came to pass in that year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah son of Azzur, the prophet from Gibeon, said to me in the house of the Lord before the priests and all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon; yet two years of days, and I will cause all the vessels of the Lord to be brought back to this place. Those whom the Hebrew calls 'prophets', that is 'nebeim', the Seventy translated 'false prophets', in order to make the understanding plainer. Indeed, in the present passage too he is called 'prophet', that is 'nebia', and not 'false prophet'. Now the word of the Lord comes under King Zedekiah, in the fourth year of his reign and in the fifth month — while the prophet Ezekiel was not yet prophesying in Babylon to those who had gone into exile with Jeconiah — and he has the confidence to speak in the temple of the Lord against the prophet, because he promises prosperity to the people, and lies are gladly heard, especially those that promise joyful things. Jeremiah had said that the rest of the vessels too, whether of the temple or of the royal house and of the whole people, which Nebuchadnezzar had left behind, were to be carried over to Babylon; but this man, on the contrary, promises that even those which had been carried over are to be brought back.

Which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took from this place and carried over into Babylon. Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exile of Judah, who went into Babylon, I will bring back to this place, says the Lord; for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon. For which the Seventy translated: Jeconiah and the exile of Judah, because I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon, briefly setting down the sense of the Hebrew truth rather than its words. Now Hananiah the 'prophet' — as he then seemed to the people — promises that not only the vessels but also King Jeconiah is to be brought back to Jerusalem, and that the yoke of the Babylonian king is to be broken, that is, his empire destroyed, and that this would come about before two years were yet completed, so that the nearness of the time of the promise might increase the greatness of the joy.

And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet in the eyes of the priests and in the eyes of all the people who stood in the house of the Lord, and Jeremiah the prophet said: Amen, so may the Lord do; may the Lord raise up your words which you have prophesied, that the vessels may be brought back from the house of the Lord, and all the exile of Babylon, to this place! He wishes 'to be done' what the false prophet lyingly tells — for this is what 'amen' means, a word the Lord often uses in the Gospel: amen, amen I say to you —, and for the sake of the prosperity of affairs he desires that the other rather than himself be speaking the truth. Hence another prophet too testifies, saying: would that I were not a man having the spirit, and spoke a lie rather! Jonah, on the contrary, is grieved that he has lied, and is rebuked by the Lord, being shown that a lie on the prophet's part is more useful than the ruin of so great a multitude. And lest he should seem to approve the false prophet's prophecy, he adds the truth under the example of others, without insulting the liar:

Nevertheless hear this word which I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people: the prophets who were before me and you from the beginning, and prophesied over many lands and over great kingdoms of battle and of affliction and of famine; the prophet who prophesied peace, when his word comes, the prophet will be known whom the Lord has sent in truth. Jeremiah could have said to Hananiah: 'You speak falsely, you deceive the people, you are not a prophet but a false prophet.' But had he said that, the false prophet too could have turned the same words back upon Jeremiah; therefore he does him no insult and speaks as though to a 'prophet'. 'Not only,' he says, 'am I a prophet, and you, but before me and you there were many others, among whom were Isaiah, Hosea, Joel and Amos and the rest. They prophesied,' he says, 'against many lands and kingdoms not small but great, announcing to them war and adversity and want of all things; and on the contrary there were others who promised peace and prosperity. The pronouncement of both was proved not by the flattery of a lie but by the outcome of events.' Under the example of others, then, he speaks of himself and of Hananiah: that when the end of events has come, then the truth of the prophets is shown. The Lord also said this same thing through Moses, that a prophet is shown by the fulfilment of his prophecy. And this must be noted, that not threateningly, not savagely, but with the confidence of truth he rebukes the liar and defers the matter to the future, so that those who hear may await the outcome of events.

And Hananiah the prophet took the chain — or the fork, which in Hebrew is called 'muthoth', — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it. And Hananiah spoke in the sight of all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord: so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in two years of days, from the neck of all the nations. And Jeremiah went on his way. The Seventy did not translate 'two years'; nor did they call Hananiah 'prophet', lest, that is, they should seem to call a prophet one who was not a prophet — as if many things in the holy Scriptures were not said according to the opinion of the time to which the events reported belong, and not according to what the truth of the matter held; thus Joseph too is called in the Gospel the 'father' of the Lord, and Mary herself, who knew that she had conceived of the Holy Spirit and had answered the angel: how will this be, since I have not known a man?, says to her son: son, why have you done so to us? behold, your father and I, sorrowing, were seeking you. And at the same time the prudence of Jeremiah, and his humility and patience, are to be considered. The false prophet does him injury by deed and, snatching the fork from his neck, breaks it — which he certainly could not have done with an iron one —; this man is silent and conceals his pain; for it had not yet been revealed to him by the Lord what he should say, so that holy Scripture might tacitly show that the prophets by no means speak by their own will alone, but also by the will of the Lord, above all concerning things to come, the knowledge of which belongs to God alone. He went, he says, and withdrew on his way, as though defeated, and fulfilling that prophetic word: I became as a man who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth.

About four hundred years have passed since the preaching of Christ burst on the world, and during that time in which his robe has been torn by countless heresies, almost the whole body of error has been derived from the Chaldaean, Syriac and Greek languages. Basilides, the master of licentiousness and the grossest sensuality, after the lapse of so many years and like a second Euphorbus, was changed by transmigration into Jovinian, so that the Latin tongue might have a heresy of its own. Was there no other province in the whole world to receive the gospel of pleasure and into which the serpent might insinuate itself, except that which was founded by the teaching of Peter, on the rock Christ? Idol temples had fallen before the standard of the cross and the severity of the gospel. Now, on the contrary, lust and gluttony endeavor to overthrow the solid structure of the cross. And so God says by Isaiah, "O my people, they which bless you cause you to err, and trouble the paths of your feet." Also by Jeremiah, "Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and save every one his life," and do not believe the false prophets who say, "Peace, peace, and there is no peace," who are always repeating, "The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord." "Your prophets have foreseen false and foolish things for you. They have not exposed your iniquity in order to call you to repentance. They devour God's people like bread. They have not called on God. Jeremiah announced the captivity and was stoned by the people. Hananiah, the son of Azzur, broke the bars of wood for the present but was preparing bars of iron for the future. False prophets always promise pleasant things and please for a time. Truth is bitter, and those preaching it are filled with bitterness. For with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth the Lord's Passover is kept, and it is eaten with bitter herbs.

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after Hananiah the prophet had broken the chain — or fork — from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Go, and you shall say to Hananiah: Thus says the Lord: the chain — or fork — of wood you have broken, and you will make — or I will make — in their place forks — or chains — of iron. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have put a yoke of iron upon the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. And what follows: and they will serve him; moreover I have also given him the beasts of the earth, is not found in the Seventy. And in the present passage, according to the Seventy, Hananiah is not written 'prophet', nor in what follows, lest, that is, as I said before, they should seem to call a 'false prophet' a 'prophet'; but what is that to the Hebrew truth? After Jeremiah the prophet had gone on his way and swallowed the injury in silence, the word of the Lord came to him, so that the prophet should not speak in his own words to the false prophet glorying in his lie, but should say: thus says the Lord, although Hananiah too, in breaking the wooden fork, had spoken with the same authority in the sight of the Lord: thus says the Lord; for falsehood always imitates truth. And what he added: you have broken forks of wood and you will make — or you have made — in their place chains of iron, shows this: that by refusing a lesser penalty he became the cause of a greater punishment among the people. In this passage too the allegorical interpreter raves, calling the wooden forks and chains ethereal and aerial bodies, namely those of demons and of the hostile powers, but the iron forks or chains our grosser bodies, which are woven together of sinews and bones, flesh and veins, so that those from the heavenly Jerusalem who refused to undergo lesser torments according to the quality of their sin are condemned into the chains of our bodies, and endure the wailing of infancy, the bonds and filth of swaddling clothes, and serve the devil, the king of Babylon, that is, of this world — Scripture saying: the world is set in the evil one — together with the beasts of the earth, which are bound fast in the bodies of brute animals. That unlearned commentator and follower of the Grunnian slander has compelled me to set forth openly the vices of others, which before I used to speak of with reserve, leaving them to the reader's prudence.

Now as to the first beast, he said concerning it, that it was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle. For the first beast was the kingdom of Babylon, which was like a lion. For thus Jeremiah wrote saying:—Israel is a wandering sheep. The lions caused them to wander. First the king of Assyria devoured him. And this last was stronger than he, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. So Jeremiah called him a lion. And he said:—He has the wings of an eagle. For thus it is written that, when Nebuchadnezzar went out to the wilderness with the beasts, he grew hair like (the plumage) of an eagle. And he said:—I saw that its wings were plucked away and it stood upright upon its feet as a man, and a man’s heart was given to it. For first, in the vision of the image, he was compared to gold which is more precious than anything which is used in the world. So in the vision of the beasts he is compared to a lion which excels in its might all the beasts. And again he was compared to an eagle which surpasses every bird. Whatsoever was written about him was fulfilled in him. For the Lord said concerning him:—I have placed a yoke of iron upon the neck of all the nations, and they shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And also the beasts of the desert and the birds of heaven have I given to him to serve him. For since the king was like the head of gold, men served him as a king. And when he went out to the wilderness, the beasts served him as a lion. And when his hair was like (the plumage) of an eagle, the birds of heaven served him as an eagle. But when his heart was lifted up, and he knew not that the power was given to him from heaven, the yoke of iron was broken from the neck of men, and he went forth with the beasts, and instead of the heart of a king there was given him the heart of a lion. And when he was lifted up over the beasts, the heart of a lion was taken away from him, and there was given him the heart of a bird. And when wings grew upon him like those of an eagle, he exalted himself over the birds. And then his wings also were plucked away and there was given to him a humble heart. And when he knew that the Most High has authority in the kingdom of man, to give it to whomsoever He will, then as a man he praised Him.

And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: Hear, Hananiah: the Lord has not sent you, and you have made this people trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, I will send away — or cast out — you from the face of the earth; this year you will die. And what follows: because you have spoken against the Lord. And Hananiah the prophet died in that year, in the seventh month, is not found in the Seventy, in place of which they put only: and he died in the seventh month. Here too in the Seventy Hananiah is not called 'prophet', though — according to the Hebrew — holy Scripture calls him 'prophet', even if, where Jeremiah rebukes him, saying: hear, Hananiah, the Lord has not sent you, he left out 'prophet'; for how could he call him 'prophet' whom he denied had been sent by the Lord? But the truth and order of the history are kept, as we said above, not according to what was, but according to what was thought at that time. 'You have deceived,' he says, 'the people with a lie, so that they would not acquiesce in God's sentence; know, therefore, that you will die this year!' If, when we die, we are freed from the prisons of our bodies, according to that testimony which the heretics interpret wrongly: bring my soul out of prison, how is death now inflicted on the false prophet as a punishment? And this too must be noted, that Jeremiah, having suffered injury from the false prophet, is silent while the word of the Lord had not yet come to him, but afterwards, sent by the Lord, boldly rebukes the liar and announces his approaching death. And as to his dying in the 'seventh' month: those who are always accustomed to interpret this number as showing 'rest' will perhaps falsely claim that he died in the 'seventh' month for this reason, that he might be freed from the evils of the body, according to the saying they bring forward as written: 'death is rest to a man'. But we know that the bodies of believers are temples of God, if indeed the Holy Spirit dwells in them.
29: And these are the words of the book which Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the remnant of the elders of the exile, and to the priests, and to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried over from Jerusalem into Babylon, after Jeconiah the king went out, and the lady — or the queen — and the eunuchs and the princes of Judah and Jerusalem — or from Jerusalem or the nobles — and the craftsmen from Jerusalem, by the hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and of Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, into Babylon, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exile which I carried over from Jerusalem into Babylon: Build houses and dwell, and plant gardens — or orchards — and eat their fruit! Take wives and beget sons and daughters; give wives to your sons and give your daughters to husbands, and let them bear sons and daughters; and multiply, and do not be few in number! And seek the peace of the city — or of the land —, to which I have carried you over, and pray for it to the Lord, for in its peace there will be peace for you! This letter, nay rather little book, of Jeremiah the prophet is sent into Babylon through Zedekiah's envoys, Elasah and Gemariah, to those who had been carried over by Nebuchadnezzar with Jeconiah and his mother, so that, taking the occasion of the royal embassy, the prophet might also accomplish his own work and admonish the exiled people of the things that had been commanded him by the Lord. And he said finely: Jeconiah the king went out, and the lady, the eunuchs and the princes of Judah and the rest, and: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exile which I carried over from Jerusalem into Babylon, so that they may be seen to have been carried over not by the power of the king of Babylon but by the will of the Lord. And the word of God is directed first to the elders, then to the priests, third to the prophets, fourth to all the people, so that the prophet's letter too might reach those who were being admonished according to the order of age.

But he admonishes them not with his own words but with the Lord's, that they should build houses and dwell in them, and plant gardens or orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and beget sons and daughters, and multiply in the place of exile and not be few in number, and seek the peace of the city or land to which the Lord had carried them over, and pray for it to the Lord. And giving the reasons he says: 'for in the peace of that land there will be peace for you'. To Jeremiah, because captivity was to overtake Jerusalem after a short time, it is commanded that he not take a wife, that he not beget sons. Hence to us also it is said through the Apostle: the time has been shortened; it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none. But if, because of the narrowness of the time, the use of wives is taken away from those who have them, how much more is it commanded to those who do not have them that they not take them! Now the prophet's prophecy commands all this so that they may not give in to the false prophets, who were promising them a return to Jerusalem after a short time, but that they may know that they will stay a long time in Babylon, so that they ought to take wives, plant orchards and sow gardens, build houses and beget sons. And in what he added: seek the peace of the city or of the land, and again: for in its peace there will be peace for you, that saying of the Apostle is confirmed in which he enjoins: I beseech therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and all who are in high station, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity. Further, according to the mystical senses: after we have been cast out of Jerusalem, that is, the Church, because of our sins, and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar — of whom the same Apostle says: 'I have handed over such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord' and again: whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme —, we ought not to be secure, nor, sluggish with idleness, to despair utterly of salvation, but first to build houses — not upon sand, but upon rock — and such houses as the midwives too built in Exodus, because they feared the Lord; Then to plant gardens or orchards, such a paradise as the Lord too planted in Eden, and set in it the tree of life, of which it is written: it is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; and he who holds her fast, blessed; third, to take wives, of whom one is wisdom, of whom Solomon writes: love her, and she will keep you; encircle her, and she will exalt you, and in another place: her I sought to take as a bride for myself, and I became a lover of her beauty. Nor does one spouse, wisdom, suffice us, unless we have the rest also: fortitude, temperance and righteousness, so that from them we may beget more sons. Let us also give our daughters to husbands, so that the truth of faith, which is understood in the sons, may be coupled with good works, which are referred to the daughters, and good works may be joined to the soundness of faith. And begetting such sons and daughters, let us be multiplied in number, so that, putting away the things of a little child and growing up to the perfect man, we may deserve to hear: I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning, and may say with the Apostle to our children: for in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I have begotten you. Let us also seek peace for the Church, our city and our land, so that we may deserve to return to it, from which by the Lord's judgment we have been carried over to dwell in the error of 'confusion'; for if it receives us, we shall have peace. And at the same time the clemency of the Lord is to be considered: he commands us to pray for our enemies and to do good to those who persecute us, so that we may not be content with our own salvation only, but may seek the salvation of our enemies also.

[Daniel 4:27] "'Wherefore, O king, let my counsel meet with thy favor, and make up for thy sins by deeds of charity, and thine iniquities by showing mercy to the poor. Perhaps God will forgive thy transgressions.'" Since he had previously pronounced the sentence of God, which of course cannot be altered, how could he exhort the king to deeds of charity and acts of mercy towards the poor? This difficulty is easily solved by reference to the example of King Hezekiah, who Isaiah had said was going to die (Isaiah 38:1); and again, to the example of the Ninevites, to whom it was said: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed" (Jonah 3:4). And yet the sentence of God was changed in response to the prayers of Hezekiah and the city of Nineveh, not by any means because of the ineffectualness of the judgment itself but because of the conversion of those who merited pardon. Morever in Jeremiah God states that He threatens evil for the nation (Jeremiah 18:7-8), but if it does that which is good, He will alter His threats to bestow mercy. Again, He affirms that He directs His promises to the man who does good; and if the same man thereafter works evil, He says that He changes His decision, not with regard to the men themselves, but with regard to their works which have thus changed in character. For after all, God is not angered at men but at their sins; and when no sins inhere in a man, God by no means inflicts a punishment which has been commuted. In other words, let us say that Nebuchadnezzar performed deeds of mercy toward the poor in accordance with Daniel's advice, and for that reason the sentence against him was delayed of execution for twelve months. But because he afterwards while walking about in his palace at Babylon said boastingly: "Is this not the great Babylon which I myself have built up as a home for the king by the might of my power and the glory of my name?" therefore he lost the virtue of his charitableness by reason of the wickedness of his pride.

"It may be that God will forgive thy sins." In view of the fact that the blessed Daniel, foreknowing the future as he did, had doubts concerning God's decision, it is very rash on the part of those who boldly promise pardon to sinners. And yet it should be recognized that indulgence was promised to Nebuchadnezzar in return, as long as he wrought good works. Much more, then, is it promised to other men who have committed less grievous sins than he. We read in Jeremiah also of God's direction to the people of the Jews, that they should pray for the Babylonians, inasmuch as the peace of the captives was bound up with the peace of the captors themselves (Jeremiah 29:7).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FOUR

Because the life of the flesh is the soul, so the blessed life of humankind is God, of whom the sacred writings of the Hebrews say, "Blessed are people whose God is the Lord." Miserable, therefore, are people who are alienated from God. Yet even this people has a peace of its own that is not to be lightly esteemed, though, indeed, it shall not in the end enjoy it, because it makes no good use of it before the end. But it is our interest that it enjoys this peace meanwhile in this life. As long as the two cities are combined, we enjoy the peace of Babylon. For from Babylon the people of God is so freed that it meanwhile travels in its company. Therefore the apostle also admonished the church to pray for kings and those in authority, assigning as the reason "that we may live a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness and love." And the prophet Jeremiah, when predicting the captivity that was to befall the ancient people of God and giving them the divine command to go obediently to Babylonia and thus serve their God, counseled them also to pray for Babylonia, saying, "In its peace you will have peace"—the temporal peace that the good and the wicked together enjoy.

Remember then, that Jeconiah, rejected without any fault of his own, ceased to reign and passed into the custody of the Gentiles when the exile to Babylon took place. Now observe the symbol of things to come in the Lord Jesus Christ revealed in advance. For the Jews did not want our Lord Jesus Christ to reign over them, yet they found no fault in him. He was rejected in his own person and in that of his servants also, and so they passed into the custody of the Gentiles as into Babylon symbolically.… How then do the people of Israel, not now in symbol but in truth, pass into the custody of Babylon? Where did the apostles come from? Were they not from the nation of the Jews? Where did Paul come from? He said, "I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin." Many of the Jews then believed in the Lord. From these were the apostles chosen. From these were the more than five hundred brothers, who were allowed to see the Lord after his resurrection. From these were the 120 in the house when the Holy Spirit came down.But what does the apostle in the Acts of the Apostles say, when the Jews refused the word of truth? "We were sent to you, but seeing you have rejected the word of God, see, we turn to the Gentiles." The true passing over into Babylon, which was prefigured in the time of Jeremiah, took place in the spiritual dispensation of the time of the Lord's incarnation. But what does Jeremiah say about these Babylonians to those who were passing into their custody? "For in their peace shall be your peace." When Israel then went into exile in Babylon by Christ and the apostles, that is, when the gospel came to the Gentiles, what did the apostle say, as though by the mouth of Jeremiah in ancient times? "I exhort therefore that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions and giving of thanks be made for all people. For kings, and for all that are in authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty." For they were not Christian kings, yet he prayed for them. Israel then praying in Babylon has been heard. The prayers of the church have been heard, and the kings have become Christian, and you see now fulfilled what was then spoken in symbol: "In their peace shall be your peace," for they have received the peace of Christ and have ceased persecuting Christians, that now in the secure quiet of peace, the churches might be built up and peoples planted in the garden of God, and that all nations might bring forth fruit in faith and hope and love, which is in Christ.

For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Let not your prophets who are in your midst, and your diviners, lead you astray, and do not attend to your dreams which you dream, for these prophesy falsehoods to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord. That there were prophets, nay rather false prophets, and diviners and dreamers in Babylon among those whom Nebuchadnezzar had led away with Jeconiah and his mother, the prophet Ezekiel testifies, writing against those whom Jeremiah too commands are not to be believed. But at the time when this letter was being sent, Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon; for this word is sent at the beginning of King Zedekiah, while Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of the exile of Jeconiah, which was the same year of Zedekiah's reign. Further, according to tropology, we ought to take as false prophets those who take the words of the Scriptures otherwise than the Holy Spirit sounds them, and as diviners those who pronounce the conjectures of their own mind and the uncertainties of things to come as though true, without the authority of the divine words; and as dreamers, those who do not hear that which is written: give no sleep to your eyes nor slumber to your eyelids, of whom Jude the Apostle too speaks: likewise these also, dreaming, defile the flesh, but despise dominion, whose mind is by no means awake, but, weighed down by the slumber of arrogance and error, is surrounded by the horror of night; to whom the Apostle Paul also speaks: rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.

Only pray, I beseech you, that the Lord may not deliver us for aye to the enemies of the Cross of Christ, but that He will keep His Churches, until the time of that peace which the just Judge Himself knows when He will bestow. For He will bestow it. He will not always abandon us. As He limited seventy years for the period of captivity for the Israelites in punishment for their sins, so peradventure the Mighty One, after giving us up for some appointed time, will recall us once again, and will restore us to the peace of the beginning—unless indeed the apostasy is now nigh at hand, and the events that have lately happened are the beginnings of the approach of Antichrist. If this be so, pray that the good Lord will either take away our afflictions, or preserve us through our afflictions unvanquished.

For thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you, and I will raise up over you my good word, to bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts which I think over you, says the Lord, thoughts of peace and not of affliction, to give you an end and patience — or hope —. And you will call upon me and you will go — or, according to Symmachus, you will find — and you will pray to me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and you will find, when you seek me with your whole heart, and I will be found by you or I will appear to you. 'Do not,' he says, 'believe your false prophets, diviners and dreamers, who promise you a near return to Jerusalem! For unless the seventy years have been completed — Cyrus, king of the Persians, releasing the captives —, you will by no means return to your fatherland; and then I will fulfill my promises, to bring you back to this place; for I know the thoughts which I think over you, says the Lord'. He says that he knows what he thinks, but that they, with their prophets, diviners and dreamers, do not know; the knowledge of things to come therefore belongs to God alone. 'To give you,' he says, 'an end and patience: an end of the captivity and patience in the present labors, or hope of things to come. Then you will call upon me and you will go to Jerusalem and you will pray, and I will hear you.' Certainly the Lord could have fulfilled what he had promised without the invocation and prayer of the captives, but he exhorts them to prayers, so that they may deserve to receive what has been promised.

According to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense], we dwell in the 'confusion' of this world for as long as it takes until we deserve to receive the 'rest' of the number seven, and, repentance having been received, God fulfills what he promised, and we are brought back to our place, the Church; for this is why the Lord seemed to strike, that he might heal, and he will give us an end of our labor and of our patience. And we shall call upon him and shall return to the Church and shall pray, and we shall be heard. We shall seek and shall find him, when we have sought him with our whole heart, and then he will appear to us. A certain one interprets the 'seventy years' according to that which is written: the days of our years, in them seventy years; and when these have been completed, then we may return to the Lord with our whole heart and be heard, and there may be an end of our labor and patience; for now we possess all things in shadow and image.

[Daniel 9:2] "I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to the prophet Jeremiah, that seventy years would be accomplished for the desolation of Jerusalem." Jeremiah had predicted seventy years for the desolation of the Temple (Jeremiah 29:1-10), at the end of which the people would again return to Judaea and build the Temple and the city of Jerusalem. But this fact did not render Daniel careless, but rather encouraged him to pray that God might through his supplications fulfil that which He had graciously promised. Thus he avoided the danger that carelessness might result in pride, and pride cause offense to the Lord. Accordingly we read in Genesis that prior to the Deluge one hundred and twenty years were appointed for men to come to repentance (Genesis 6:3); and inasmuch as they refused to repent even within so long an interval of time as a hundred years, God did not wait for the remaining twenty years to be fulfilled, but brought on the punishment earlier which He had threatened for a later time. So also Jeremiah is told, on account of the hardness of the heart of the Jewish people: "Pray not for this people, for I will not hearken unto thee" (Jeremiah 7:16). Samuel also was told: "How long wilt thou mourn over Saul? I also have rejected him" (1 Samuel 16:1). And so it was with sackcloth and ashes that Daniel besought the Lord to fulfil what He had promised, not that Daniel lacked faith concerning the future, but rather he would avoid the danger that a feeling of security might produce carelessness, and carelessness produce an offense to God.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER NINE

You will seek and you will find me, when you seek with your whole heart, in accordance with that saying of the Gospel: ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

And in this place a delirious interpreter dreams of the ruin of the heavenly Jerusalem and supposes that the prophecy is directed to those who dwell in the Babylonian region of this world, that they did well to descend of their own accord into these bodies and in the land of the Chaldeans to build houses, plant orchards, take wives, beget sons, and by good works to be restored after seventy years to their former place and to the heavenly Jerusalem; but that those who were unwilling by their own will to descend to earthly things would suffer these things which the Lord threatens against Zedekiah and his people, who were unwilling to imitate their brothers or to come into Babylon: that he sends upon them the sword and famine and plague, that is, the want of all things, and makes them like very bad figs, which utterly cannot be eaten, and pursues them with an everlasting sword and gives them over to vexation to all the kingdoms of the earth, so that, namely, they become not men at all but demons, aerial powers, and are, before all the angels who preside over the several provinces, for a curse and for astonishment and for hissing and for a reproach to all the nations. And that they would suffer this for the reason that they were unwilling to hear, in the heavenly Jerusalem, the words of the prophets, who exhorted them to descend to earthly things and take up the body of humiliation, and, having done penance, after the true sabbath-rest to possess their former place. So much he may say; and when his disciples and the dung of the Grunnian household hear it, they think they are hearing divine mysteries, and us, who despise these things, they hold as brute animals and call pēlousiōtas [men of mud], because, set in the mud of this body, we cannot perceive heavenly things.

※ And I will be found by you, says the Lord, and I will bring back your captivity and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I drove you out, says the Lord, and I will make you return from the place to which I made you go into exile, because you have said: The Lord has raised up prophets for us in Babylon. For thus says the Lord to the king who sits upon the throne of David, and to all the people, the inhabitant of this city, and to your brothers who did not go out with you into exile; thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will send upon them the sword, famine and plague, and I will make them like bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are very bad. And I will pursue them with the sword, with famine and with pestilence, and I will give them over to vexation to all the kingdoms of the earth, for a curse and for astonishment and for hissing and for a reproach to all the nations to which I am casting them out, because they did not hear my words, says the Lord, which I sent to them through my servants, the prophets, rising up by night and sending; and you did not hear, says the Lord. You, therefore, hear the word of the Lord, all the exile, which I sent out from Jerusalem into Babylon! ※ Up to this point, what I have marked beforehand with asterisks is not found in the Seventy; for the rest, in which either single verses or a few words have been passed over by them, I was unwilling, overcome by weariness, to note them, lest I should cause the reader disgust. Now the Lord promises those who were in exile that after seventy years of captivity he will make them return from all the nations and from all the places to which he had driven them out, and that, the captivity being released, they would recover their former state and fatherland.

'And since I,' he says, 'am going to do these things of my own accord and to restore you at a fixed time, you are deceived in vain and think that you have prophets in Babylon who promise you false things; so know, then, that you ought by no means to hope for a return now, but to build houses, plant orchards, take wives and beget sons and multiply in number and await the promised time. Hear what the Lord says to Zedekiah, who now reigns in Jerusalem, and to all the inhabitants of his city, that is, to your brothers, who were unwilling to obey my sentence and to migrate to Babylon with you: that they can by no means escape captivity, but will die by sword and famine and plague, and that he will make them like bad figs', which Theodotion and Aquila's first edition translated 'sudrinas', the second 'very bad', Symmachus 'last'; in Hebrew they are called 'suarim' [vile], but by the fault of copyists, in place of the middle syllable or letter 'alpha', the Greek 'delta' has crept in, so that 'sudrim' is read in place of 'suarim'. And just as the basket or hamper which had good figs is said to have had 'first-ripe' ones, so the other basket, which had bad figs, is written to have had 'last' figs.

'And I will pursue,' he says, 'them, who now dwell in the city of Jerusalem, with sword, famine and pestilence, so that, first by the siege, and then at once, those who have been able to remain and escape may be scattered into all lands and be an example of curse, astonishment and hissing and reproach to all among whom I shall cast them out, because they did not hear my words, says the Lord, which I spoke to them through my servants, rising up by night and sending, and I never ceased admonishing them to imitate you, who now in exile enjoy a secure leisure until the Lord's promise is fulfilled. But you, who obeyed my sentence and handed yourselves over to the Babylonian king, hear what I am about to say'.

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to Ahab son of Kolaiah and to Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy to you in my name falsely: Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them before your eyes. And from them a curse will be taken up by all the exile of Judah that is in Babylon, saying: May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon fried in the fire, because they did folly — or iniquity — in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their friends — or fellow citizens — and spoke a word in my name falsely, which I did not command them; I am judge and witness, says the Lord. The Hebrews say that these are the elders who did folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens, to one of whom Daniel says: you who have grown old in evil days and to the other: seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you and lust has perverted your heart! Thus you did to the daughters of Israel, and they in fear spoke with you; but a daughter of Judah did not endure your iniquity. And what the prophet now says: and they spoke a word in my name falsely, which I did not command them, they think signifies this: that they so deceived wretched silly women, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, as to tell them that, since they were of the tribe of Judah, Christ was to be begotten of their seed; and these women, enticed by desire, offered their bodies as if they would be the mothers of Christ. But what is said in the present passage: whom the king of Babylon fried in the fire, seems to contradict the history of Daniel. For that asserts that they were stoned by the people at Daniel's sentence; but here it is written that the king of Babylon fried them in the fire. Hence by many, indeed by almost all the Hebrews, that very story is not received, being taken as a fable, nor is it read in their synagogues. 'For how,' he says, 'could it be that captives had the power of stoning their princes and prophets?' And they affirm that this is rather the truth, which Jeremiah writes: that the elders were indeed convicted by Daniel, but that sentence was pronounced against them by the king of Babylon, who as victor and lord had authority over the captives. How many from our own flock too, like Ahab and Zedekiah, prophesy falsehood in the name of the Lord and do folly in Israel and commit adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens, who were begotten in the same city of the Church! These the true Nebuchadnezzar fries in the fire of sin, as the prophet Hosea says: all who commit adultery are like an oven kindled by the one who bakes. Happy he who takes up the yoke from his youth and sits alone, because he is filled with bitterness, and can say with David: I have not sat in the council of the malignant, and with those who do iniquity I will not go in! And what the prophet has now added: I am judge and witness, says the Lord, has this sense: 'these things which I say about the two false prophets, who speak a word in my name falsely which I did not command them, I have by no means come to know by opinion, but I myself know them to be true, I from whom no one can hide nor escape the truth of my judgment'.

Not everyone who prophesies is holy, nor is everyone who casts out devils religious. Even Balaam the son of Beor the prophet did prophesy, though he was himself ungodly, as also did Caiaphas, the falsely named high priest. No, the devil foretells many things, and the demons, about Christ. Yet for all that, there is not a spark of piety in them. They are oppressed with ignorance, by reason of their voluntary wickedness. It is clear, therefore, that the ungodly, although they prophesy, do not by their prophesying cover their own impiety. Nor will those who cast out demons be sanctified by the demons being made subject to them. They only mock one another, as they do who play childish tricks for mirth, and destroy those who give heed to them. For neither is a wicked king any longer a king but a tyrant. Nor is a bishop oppressed with ignorance or an evil disposition a bishop, but he is called so falsely. He is not one sent out by God but by people, as Ananiah and Samoeah in Jerusalem, and Zedekiah and Achiah the false prophets in Babylon. Indeed, Balaam the prophet, when he had corrupted Israel by Baalpeor, suffered punishment. Caiaphas at last was his own murderer. The sons of Sceva, endeavoring to cast out demons, were wounded by them and fled away in an undignified way. The kings of Israel and of Judah, when they became impious, suffered all sorts of punishments. It is therefore evident how bishops and elders, also called so falsely, will not escape the judgment of God. For it will be said to them even now, "O priests that despise my name, I will deliver you up to the slaughter, as I did Zedekiah and Achiah, whom the king of Babylon fried in a frying pan," as says Jeremiah the prophet. We say these things, not in contempt of true prophecies, for we know that they are wrought in holy people by the inspiration of God, but to put a stop to the boldness of conceited people, and add this, that from such as these God takes away his grace. "God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble."

[Daniel 13:5] "And there were two of the elders of the people (the Vulgate omits: of the people) who were appointed judges that year." There was a Jew who used to allege that these men were Ahab and Zedekiah (variant: Alchias and Zedekiah), of whom Jeremiah wrote: "The Lord do to thee as Ahab and Zedekiah, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire because of the iniquity they had wrought in Israel and because they had committed adultery (variant: were committing adultery) with the wives of their citizens" (Jeremiah 29:22-23).

"It was concerning them that the Lord said that iniquity came forth from Babylon on the part of the ancient judges who appeared to govern the people. They used to frequent the house of Joakim..." Very appropriately it is not said of these sinful elders, "They governed the people," but rather, "They appeared to govern." For those who furnish good leadership to the people are the ones who govern them, but those who merely have the title of judge and lead the people unjustly only appear to govern the people rather than actually doing so.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER THIRTEEN

[Daniel 13:60] "And the whole congregration (Vulgate: assembly) cried out with a great voice and blessed God, who saveth those who trust in Him..." If the whole congregation put them to death, the view which we mentioned earlier is apparently refuted, namely that these were the elders Ahab and Zedekiah, in conformity with Jeremiah's statement (Jeremiah 29:22). The only other possibility is that instead of taking the statement, "They killed them," literally, we interpret it as meaning that they gave them over to the king of Babylon to be put to death. That would be just like when we say that the Jews put the Savior to death; not that they smote Him themselves, but they gave Him over to be slain and cried out, "Crucify Him! Crucify Him!" (John 19:15).
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER THIRTEEN

So long as we are held down by this frail body, so long as we have our treasure in earthen vessels, so long as the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, there can be no sure victory. "Our adversary the devil goes about as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour." "You make darkness," David says, "and it is night, in which all the beasts of the forest do creep forth. The young lions roar after their prey and seek their meat from God." The devil does not look for unbelievers, for those who are outside, whose flesh the Assyrian king roasted in the furnace. It is the church of Christ that he "hurries to spoil." According to Habakkuk, "His food is the choicest." Job is the victim of his scheming, and after devouring Judas he seeks power to sift the other apostles. The Savior came not to send peace on the earth but a sword. Lucifer fell, Lucifer who used to rise at dawn, and he who was raised in a paradise of delight had the well-earned sentence passed on him, "Though you exalt yourself as the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord." For he had said in his heart, "I will exalt my throne above the stars of God," and "I will be like the most High." Therefore God says every day to the angels, as they descend the ladder that Jacob saw in his dream, "I have said you are gods, and all of you are children of the most High. But you shall die like mortals and fall like one of the princes." The devil fell first, and since "God stands in the congregation of the gods and judged among the gods," the apostle writes to those who are ceasing to be gods, "Since there is among you envy and strife, are you not carnal and walk as humans?"

And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say; and what follows: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you have sent books in your own name to all the people that is in Jerusalem, is not found in the Seventy; and again they added of their own: I did not send you in my name, and consequently, in order: and to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, and again from the Hebrew: and to all the priests; and then the story is woven on: The Lord has made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, that you may be leader — or instructor and overseer — in the house of the Lord over every man who is possessed and prophesies, that you may put him in the stocks and in prison — or in custody and in the cataract, for which Symmachus put mochlon [a bar], and Aquila put the Hebrew word itself, 'sinac' —. And now why have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite, who prophesies to you? For on this account he sent to us in Babylon, saying: It is long; build houses and dwell, and plant gardens and eat their fruit! So Zephaniah the priest read this book in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet. Shemaiah, from the place 'Nehellami', which means 'torrent', had been led to Babylon with King Jeconiah and was prophesying falsely to the people that they would quickly return to Jerusalem. That he was a false prophet the following words of Jeremiah show: thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: because Shemaiah has prophesied to you and I did not send him. Since, therefore, Jeremiah had sent a letter to those who were in Babylon, saying: build houses and dwell; plant gardens and eat their fruit; take wives and beget sons! And after other things had added: let not your prophets who are in your midst, and your diviners, lead you on! And then: for these prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord, Shemaiah, understanding that it had been written against him under the common name of the false prophets, sends a letter to Jerusalem, to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, the priest, and to the rest of the priests, against Jeremiah, asking why he was not rebuked by Zephaniah the priest, whose office it is to discern between prophets, which speak by the Holy Spirit and which by the contrary one, and why he was not ordered to be shut up in prison, that he might pay the penalty of his lie and cease to trip up the people any further. Jehoiada was the priest who handed the rule to Joash after the killing of Athaliah and killed the priest of Baal. This, then, is what he writes: 'why do you not imitate Jehoiada the priest and kill Jeremiah the false prophet? For the Lord has appointed you in place of Jehoiada, that you may have care of the temple and especially discern who speak by the Holy Spirit and who by a demonic one' — and the Apostle too records that the discernings of spirits belong to the Lord's grace —; 'why,' he says, 'have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite?' What he himself deserved as a false prophet he turns back upon the prophet, and he forestalls the truth with a lie. Hence too the sons of darkness are thought more prudent than the sons of light in this generation, and while we act patiently and wait for the salvation of the wretched, the heretics forestall us and call us by their own name, the blind leading the blind into the pit.

He sent, he says, to us in Babylon, saying: It is far off. This is all that grieves him: that against his lie Jeremiah wrote the truth, that the return was far off and that they would return to Jerusalem after seventy years; and that therefore they ought to build houses, plant orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and beget sons, as the preceding discourse related.

When Zephaniah the priest had received this letter, which was written specifically in his name, he read it to Jeremiah, in a way insulting him and rebuking him by the very reading, as to why he dared to write such things to Babylon.

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Send to all the exile, saying: Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you and I did not send him, and he has made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite and upon his seed; there shall not be a man sitting in the midst of this people, and he shall not see the good which I will do to my people, says the Lord, because he has spoken transgression against the Lord. The false prophet Shemaiah, truly a 'Nehellamites', who had taken up foreign and troubled waters from the 'torrent', is angry that Jeremiah has written true things against his lie, and he sends letters to Zephaniah the priest, asking why the prophet dared to write the truth, and he desires that he be shut up in prison so that he may not speak. Zephaniah too secretly accuses the prophet, while he reads the letter of the liar and boasts that he holds his accusation. How much more guilty of crime are those who defend false prophets and cherish liars and make the evil inventions of others their own sins!

Let the false prophet therefore hear, let the priest understand what he himself also deserves to hear through him: thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit upon Shemaiah. This the Lord speaks, not the prophet: that he will visit upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite, not for remedy but for the punishment of the liar, according to that which is written: I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges. Nor does he visit upon the false prophet alone, but also upon his seed, all the disciples whom he deceived by his error. There shall not be, he says, a man sitting in the midst of this people. Let the worst stock be blotted out of the assembly of the saints, and let him not sit in the midst of those at rest, who could not stand with those who stand, nor heard that saying: if he had stood in my substance. And whereas the Lord promises the perfection of all virtues when the sevenfold time is ended, he will not see the good which he claimed for himself in the present time. Now all this will come about because he has spoken transgression against the Lord, in saying that, the captivity of sins being already loosed, they would return to Jerusalem; such men the Apostle threatens: already you are filled, already you have become rich, without us you have reigned; and would that you did reign, that we also might reign with you!
30: This word, which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel, saying: Write for yourself in a book all the words which I have spoken to you! For behold, days will come, says the Lord, and I will turn back the turning of my people Israel and Judah, says the Lord, and I will turn them back — or I will make them settle — into the land which I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it. While the false prophets in Babylon were promising that the people who had been taken captive with Jeconiah would soon return, and while Hananiah son of Azzur was preaching the same things in Jerusalem, Jeremiah the prophet both asserted that this would indeed come to pass, not within two years, as they lied, but when the seventy years were finished, and now he is ordered to write in a book and to hand down to remembrance the things which the Lord foretells are to come. From this it is plain that the time of the prophecy is by no means near, but that these things are to be fulfilled after a long time, when Israel and Judah are to return to their land, and that what Ezekiel prophesied is to be fulfilled: that the two rods are to be joined together with each other, and that David the king will rule, of whom he writes: and my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd of them all. Whatever, therefore, we said on that prophecy must be understood in the present passage as well, especially since Ezekiel in Babylon and Jeremiah in Jerusalem prophesied the same things, and at the same time.

The length of the book of Jeremiah the prophet overcomes our purpose, so that, however briefly, we nonetheless say much. Hence the present sixth book of the commentaries on Jeremiah will also contain the mystical promises which the Jews, and our Judaizers, think are to be fulfilled at the consummation of the world; for they cannot prove that they were already fulfilled under Zerubbabel. We, however, following the authority of the apostles and evangelists, and above all of the Apostle Paul, show that whatever is promised carnally to the people of Israel has been fulfilled spiritually in us and is being fulfilled today, and that there is no other contest between Jews and Christians but this: that, while they and we both believe that Christ the Son of God has been promised, the things that are to be under Christ are said by us to have been fulfilled, by them to be yet fulfilled. We, therefore, who believe that Christ has already come, must teach that the things which are said to be going to take place under Christ have been fulfilled, and that we are the sons of Abraham, of whom it is written: God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham, to whom the promise was made: and in your seed all the nations shall be blessed. Teaching that this blessing was fulfilled in Christ, the vessel of election says: he did not say, he says, in seeds, but in seed, which is Christ. Pray, therefore, brother Eusebius, to the Lord Jesus Christ, that with the same labor and grace of the Spirit with which we have interpreted the promises of the other prophets, and especially of Isaiah, we may be able to explain those of this prophet also, who, as much as he seems simple and easy in his words, is in the same measure most profound in the majesty of his meanings.

And these are the words which the Lord spoke to Israel and to Judah, for thus says the Lord: We have heard a voice of terror — or of fear —; dread, and there is no peace. Ask and see whether a male gives birth! Why then have I seen the hand of every man upon his loins, as of a woman giving birth, and all faces have been turned into jaundice? First sad things are announced, so that after the greatness of the evils glad things may follow; for health is more welcome when sickness has been driven off, and the greatness of pain is turned into a greatness of joys. What he says, then, is this: so great will be the fear and so great the dread that, peace having been put to flight, all things will be filled with wars and blood, and that a womanish terror will take hold even of the men, whose proper task is to fight against adversaries, and they will put their hands by no means to arms but to holding their kidneys, as if a woman giving birth were clutching her flanks and loins. Hence also the faces of all will be turned into jaundice, testifying by the pallor of the countenance to the terror of the heart. Some interpret this passage according to tropology in such a way that they set down that testimony: From your fear, O Lord, we have conceived and travailed and brought forth; we have made the spirit of your salvation upon the earth, and they compare to this example that saying of the Apostle in which he says: My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ be formed in you; which plainly pertains not to terror but to joy, whereas the present Scripture signifies the time of the devastation and ruin of Israel.

Woe, for great is that day, nor is there any like it, and it is the time of the tribulation of Jacob! and from it he shall be saved. He foretells the time of misery in order to bring in the time of joy. 'Although,' he says, 'such great evils have gone before that the pain of all the men is compared to the pain of a woman giving birth, yet the time of the tribulation of Jacob, that is, of the people of God, will be changed into prosperity, and from it too he shall be saved' — 'time' is understood —, 'of which the discourse had spoken'. But by 'Jacob' understand the twelve tribes, which were saved by no means under Zerubbabel, as some falsely suppose, but by the calling of the Gospel.

And God promises that He will break from those who are thus to be saved the old heavy yoke of bitter daemons and shatter the bonds of the sins by which they were held of old, so that they will no more serve strange gods, but bear fruit and please Him only. Compare with this the oracle in the Second Psalm concerning the Coming of Christ and the calling of the Gentiles, which says: "Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast off their yoke from us." To which, I think, this we are considering is akin when it says:

"In that day, saith the Lord, I will break the yoke from off their necks, and shatter their bonds, and they shall not serve other gods, but shall serve the Lord their God."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 3

And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will break his yoke from off your neck and I will burst his bonds, and strangers shall no longer rule over him, but they shall serve — or work for — the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them. This is the David whom the Gospel also mentions: that he would grant us that, without fear, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. For just as a first Adam and a second Adam are written of according to the truth of the body, so also the Lord and Savior is David, because according to the flesh he is from David, holy Mary contributing to him wholly whatever was of the stock of David, while she had the origin and conception from the Holy Spirit. And as for his saying: I will break his yoke from off your neck and I will burst his bonds, there is no doubt that under the type of Nebuchadnezzar it must be understood of the devil.

"I shall raise up David their king for them." Christ the Lord brought fulfillment to the prophecy. He sprang from David according to the flesh, and he no longer shepherds only Israel but all the nations. The prophecy had a kind of outcome by way of shadow and type in the time of Zerubbabel as well.

[Passages quoted, Jer. xxiii. 6-8, xxx. 8, 9.]

Jeremiah prophesies thus long after the death of David and even the time of Solomon concerning a king who is to arise from the seed of David, whom he first calls "the rising," not simply but with the adjective "just," as though he were to shine forth from the sun of righteousness, of whom I treated in my evidences about the Second Cause, where I shewed that the pre-existent Word of God besides many other names was called Sun of Righteousness, quoting the prophecy which said, "To them that fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise." Therefore the prophecy in the present passage is that God will raise up "a righteous rising" to David, in the sense of a sun of righteousness. And he calls the same Being an understanding king, and one who does judgment and justice on the earth. He gives him too the same name as David, who died very long before. For you must note carefully how at the beginning he says, "And I will raise up to David a righteous rising," and adds at the end, "And I will raise up David to be his king." Whose, but David's?—for it was to him that he said He would raise up a righteous rising.

And Zechariah prophesying of the same Being likewise calls Him "arising," saying, "Behold I will raise up my servant, the rising," and also, "Behold a man whose name is 'The Rising,' and beneath him springs righteousness."

But no one, it is certain, arose after the time of Jeremiah among the Jews who could be called "a righteous rising" and "an understanding king doing judgment and righteousness on the earth." For if it be suggested that Jesus son of Josedec is meant, it must be answered that the prophecy is inapplicable to him. For he was neither of David's seed nor did he reign as king. How could this apply to him, "And I will raise up David to be his king," when he was of the tribe of Levi, and of high-priestly rank, and of another tribe than David, and is never recorded to have been king? We conclude that, as no other can be discovered, we must agree that the subject of this prophecy can only be our Lord and Saviour, called in other places "the light of the world," and "the light of the nations." He therefore must be the subject of this prophecy, and the prediction is absolutely true. For He alone of David's seed and figuratively named after his ancestor, for David means "strong-handed," preached judgment and justice by His teaching to all men on earth, and alone of all that ever lived is king not of one land only, but of the whole world, and alone has caused righteousness to arise over all the world, according to what is said of Him in the Psalm: "Righteousness shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace."
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 7, Chapter 3

You therefore, do not fear, my servant Jacob, says the Lord, nor be afraid, Israel, for behold, I will save you from a far-off land, and your seed from the land of their captivity, and Jacob shall return and be at rest and abound in all things, and there shall be none whom he fears, since I am with you, says the Lord, to save you. For I will make a full end among all the nations among which I have scattered you; but you I will not bring to a full end, but I will chastise — or instruct — you in judgment, so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless or and cleansing, I will not cleanse you. This perikopē [passage] is not found in the Seventy, and in very many manuscripts of the common edition it has been added under asterisks from Theodotion. The divine word makes a promise and, more familiarly, calls Jacob and Israel 'his servant', just as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are called 'servants of God' — Moses too and the other prophets, and the Apostle Paul at the beginning of his epistles glories in this title —, so that both the two and the ten tribes, that is, the twelve, may know that they are to be saved from a far-off land, that the captivity is to be loosed and peace restored, and that they are to be filled with all abundance, according to what is said in the psalm: Let there be peace in your strength and abundance in your towers!

And this will come about because they will enjoy the presence of the Lord, when the hostile nations which had captured them will perish and these will be set free from among the nations. And he teaches that they were handed over by no means to punishment but to instruction, so that they might be judged as his own, not destroyed as strangers; for he who does not believe has already been judged, that is, judged beforehand unto destruction. And what he added: so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless, or according to Symmachus: and cleansing, I will not cleanse you, or according to Aquila: when I have instructed you through judgment, I will by no means make you innocent, signifies that the whole world stands in need of the mercy of God, and that no one, however holy he may be, goes to the judge secure; against the new heresy sprung from the old, which supposes that in this age and in this mortal flesh, before this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality, there is perfection in anyone, and that the righteous man can fulfill all the virtues at once.

But that "contrition" and "a sore of pain through chastisement" are imposed on the soul for the sake of cure, Jeremiah teaches, saying: "Thus said the Lord: I have raised up contrition, thy sore is with pain, there is none that judges thy judgment, thou art cured with pain, there is no profit in thee. All thy friends have forgotten thee, nor will they now inquire concerning thee; because I have smitten thee with the wound of an enemy, with strong chastisement, for all thy iniquity, since thy sins are multiplied. Why criest thou out over thy contrition? Thy pain is violent, because of the multitude of thy iniquities thy sins have prevailed and have done these things to thee. Therefore all who devour thee shall be devoured, and all thine enemies shall devour their own flesh; and those who afflicted thee shall be in affliction, and all who devastated thee I will give over to plunder; for I will recall thy health, and from the pain of thy wound I will recall thee, said the Lord."

For thus says the Lord: Incurable is your fracture, most grievous your wound. There is none who judges your judgment for binding up; there is no benefit of healings for you. All your lovers have forgotten you, they will not seek you; for I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, with cruel chastisement — or strong —. Because of the multitude of your iniquity have become hard — or have been multiplied — your sins. Why do you cry out over your crushing? Incurable is your pain; because of the multitude of your iniquity and because of your hard sins I have done these things to you. He speaks as to a beautiful woman, to whom he had said above: I will chastise you in judgment, so that you may not seem to yourself guiltless or innoxia [guiltless, in the feminine]; and by metaphoran [metaphor] he speaks to Jerusalem, that she has been most grievously wounded by the judgment of God and can be healed by no other curing her except him who had struck her — there is none, he says, who judges your judgment — nor draw the skin of a scar over the deepest wound. 'Wherever you turn, there is no benefit for you, because you have offended him who is the true and only physician. All your lovers have forgotten you, whether the priests or the princes, or at any rate the protection of the angels by which, before you offended the Lord, you were walled about. They will not seek you, acting contrary to the Apostle, who sought the believers and not the things which were the believers'; for I have struck you with the blow of an enemy, with cruel chastisement.' A friend strikes in one way, an enemy in another; a father in one way, a foe in another. The one beats in order to correct, the other strikes in order to kill; hence the prophet too says tearfully: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your wrath! But this has happened because because of the multitude of your iniquity your sins have become hard. And what follows: Why do you cry out over your crushing? Incurable is your pain because of the multitude of your iniquity, is not found in the Seventy, evidently because it is said a second time: because of the multitude of your iniquity and your hard sins, and those who copied from the beginning thought it had been added. And the sense is: 'That I struck you with the blow of an enemy, that I beat you with cruel chastisement, the multitude of your iniquity and your hard sins brought about, which could not be healed except by the most biting powder and the burning cautery and the sharpest steel, with which I might cut away the putrid and incurable flesh. And yet because of the multitude of your iniquity and your hard sins I have done this to you, not by my own will, but because the method of medicine compelled me'.

Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your enemies shall be led into captivity, and those who lay you waste shall be laid waste, and all your plunderers I will give up as plunder. For I will draw a scar over you and from your wounds I will heal you, says the Lord, because they have called you cast out — or scattered —, Zion: this is she who had no one seeking her. And we know that these things were done under Zerubbabel too. When the Babylonians and Chaldeans laid waste the Assyrians, that is, Nineveh, and the Medes and Persians in turn captured the Babylonians and Chaldeans and Babylon was destroyed, then Zion began to have the Lord seeking her, and a scar was drawn over her wound and she was healed of her blows; which is fulfilled more fully and more perfectly in Christ.

Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn back the turning of the tents of Jacob, and on the dwellings — or captivity — of them I will have mercy, and the city shall be built on its height, and the temple shall be founded according to its order.
