And from them shall go forth praise and the voice of those playing, and I will multiply them and they shall not be diminished; and what follows: and I will glorify them and I will not make them few, is not found in the Seventy. And his sons, he says, shall be as from the beginning, and his assembly shall abide before me, and I will visit against all who afflict him. And his leader shall be from himself, and a prince shall be brought forth from his midst, and I will draw him close and he shall approach me; for who is this who draws his heart close so as to come near to me?, says the Lord; and again, what follows in the Hebrew is not found in the Greek: and you shall be, he says, my people, and I will be your God. A type of these things went before in Zerubbabel and Ezra, when the people returned and the city began to be built on its height and the worship of the temple to be observed, and the other things which are contained in the book of Ezra himself; but it was fulfilled more fully and more perfectly in the Lord and Savior and the apostles, when there was built the city on its height — of which it is written: a city that is set on a mountain cannot be hidden — and the temple according to its order and ceremonies was founded, so that whatever was done carnally among the former people might be fulfilled spiritually in the Church.

"I will multiply them, and they will not be diminished. Their congregation will be before my face," as during the time of Moses, Aaron and Joshua. All this and what would follow in the prophecy below was fulfilled and was accomplished in the coming of our Lord, as we have already noted above. Like many other things in the Lord's divine plan predicted by the prophet and fulfilled by the redemption and restoration of the people of God, this passage also should not be simply understood in the sense of Israel but of people that the divine Paul calls the Israel of God who consisted of, and were gathered from, Jews and people of other nations. This passage is not simply about biological children of Abraham but about children of promise, and Paul teaches the same. Only in this more mysterious sense was the word of Jeremiah fulfilled, "They would no longer serve foreigners, but they shall serve the Lord their God and king David, whom I will raise up for them." The Jews did not have peace. After they were conquered by the Chaldeans, they never were free from fear and oppression from other foreign nations. Rather, at various times they were enslaved by Persians, Greeks and Romans. These words of the prophet, "Jacob shall return, have rest and should not be afraid," were not fulfilled for Jews. All prophets who prophesied after the Babylonian captivity say that during their time Jews were not free from fear and wars with neighboring nations, and they did not have even a moment of rest but were instead in fear of other peoples. And even though they served the Lord their God and did not worship pagan gods, they were oppressed.

Then there went forth praise or thanksgiving — for this is what 'thoda' signifies —, so that all the apostles said: grace to you and peace, and the voice of those playing, not with that play with which the people ate and drank and rose up to play, but with that with which David played before the ark of the Lord. And they were multiplied and not diminished, so that the whole world believed in God the Savior, and they were glorified, so that what is written was fulfilled: Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God!

And his sons, that is, the apostles, were as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the princes of the race of Israel, were from the beginning. Then the Lord visited against all who afflicted the people of God, namely the adverse powers.

And there was his leader from himself — no doubt the Lord and Savior, according to the flesh from the race of Israel — and a prince from his midst was brought forth. The Father drew him close to himself, and he approached him, so that the Son might say: I in the Father and the Father in me, because no one can so draw his heart close to the Lord, nor be joined to him as the Son is to the Father.

And what he says according to the Hebrew only, but not according to the Seventy: and you shall be my people, and I will be your God, we see fulfilled in deed, in part in Israel and wholly in the multitude of the nations.

Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord, fury going forth, a storm rushing down, shall come to rest upon the head of the wicked. The Lord will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he does and fulfills the purpose of his heart; in the last of days you will understand these things. The whirlwind of the Lord's fury and the rushing storm and tempest will rest upon the head of the wicked, whether of the demons or of those who blasphemed the Son of God; and he will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he does and fulfills the purpose of his heart, and until Jerusalem is surrounded by an army and utterly destroyed. Now just as a craftsman cannot be understood except when the work is completed, nor the diligence of medicine except after health has been attained, so, when the overthrow of Jerusalem and the casting off of the former people have come about, then believers will understand that the rejection of the Jews is the occasion of our salvation.
31: At that time, says the Lord, I will be God to all the families of Israel — or to the race of Israel — and they shall be to me for a people. Unless the thought of the Lord has been fulfilled and his fury has come to rest upon the head of the ungodly, the Lord of the universe cannot be God to the families of Israel; but this he says to the remnant, which has been saved. But if what is said is set against us: I will be God to the race of Israel or to all the families of Israel, let us take up an example: 'if you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of your father'; and the Apostle writes: behold Israel according to the flesh. From this he teaches that there is another Israel according to the spirit. That one, then, is Israel who discerns God with the mind, or is the most upright one of the Lord, and an Israel of this kind will be the people of God.

With this sense the words of Jeremiah also agree, spoken in the person of the Lord: As something warm in the desert, I found Israel with those slain by the sword (Jer 38:2 LXX; Vulg. 31:2). For when, he says, the whole world lay lifeless, wounded by the swords of idolatry, I found Israel in Abraham to have the warmth of faith, like a physician who after a battle, among the corpses of the dead, where he perceives that someone still has something of life in his beating veins, applies care to his wounds to restore him to health. For what is written ὡς θερμὸν, that is, as something warm, the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, rendered lupine, and in this most of the Greeks also err. And yet it should be known that in the Hebrew, for warmth, THODA (תודה) is written, which means grace: namely, that Israel was saved by the grace of God, and not by the merit of its own works.

Thus says the Lord: the people that had remained from the sword found grace in the desert; Israel shall go to its rest. LXX: thus said the Lord: I found warm in the desert with those who had perished by the sword; go, and do not kill Israel! Ridiculously, in this place the Latin codices, through the ambiguity of the Greek word, translated 'lupines' for 'warm'; for the Greek THERMON signifies both, and it is not itself found in the Hebrew. For there is written 'hen', which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion translated as charin, that is, 'grace'; the Seventy alone put 'warm', thinking that the last letter was 'm'. For if we read 'hen' with the letter 'n', it means 'grace'; if with 'm', it is interpreted 'heat'. Now the sense according to the Hebrew is this: the people of the Jews, which had remained from the Roman sword, or at any rate had been able to escape the wrath of the Lord's fury, found grace in the desert of the nations, so that amid the crowd of the nations it might be saved in the Church; whence Israel shall go and shall find its rest, which it had always hoped for, which the prophecies of the prophets had promised it. Further, according to the Seventy this is the understanding: the Lord found the apostles and their companions warm and living in the desert of the nations, among those who had been killed by their own unbelief and did not have the warmth of life. Hence it is commanded to the angels and to those who are in the ministry of God that they should not kill all, that Israel should not be utterly destroyed, and it is said to them: 'go, and do not kill Israel; let there be some who live, let there be those who are warm with the ardor of faith, let there be those who escape the cold of unbelief and of death, whom the Lord may find in the desert!'

From afar the Lord appeared to me — or to him — : and with an everlasting love I have loved you; therefore I have drawn you, having pity. And again I will build you and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Again you shall be adorned with your timbrels — or you shall take up your timbrels — and you shall go forth in the dance of those who make merry. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; plant plantings and gather the vintage! for there shall be a day on which the watchmen on Mount Ephraim shall cry: arise, and let us go up into Zion to the Lord our God! Because Israel had offended the Lord and had said: we have no king but Caesar, and: come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours, and had withdrawn far from God, therefore the Lord after a long time appeared to him — not in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, after they were taken captive again —, but with an everlasting love, which will be blotted out by no end, he loved him, and drew him, having pity; for he was saved not at all by merit, but by clemency.

And again, he says, I will build you and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Let us understand this properly of the Church; for they rave who sigh for a golden and jeweled Jerusalem, consecrating their own avarice in the mystery of the Lord's city. 'Again you shall be adorned with your timbrels, so that you may sing to the Lord in the churches, all the flesh of evil works in you having been consumed, and you shall go forth in the dance of those who make merry with the crowds of the nations, you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria', not at all in the valleys and low places, but on the mountains of Samaria, which after the captivity of the people of Israel were possessed by foreigners, to whom it is said: plant plantings and gather the vintage!

Then was the day of the Lord, on which the watchmen — namely the apostles and apostolic men — cried on mount 'Samaria' and on mount 'Ephraim', of which the one sounds 'guard', the other 'fruitfulness'; but what do the watchmen of Samaria say, nay rather, what do they cry on Mount Ephraim? 'Arise, you who lie down, leave lowly things, spurn the offerings of victims' — a sacrifice to the Lord is a troubled spirit —, 'let us go up into Zion, that is, into the Church, where there is 'contemplation' and the beholding of God; and when we are in Zion, nay rather have gone up to it, we shall go up likewise to the Lord our God'.

For thus says the Lord: exult with gladness, Jacob, and neigh against the head of the nations; sound aloud, sing and say: save, O Lord, your people, the remnant of Israel! Significantly, not the whole of Israel is saved, but the remnant of Israel, the Lord commanding and saying: 'exult with gladness, you who are of Jacob, and neigh toward the head of the nations, referring all things to it, because the tail was once turned into the head; sound aloud and sing and say!' What is it that they are bidden to say? Save, O Lord, your people. Which people? Surely the remnant of Israel, which has been saved according to election, of whom Paul too speaks, taking up the testimony of Isaiah: unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have become as Sodom and we should have been made like Gomorrah.

When Jeremiah says, "And I will gather them together from the extremities of the land in the feast day," he signifies the day of the Passover and of Pentecost, which is properly a "feast day." However, every day is the Lord's. Every hour, every time, is apt for baptism. If there is a difference in the solemnity, there is no distinction in the grace.

Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north and will gather them from the ends of the earth; and what follows: at the solemnity of the Passover; and it shall beget many sons, is not found in the Hebrew, but is read only in the Seventy, in place of which among the Hebrews is written: among whom shall be the blind and the lame and the woman with child and the woman giving birth together, a great church of those returning hither. The remnant of the people of Israel is gathered through the apostles and apostolic men, of whom we read above: the watchmen shall cry on the mount, and to whom it is commanded: sound aloud and sing and say, so that the remnant of Israel may be saved. And the Lord himself promises that he will bring them back from the land of the north, which is a most harsh wind, but by name is called right, from unbelief, from the cold of the Lord's love, and will gather them from the ends of the earth, not at another time, but at the solemnity of the Passover, that is, on the festal days of the Lord's passion, when the Lord was crucified and that was fulfilled which he himself promised in the Gospel: when I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself. Then it begot a great people, so that that saying of Isaiah might be fulfilled: for a nation is born at once; for in one day three thousand and five thousand men believed. And what is written in the Hebrew: among whom shall be the blind and the lame and the woman with child and the woman giving birth together, a great church of those returning hither, although it has also been fulfilled according to the letter, in that the blind saw and the lame walked, yet it can better be understood according to anagōgēn [the higher, spiritual sense]: that those who before were blind with faithlessness afterwards believed in the Savior, and those who were lame, to whom Elijah once spoke: how long do you limp on both feet?, afterwards walked, and the people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light, and the lame ran, and the woman with child bore sons, a great church of those returning to the faith. The Jews think that this was fulfilled when under Ezra, after the day of the Passover, they went out from Babylon to return to Jerusalem, in which there was a type and not the truth; for they will not be able to prove that at that time all the things which we have read and are going to read were fulfilled.

Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?  And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?  And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.  Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,  And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty. [Jeremiah 31:9]

With weeping they shall come — or they shall go out — and in mercy I will lead them back, and I will bring them through torrents of waters in a straight way, and they shall not stumble — or they shall not go astray — in it, for I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn. If we read according to the Hebrew: with weeping they shall come — for this is what 'iabu' indicates —, we shall say that sometimes weeping is also a sign of excessive joy, according to that saying: I weep for joy. But if according to the Seventy, who said: with weeping they shall go out and in mercy — or in consolation — I will lead them back, we shall set down that sense which is also spoken in the Psalms: going they went and wept, carrying their seeds; but coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves. For they wept when they were led away captive, and they received the greatest consolation when they were led back by the mercy of the Lord. And the Lord brought them, through the apostles and apostolic men, full of waters and of a most abundant river, in a straight way, namely that of faith, not in the faithlessness of the Jews. And they shall not, he says, stumble in it, because they have ceased to be blind, to whom it was once said: if you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, We see; your sin remains. We can also understand the 'straight way' as Christ, in whom whoever walks will not stumble. I have become, he says, a father to Israel, who has been led back, and Ephraim is my firstborn; for where once sin abounded, grace abounded the more. And Scripture testifies that Ephraim is in the type of the people gathered from the nations. For he was the younger son of Joseph and stole away the birthright of Manasseh, who by nature was the firstborn; but in the mystery of the cross, the hands being crossed, he who stood at Jacob's left received the blessing of his right hand, and he who had stood at the right, blessed with the left, was reduced to the second rank. And as Jacob from Esau, so Ephraim snatched the birthright from Manasseh, and the whole people of the ten tribes was called Ephraim, because Jeroboam son of Nebat, from this tribe, was the first to obtain the kingdom in Samaria.

Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it to the islands that are far off, and say: he who scattered Israel will gather him and will keep him as a shepherd his flock, for the Lord has redeemed Jacob and has delivered him from the hand of one more powerful — or stronger —. And they shall come and shall praise on Mount Zion and shall flow together to the good things of the Lord, over grain and wine and oil and the young of flocks and of herds. Their soul shall be like a watered garden — or like a fruit-bearing tree — and they shall hunger no more. Then the virgin shall rejoice in the dance — or virgins — and young men and old together, and I will turn their mourning into joy and will console them and make them glad from their sorrow, and I will inebriate the soul of the priests with fatness — or of the sons of Levi — and my people shall be filled with my good things, says the Lord. The calling of the nations is clearly shown, Scripture saying: hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it to the islands that are far off, and say! What do they declare to the islands that are situated far off? That the Lord, who scattered Israel, himself will gather him — it was not at all, then, of the power of the adversaries that they were scattered, but of the Lord's will — and will keep him as a shepherd his flock — for the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep —, for the Lord has redeemed Jacob at the price of his own blood and has delivered him from the hand of one more powerful or stronger. By this it is shown that the adversary powers are stronger than the nature of human frailty, and, as to the strength that is in each, that they are stronger by nature, but we stronger by faith, if only we deserve to be delivered by him who can bind the strong man and plunder his house.

And they shall come, he says, — no doubt delivered from the hand of the powerful — and shall praise their deliverer on Mount Zion, that is, in the Church, and shall flow together to the good things of the Lord, the abundance of all things, which is perceived not in the fruits and foods of this flesh, but in the variety of the virtues. Over grain, he says, and wine and oil — from which the bread of the Lord is made, and the type of his blood is fulfilled, and the blessing of sanctification is shown, Scripture saying: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows — and the young of flocks, who are the simple in the Church, and of herds, which are horned and toss the adversaries. But that we may know that these blessings do not pertain at all to the body but to the soul, there follows: and their soul shall be like a watered garden or like a fruit-bearing tree, which is planted beside the streams of waters, and the paradise of the Lord in delights. And no more, he says, shall they hunger; not at all with that hunger of which it is written: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, but with that which is changed by satiety and shuts out the want of all things.

Then the virgin shall rejoice in the dance — of whom the Apostle writes: for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ — and the young men — to whom John speaks: I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one — and the old, to whom the same testifies in mystical speech: I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. And I will turn, he says, their mourning into joy — so that the resurrection may gladden those whom the cross had terrified — and I will console them and make them glad from their sorrow — according to what the Lord says: blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled — and I will inebriate the soul of the priests, who have the knowledge of God, from whose mouth they ask the law of the Lord, who believe in him to whom the prophet sings: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. But what follows according to the Seventy: of the sons of Levi, is not found in the Hebrew, and it is clear that here it is not at all said of those priests who are sons of Levi, but of those in whose type Melchizedek went before. And the 'inebriation' of the priests is proved in the apostles too, when they were fervent in faith and were said to be full of new wine; whence also the place in which the Lord was seized is called 'Gessemani', which in our language sounds 'valley of fatness'. And when the priests have been made fat with the teaching of the Lord and, inebriated at the banquet of Joseph, have said: your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is!, then this too will come about which the Lord now promises: and my people shall be filled with my good things. All these things are now granted in part; but then they will be given in full, when we see face to face and the body of our lowliness has been changed by the glory of the resurrection.

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men.  Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying,  In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not. [Jeremiah 31:15]

"Thus says the Lord: A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, sobbing and weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children." In a historical sense this prophecy speaks about sons of Judah and Benjamin living in Jerusalem and Bethlehem. Jeremiah later on describes the fulfillment of this prophecy, saying that tribes of Judah and Benjamin were sent to Ramah, the city of Benjamin's tribe, and then they were sent to captivity in Babylon. But in a spiritual sense, these words were fulfilled when Herod killed infants in Ephrathah and in its suburbs. It was said that Rachel was crying in Bethlehem and her voice was heard in Ramah because her body was buried in Bethlehem. But the people of Bethlehem were captured and sent to Ramah, and from there they had to go into a foreign land, to Babylon. It is why the prophet comforts mothers of killed infants when referring to Rachel.

Why then need I watch the rising and setting of the stars, at whose rising the fallows should be ploughed up and pierced by the hard plough-shares, and at whose setting the fruitful crop should be cut down by the sickle? One star suffices for me in the place of all others, the bright and morning Star, at Whose rising was sown the seed not of corn but of martyrs; when Rachel wept for her children, and offered in the stead of Christ her children washed in her own tears. The setting of this Star raised from the tomb not the senseless relics of the funeral pile, but the triumphant bands of the re-animated dead.

Herod sought him after his birth. He was to kill all the children in that place. And the prophet revealed this, too, foretelling it long beforehand when he said, "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, mourning and much weeping, of Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are not." The Scriptures also predicted that he would come to Egypt when they said, "Out of Egypt I called my son."

Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great wailing, Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not be consoled, because they are not. Of Rachel was born Benjamin, in whose tribe Bethlehem does not lie. It is asked, therefore, how Rachel weeps for the sons of Judah, that is, of Bethlehem, as if they were her own. We shall answer briefly: because she was buried near Bethlehem in Ephrathah (from the inner lodging of her little body she received the name of mother); or else because Judah and Benjamin were two joined tribes, and Herod had commanded that the boys be killed not only in Bethlehem but in all its borders round about; by occasion of Bethlehem we understand that many of Benjamin also were slain. And she weeps for her sons and does not receive consolation according to a twofold understanding: either because she thought them dead for ever, or because she would not be consoled for those whom she knew would live. And as for the saying: in Ramah, let us not think it is the name of the place which is near Gibeah; but Ramah is interpreted height, so that the sense is: A voice was heard on high, that is, spread far and wide.

Thus says the Lord: a voice of lamentation was heard on high, of weeping and mourning, of Rachel bewailing her sons, and she would not be consoled over her sons, because they are not. LXX: thus said the Lord: a voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and mourning, of Rachel bewailing her sons, and she would not be quieted, because they are not. Matthew took the testimony neither according to the Hebrew nor according to the Seventy; for we read in him, after the description of the slaughter of the infants: then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: a voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and much howling, of Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not be consoled, because they are not. From this it is clear that the evangelists and apostles did not at all follow anyone's translation from the Hebrew, but, as Hebrews from Hebrews, expressed in their own words what they read in Hebrew. Rachel, the mother of Joseph, when she was coming to Bethlehem, was suddenly seized with the pain of childbirth and bore a son, whom the midwife, because she was dying in giving birth, called Benoni, that is, son of my sorrow; but his father Jacob changed the name and called him Benjamin, that is, son of the right hand. It is asked, then, how Matthew the evangelist transferred the testimony of the prophet to the killing of the little ones, when it is clearly written of the ten tribes, whose chief was of Ephrathah, and it is not at all in the tribe of Ephraim, but in the tribe of Judah. For this same place is also Bethlehem, diōnymos [double-named], whence also the names of both agree; 'Bethleem' is called 'house of bread', 'Ephratha' karpophoria, which we can call 'fruitfulness'. Since, then, Rachel was buried in Ephrathah, that is, in Bethlehem — as both holy Scripture and the inscription of her tomb testify to this day —, she is said to weep for the children who were killed near her and in her own regions. Some of the Jews interpret this place thus: that, when Jerusalem was taken under Vespasian, countless thousands of captives were sent to Rome by this road, by Gaza and Alexandria; others, that in the last captivity under Hadrian, when the city of Jerusalem too was overthrown, a numberless people of various ages and of both sexes was sold at the market of the Terebinth; and that for this reason it is abhorrent to the Jews to visit that most frequented market. Let them say what they will; we shall say that the evangelist Matthew rightly took the testimony for the place in which Rachel was buried and wept for the sons of the neighboring villages round about as if they were her own.

Ramah belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, and the tomb of Rachel is in the hippodrome of Chaphratha on the way to Ephrath. While the prophecy had its fulfillment in the time of Herod the Great, who did away with the babies in the hope of doing away at the same time with the newborn Savior, the prophet places it here in the context of the promise of good things so as to emphasize that the birth of our Lord and Savior according to the flesh was the real good and the summit of salvation, though on account of it the babies met that unjust end.

Today we are celebrating the feast of all those infants who, the Gospel text tells us, were killed by King Herod, and for this reason our land, the fruitful mother of heavenly soldiers and such great virtues, should rejoice with the greatest exultation. Behold, the wicked enemy could never have helped the blessed infants as much by submission as he did by his hatred. As today's most sacred feast shows us, the grace of benediction shone forth in the blessed infants as much as cruelty against them abounded. For we heard a little while ago that when King Herod was pursuing Christ, thousands of happy boys were killed. As the prophet said, "Rachel mourns her children; she refuses to be consoled because her children are no more." The blessed mother of the triumphant, the land of illustrious warriors, rich in children, for a short time seemed to the eyes of the foolish to be bereaved. But she never was in need of consolation, nor did she bewail the sons whom she acquired with enviable sorrows, even while she lost them. Blessed are you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, who suffered the cruelty of King Herod in the death of your sons and at the same time merited to offer to God a white-clad group of peaceable, sinless infants.

According to the oracle of Jeremiah, "A voice was heard in Ramah," that is, "on high," "of lamentation and great wailing." This clearly denotes that holy church's mourning, by which it grieves for the violent death of its members, does not, as our enemies foolishly claim, pass away into a void, but it ascends right to the throne of the heavenly judge.

Thus says the Lord: let your voice cease from wailing and your eyes from tears, for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord, and they shall return from the land of the enemy — or of the enemies — and there shall be hope for your last end, says the Lord, and the sons shall return to their borders. This has not yet happened according to the letter — for we do not read that the ten tribes, which are in exile in the cities of the Medes and of the Persians, have returned to the land of Judea —, but according to the spirit it was fulfilled in the passion of the Lord and is being fulfilled up to now, when Israel is saved from the whole world and it is said to Rachel: let your voice cease from wailing and your eyes from tears!, and the sense is: 'cease to wail — for the Lord has looked upon your former works — and your sons shall return from the land of the enemy, and do not be held by present sorrow! for there is hope in your last end, says the Lord, and your sons shall return to their borders, which their fathers had, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob'. But we understand it better of the little ones: that they have the reward of their blood shed for Christ, and in place of the land of Herod the enemy they hold the kingdoms of heaven, and they will return to their former seat when, in place of the body of lowliness, they receive a glorious body. This is the last hope, when the righteous shall shine like the sun, and the infants, once little ones and sucklings, rise again without the increase of years and without the injuries and toil of the body. Into the perfect man, into the measure of the fullness of Christ.

Let us purify ourselves by tears, that the Lord our God may hear us when we lament, as he heard Ephraim when weeping, as it is written: "I have surely heard Ephraim weeping." He expressly repeats the words of Ephraim: "You have chastised me, and I was chastised; like a calf I was not trained." For a calf shows itself off and leaves its stall, and so Ephraim was untrained like a calf far away from the stall, because he had forsaken the stall of the Lord, followed Jeroboam and worshiped the calves, which future event was prophetically indicated through Aaron, namely, that the people of the Jews would fall after this manner. And so repenting, Ephraim says, "Turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are the Lord my God. Surely in the end of my captivity I repented, and after I learned I mourned over the days of confusion and subjected myself to you because I received reproach and made you known."

Hearing I heard Ephraim going into exile — or lamenting — : you have chastised me and I was instructed like an untamed bullock — or like a calf, and I did not learn — ; convert me, and I shall be converted, for you are the Lord my God. For after you converted me — or I was taken captive —, I repented, and after I knew — or you showed me —, I struck my thigh — or I groaned — ; I was confounded and blushed — or from the day of confusion and I showed you —, because I bore the reproach of my youth. God says what he heard Ephraim saying and lamenting. Now no one doubts that it signifies the ten tribes, over which Jeroboam son of Nebat first ruled, who also made the golden calves in Dan and Bethel, so that the people, seduced by this error, might cease to worship and adore the God of Israel. You have chastised me, he says, and I was chastised. Every correction, which for the present seems to be of sadness, profits for salvation and afterwards brings peaceable fruits. And what he says: like an untamed bullock or a calf, and I did not learn, signifies this: that he was instructed with much toil and with blows, so that he might be turned to repentance, and he did not profit. 'Convert', he says, 'me, and I shall be converted' — therefore even this very thing, that we repent, we cannot accomplish unless we rely on the help of God — ; 'for after you have converted me and I have been converted to you, then I shall know that you are the Lord my God, and not at all my errors and sins. And after you converted me, I repented'.

See how great is the help of God and how frail the human condition, that this very thing, that we repent, we are not at all able to accomplish unless the Lord has first converted us. 'And after', he says, 'you showed me either repentance itself or the knowledge of you, or I knew you, I struck my thigh.' This is the sign of one grieving and lamenting and bewailing his former error: that he strikes his thigh with his hand and confesses that he was foolish before. I was confounded, he says, and blushed or from the day of confusion. For what time is not one of our confusion, if we recall our ancient sins and call to memory all the things we have done ill? And what the Seventy said: and I showed you, signifies that, after he groaned and knew his own offenses, he then came to such progress that he even showed God to others who did not know him, according to what David too says in repentance: I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you. Because I bore, he says, the reproach of my youth. He says that he sinned through the ignorance of his age, so that he may more easily obtain pardon, according to what David too sings: the offenses of my youth and my ignorances do not remember! Whence also in what follows the Lord calls him 'a little one' and 'abounding in delights'; and this he says on account of the greatness of its riches and the fertility of the land, in which the tribe of Ephraim luxuriates to this day.

Is Ephraim an honorable son — or beloved — to me, is he a delicate child? for, since I spoke of him — or my words in him —, I will still remember him; therefore my bowels are troubled over him; pitying I will have pity on him, says the Lord. Since Ephraim repents and says at the beginning: you have instructed me and I was instructed like an untamed bullock, and at the end: because I bore the reproach of my youth, the Lord answers, and sustains him, turned to him with his whole mind, with such an oracle: 'Ephraim is a beloved son to me, whom I loved so much from the beginning that I preferred him to his brother Manasseh.' An honorable son, who against the order of nature received the honor of the firstborn by the condescension of the Lord; a delicate child, of whom he writes: the sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle, against whom and to whom the whole book of the prophet Hosea is addressed, whom Jacob blesses. And let us take 'delights' in this place according to what is said in the psalm: delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart, for which in the Greek and in the Hebrew it has: abound in delights; whence also the paradise in Eden is called the paradise 'of delights'. 'For', he says, 'there were my words in him, with remembrance I will still be mindful of him.' Lest the blessing be thought gratuitous, and to have been conferred out of the indulgence of the giver rather than by the merit of him on whom it was bestowed, therefore he says: 'I will remember him, for my words were in him, not in his mouth, not on his lips, but in the innermost affection of the heart; for which cause also my bowels are troubled over him'. To him he speaks through Hosea too: what shall I do to you, Ephraim? what shall I do to you, Israel? shall I make you as Admah and as Zeboiim? my heart is turned within me, my bowels are troubled. I will not execute the fury of my wrath and I will not destroy Ephraim. Pitying I will have pity on him, says the Lord. 'My words indeed were in him, and he received all my commandments with an eager mind and kept them in his heart; but nevertheless pitying I will have pity on him', to show that all the righteousness of men needs the mercy of God.

The Impassible speaks as if it suffered passion, and that which contains in Itself the cause of its own and all other bliss talks as though it could be in want and yearning. "Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him."

Set up for yourself watchtowers, put for yourself bitternesses, direct your heart into the straight way in which you walked; return, virgin Israel, return to these your cities! How long will you be dissolved in delights, wandering daughter? for the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man. LXX: set up for yourself lookouts, make punishment, give your heart to your shoulders; the way in which you walked, return, virgin Israel, return to your cities mourning! How long will you turn away, despised daughter? for the Lord has created you as salvation for a new planting; in your salvation men shall go about. Where we said: how long will you be dissolved in delights?, Symmachus put: how long will you sink into the deep? Now I have set out each edition in full, in order to show that a most obscure passage, one containing the mysteries of the Church, was either unknown to or omitted by the Seventy — or whoever else translated this prophet. The Hebrew word 'sionim' is rendered either as 'lookouts' or as 'watchtowers', as Aquila and Symmachus translated. Hence I wonder what the common edition meant by putting 'Sion' in place of 'sionim', that is, 'lookouts', and so confusing the reader's understanding that he would think that after Ephraim the word of God had suddenly been addressed to Zion and to the tribe of Judah, although the discourse is continuously to Ephraim, to whom he also spoke above: hearing I heard Ephraim, and: Ephraim is an honorable son to me or a delicate child, and to whom he now also speaks: 'set up for yourself watchtowers or lookouts, to announce to you beforehand that so great a happiness of all things is coming.' And what follows, 'bitternesses', which in Hebrew are called 'themrurim', for which Symmachus translated 'changes', indicates this: that she ought to weep, either for her ancient sins or from the greatness of her joy, and to be converted to God with her whole mind, and to set or direct her heart into the way by which she set out; for by that way she will return. And what the Seventy said in place of this: give your heart to your shoulders, signifies that she ought to join her thoughts to works, or to contemplate the shoulders of those carrying her, bringing her back from captivity; which Isaiah sets out more fully in the camels and chariots and litters, asserting that they are to be brought back. 'Return', he says, 'virgin Israel, return to your cities, which you deserted when they were captive! How long will you be dissolved in negligence and wander in deep error? Look at what I am about to say, and attend diligently to whence so great a blessedness is to be hoped for by you; hear what you had never known before! The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: without the seed of a man, without any intercourse and conception, a woman shall encompass a man in the bosom of her womb, who, according to the increments of age indeed, through wailings and infancy will be seen to advance in wisdom and age, but a perfect man will be contained in a woman's belly for the usual months.' Hence both Symmachus and Aquila translated in accordance with our edition. But what the common edition meant in this place I could say, and could find some sense, were it not sacrilege to argue about the words of God with human sense. Theodotion, however, himself also agreeing with the common edition, translated: the Lord has created a new salvation, in salvation man shall go about, putting the singular for the plural; and at the same time this too is to be noted, that the nativity of the Savior and the conception of God is called 'creation'.

A figure preceded in the woman and the man, because Jeremiah says: "A woman shall encompass a man." All of this was fulfilled in the glorious Virgin. Whence Bernard says: "What was shown to Moses in the bush and fire, to Aaron in the rod and flower, to Gideon in the fleece and dew: this Solomon clearly foresaw in the strong woman and her price; more clearly Jeremiah foretold concerning the woman and the man; most clearly Isaiah declared concerning the Virgin and her son; and at last Gabriel made it manifest by greeting the Virgin."

The word of Jeremiah concerns the woman and the man: "A new thing," he says, "the Lord will make upon the earth; a woman shall encompass a man." Who brought it about that the Virgin conceived? Certainly the Holy Spirit, who is a love fervent, fruitful, undefiled, virile, incorrupt, and deifying. That he is a virile love is signified to us in the woman and the man, because the "woman encompassed the man," that is, enclosed him on every side.

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: they shall still say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity: the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain! And Judah shall dwell in it, and all its cities together, husbandmen and those who drive flocks. LXX: thus said the Lord of powers, the God of Israel: they shall still say this speech in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I bring back its exile: blessed be the Lord upon his righteous holy mountain, and those who dwell in the land of Judea and in every city of it with the husbandman; and he shall be lifted up in the flock. According to the Hebrew it is plain that at the return of Israel, its captivity having been turned back into its own land, the cities of Judah dwell, and it is said to them one by one: the Lord bless you, who is truly the beauty of righteousness and the holy mountain, in which whoever dwells will fear no snares; and Judah will dwell without iniquity in its cities, and there will be husbandmen and a multitude of cattle. This seems to have been fulfilled in part under Zerubbabel and Ezra, but let the fullness of the prophecy be referred to the times of Christ: either to the first coming, when these things were done spiritually, or to the second, when all things are fulfilled — according to us spiritually, according to the Jews and our Judaizers carnally. Further, according to the Seventy this is the sense: 'this speech shall still be spoken in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back its captivity'. What shall be spoken? Blessed be the Lord upon his righteous holy mountain. The mountain which deserves to receive the name 'of righteousness and of holiness' is no other than the Savior; for the rest, it is foolish, with Jewish error, to believe an irrational and insensible mountain 'righteous and holy'. He it is of whom it is also written in what follows: and in every city of it — understood: of the Savior — with the husbandman; no doubt it signifies God, of whom it is written in the Gospel too: I am the vine, you the branches, and my Father is the husbandman; whence also the Apostle says: you are God's husbandry, God's building. And what follows: and he shall be lifted up in the flock, shows this: that in the several flocks the righteous and holy one and husbandman, the Lord himself, is lifted up, and in his servants and believers ascends to the heights.

For I have inebriated the weary soul — or for I have inebriated every thirsting soul — and every hungering soul I have satisfied — or I have filled —, therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me. The change of persons makes the understanding of the prophets obscure. The Lord had said: they shall still say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I turn back their captivity. And what shall they say? No doubt this, which follows: the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain, and the rest. And again, while they say these things, the Lord answers: for I have inebriated the weary soul — or thirsting — and every hungering soul I have satisfied. And while he says these things, the people that had come from captivity answers: therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me. For the Lord inebriates the weary or thirsting soul, and says in the Gospel: whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and: whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water; and he satisfies every hungering and thirsting soul, of which thirst and hunger the same testifies in the Gospel: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. And it is to be noted that 'inebriation' in this place is put in a good sense, of which in the Canticle too it is said: eat, friends, drink and be inebriated, dearest ones! With this inebriation Joseph too was inebriated with his brothers at midday.

Let us, then, submit ourselves to God, and not be subject to sin, and when we ponder the remembrance of our offences, let us blush as though at some disgrace, and not speak of them as a glory to us, as some boast of overcoming modesty, or putting down the feeling of justice. Let our conversion be such, that we who did not know God may now ourselves declare Him to others, that the Lord, moved by such a conversion on our part, may answer to us: "Ephraim is from youth a dear son, a pleasant child, for since My words are concerning him, I will verily remember him, therefore have I hastened to be over him; I will surely have mercy on him, saith the Lord." And what mercy He promises us, the Lord also shows, when He says further on: "I have satiated every thirsty soul, and have satisfied every hungry soul. Therefore, I awaked and beheld, and My sleep was sweet unto Me." We observe that the Lord promises His sacraments to those who sin. Let us, then, all be converted to the Lord.

For you should not be surprised if the Prophet says that his soul is disturbed, since the Lord Jesus himself said: "Now my soul is troubled." For he who took on our weaknesses also took on our emotions, in which he was sad even unto death, not because of death; for voluntary death could not have sorrow, in which the joy and refreshment of all was to come. Of this he also said elsewhere: "And I arose, and saw, and a sweet sleep came to me." Blessed sleep that made the hungry not hunger, the thirsty not thirst, for whom he prepared the sweetness of the sacraments. So how then was his soul troubled by fear, who made the souls of others not fear? Sorrowful even unto death, until grace was perfected: which is proven by his own testimony saying of his death: "With the baptism I am to be baptized, and how am I distressed until it is accomplished?"

And those who had been weary and had hungered, inebriated and satisfied, give thanks, answering: 'I awoke and saw the Lord', namely raising them up and saying: arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you. 'And my sleep', he says, 'was sweet to me, so that I might imitate the words of my Lord, who says: I slept and was put to rest; and I rose up, because the Lord sustained me'.

Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of men and the seed of beasts. And as I watched over them to pluck up and to demolish and to scatter and to destroy and to afflict, so I will watch over them to build and to plant, says the Lord. In those days they shall no longer say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge; but each one shall die in his own iniquity; every man who eats the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge. 'House' and 'house', that is, the house of Israel and the house of Judah, is not in the Seventy, but only: Israel and Judah, so that it reads: and I will sow Israel and Judah. And what he added: with the seed of men and the seed of beasts, we ought to refer to the rational and the simple.

And as at the beginning of Jeremiah it was said to him: 'behold, I have set you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to pluck up and pull down and destroy and scatter and build and plant, — and I watched over them, to do what I threatened, — so', he says, 'now I will watch over them to build and to plant; God's indeed husbandry, God's building you are.' All promises of this kind are thought, according to the Jews and our Judaizers, to be fulfilled in a kingdom of a thousand years. But we, since the Apostle says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase, and the prophet Isaiah records that the Savior is the builder of hedges and of houses, maintain that they were fulfilled spiritually at the first coming of Christ — and fulfilled in part, not in whole, because now we see in a mirror and in an enigma, and we do not know as we ought to know; but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away — or at any rate we believe that they are to be fulfilled at the second coming, when the Lord will appear in his majesty and the fullness of the nations has come in, so that all Israel may be saved, and not at all in part, through individuals, but that God may be all in all.

In the mean time, whom will you be able to persuade that by receiving the lapsed the whole Church hath perished? That by the admission of penitents, the people of those who admit them has been made a denier of the Faith? But even if the people here or there have been too lax, have the other peoples also who approved not of their deed, but followed custom and peace, lost the Christian name? Hear the voice of Jeremiah, In those days shall they not say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge. But every one shall die for his own iniquity.

And what is brought in: in those days they shall no longer say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge, and the rest, we discussed more fully in the explanations of Ezekiel, when we interpreted that place: son of man, what is this parable to you among the sons of Israel, who say: the fathers have eaten a sour grape and the teeth of the sons are set on edge? As I live, says the Lord, if this parable shall be any longer in Israel! for all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son; the soul that sins, it shall die. By this we learn that it is not the Lord who makes death, but sin; for the soul that sins, it shall die. And this is said in the present place: that Israel will not at all stumble forever because of the sins of the fathers, but will be saved by its own merits and by faith in Christ after many ages. And it is to be observed that vices and sins are called 'a sour grape', so that the teeth of those who eat are set on edge and cannot perceive the sweetness of him of whom it is said: taste and see that the Lord is sweet! Whoever does not understand the Scriptures as the truth of the matter holds eats a sour grape; whence also all heretics, believing perverse things, cannot eat the bread that comes down from heaven, but their teeth are set on edge, not by the harshness of the foods, but by the fault of the teeth.
It is similarly impossible, he says, for children to be called to account for ancestral sins, because I promise to children the greatest blessings even when their parents sin.

All things therefore are of one and the same substance, that is, from one and the same God; as also the Lord says to the disciples "Therefore every scribe, which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven, is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old." He did not teach that he who brought forth the old was one, and he that brought forth the new, another; but that they were one and the same. For the Lord is the good man of the house, who rules the entire house of His Father; and who delivers a law suited both for slaves and those who are as yet undisciplined; and gives fitting precepts to those that are free, and have been justified by faith, as well as throws His own inheritance open to those that are sons. And He called His disciples "scribes" and "teachers of the kingdom of heaven;" of whom also He elsewhere says to the Jews: "Behold, I send unto you wise men, and scribes, and teachers; and some of them ye shall kill, and persecute from city to city." Now, without contradiction, He means by those things which are brought forth from the treasure new and old, the two covenants; the old, that giving of the law which took place formerly; and He points out as the new, that manner of life required by the Gospel, of which David says, "Sing unto the Lord a new song;" and Esaias, "Sing unto the Lord a new hymn. His beginning, His name is glorified from the height of the earth: they declare His powers in the isles." And Jeremiah says: "Behold, I will make a new covenant, not as I made with your fathers" in Mount Horeb. But one and the same householder produced both covenants, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spake with both Abraham and Moses, and who has restored us anew to liberty, and has multiplied that grace which is from Himself.

For we find in the Scriptures, as the Lord says, "Behold, I make with you a new covenant, not as I made with your ancestors in Mount Horeb." He made a new covenant with us. For what belonged to the Greeks and Jews is old. But we, who worship him in a new way, in the third form, are Christians. For clearly, as I think, he showed that the one and only God was known by the Greeks in a Gentile way, by the Jews Judaically and in a new and spiritual way by us.

And theirs is the new covenant, not according to the old. Do not allow the covenant of the pre-Mosaic Saints to be called "the old covenant,"but that which was given to the Jews by the Law of Moses. For the text which says that the new will be quite unlike the old clearly implies which one was the old:

"I will make a new covenant, not according to the covenant I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt."

"Not according to the covenant of the Mosaic Law,"he says. For that was introduced to the Jews at the exodus from Egypt. It might have seemed that he was introducing a new covenant opposed to the religious ideals of the Abrahamic Saints, if he had not distinctly said:

"Not according to the covenant, which I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt."

He prophesied that the new covenant would not be according to the one enacted at the time of the Exodus and the wanderings in the wilderness, but according to the ancient one under which the pre-Mosaic saints flourished.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 6

This new song is called by Jeremiah, another Hebrew prophet, "a new covenant"where he says:

"31. Behold the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Juda: 32. not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt: for they abode not in my covenant, and I disregarded them, saith the Lord. 33. For this is my, covenant which I will make with the house of Israel, saith the Lord, I will put my laws in their minds, and on their hearts I will write (them), and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

You see here that he distinguishes two covenants, the old and the new, and says that the new would not be like the old which was given to the fathers. For the old covenant was given as a law to the Jews, when they had fallen from the religion of their forefathers, and had embraced the manners and life of the Egyptians, and had declined to the errors of polytheism, and the idolatrous superstitions of the Gentiles. It was intended to raise up the fallen, and to set on their feet those who were lying on their faces, by suitable teaching.

"For the law, it is said, is not for the righteous, but for the unjust and disorderly, for the unrighteous and for sinners, and for those like them."

But the new covenant leads those who, through our Saviour by the grace and gift of God are raised up, to a rapid march into the kingdom promised by God. It summons all men equally to share together the same good things.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 4

And we heard just now what the ordinances of the prophet were, which we must obey, their wisdom, perfection and heavenliness, which he thought fit to inscribe, not on tables of stone like Moses, nor yet with ink and parchment, but on the hearts of his pupils, purified and open to reason. On them he wrote the laws of the new covenant, and actually fulfilled the prophecy of Jeremiah.

"I will make a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers. For this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel, I will give my laws into their mind, and upon their heart I will write them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

THE one wrote on lifeless tables, the Other wrote the perfect commandments of the new covenant on living minds.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapters 7-8

How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. They were always rebellious and disrespectful against God, and therefore they received such commandments by which their necks, which were unbending, might be pressed down. For they never wished to hope for good things from God, whose such great benefits and such wondrous powers they had come to know. Therefore it is that, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: “I lifted up my hand to them in the desert, that they should be scattered among the nations and dispersed in the lands, because they did not perform my ordinances and rejected my commandments.” And in what follows: “I gave them laws that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live in them” (Ezek. 20:23–25). He shows for what reason such great and so harsh commandments were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great benefits, and, justice dictating, they were to be pressed by more severe precepts. Therefore He called them “not good,” although they are just: because they did not lead them to justification, but to destruction; and although a punishment rightly inflicted, yet for the one who suffers it, it is not a good. After these things, however, because God is merciful, He promised that He would give the New Testament, in which the shortening of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham was justified: so that, with new moons and the sabbath and circumcision and the other precepts ceasing, not those that belong to the natural law, that is, murder, adultery, and such things, they might be justified as Abraham was. For, with the faith of Abraham renewed, He willed that all things should cease, so that the time might be such as it was when Abraham believed. But perhaps the Jews say: “If those things that were given by Moses are said to cease through the shortening of the Law, was circumcision given by Moses so that it should cease? And therefore we have the sign of our father, because we are the sons of Abraham, a sign which, for the sake of the testimony of our lineage, ought not to cease.” Circumcision indeed had to be observed in its time, that is, before the New Testament which had been promised was given. But when, by the grace of God, the burdens of the Law were ordered to cease, what need is there of circumcision? Therefore a new Law was given, that is, a spiritual one, so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign: so that just as in the Old Testament they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Testament began, so also in the New they might have the sign of the Savior, who is the institutor of the New Testament. For just as from Abraham they were called Hebrews, so from Christ they are called Christians. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the New Testament which God promised, bringing to nothing the kindness and mercy of God: for He no longer wished His people to be designated by the name of a man, but agreed to establish them under the name of His Son. With what courage, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will give thanks to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, O nations, with his people”? And to the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Judaism certainly has its own particular signs: for this people is signified either in Jacob, or in Samaria, or in Jerusalem, or in Judea, or in Israel. As for the nations, however, it is clear that He signifies them in a different way than He does the Jews. Therefore Jeremiah is our prophet. For although in all the Prophets God showed that the nations would share in His gift, yet to Jeremiah in particular He says that He has given him to us as a prophet. For he signified that the New Testament would come, which would profit the Gentiles more than the Jews, as now appears clearly. For since the preaching of the New Testament is spread over the whole earth, a faithful Jew is so rarely and with such difficulty found that all the Churches of the New Testament are called “of the nations,” as it was said in the prophet Hosea: “I will call that which is not my people, my people; and her that was not beloved, beloved” (Hosea 2:24; Rom. 9:25). Therefore, the Jews having been rejected, He calls the nations with the same mercy and grace with which He agreed to call Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. Therefore, He who agreed to call Abraham likewise agreed to call the nations. Why then do they say, “The Law is ours,” when it is clear that the gift of God is for all who are willing? Let this careless violation cease, since the grace of God is common to all. With what shame do they deny that our Christ was promised in the Law, when they see in Him all the signs which the Law foretold as to come? For both according to the promise made to Abraham all nations are justified by believing in Him (Gen. 22:18); and according to the prophet Isaiah He was born of a Virgin (Isa. 7:14) in Bethlehem from the tribe of Judah, as was promised, from the seed of David (Micah 5:2); and in accordance with what Jeremiah prophesied (Jer. 31:31–32), He proclaimed the New Testament which God then promised would come; and after all the signs of power had been shown, He humbled Himself, according to the words of the Prophets; and having suffered all that had been foretold, He rose on the third day, as it is written in the prophet. And if they inquire about the time of the promise, as it is shown in the prophet Daniel (Dan. 9:24 ff.), they will find it fulfilled in the time when Christ was born and suffered: for from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, down to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, chief of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were completed, which are four hundred and ninety years, a reckoning made clear through the kingdoms and the successors of the empire. Therefore also it is found calculated by Tertullian in the book which he wrote against the Jews; but, lest this should backfire to his disadvantage, although he calculated correctly, we have passed it over in silence. And who can doubt this number, when now about three hundred years are found in addition to that number? It is therefore shameless, after so many years have been added beyond the time of the coming of the Saviour, to say, “He has not come.” Under the Apostles, or at the time when the Lord was living among men, hatred opposing the truth could still hide itself; so that, although it saw all the signs of the Christ who had been promised in the Savior, it could say that it doubted about the time, to conceal its unbelief. But afterwards, when many years began to exceed the promised number, what shamelessness it is to deny that He has come, whose coming is known to have been fulfilled both by signs and by times! For when something is full and does not overflow, a combative person may say that it is not full; but overflow closes the mouth of the argumentative. So the Jews, in the time of the Saviour, could say, though deceitfully, that the calculation from the time of Darius to the Lord Christ was not correctly made, so that He might not be acknowledged as the one who had been promised. We are mistaken, they might say, in the years and in the months and in the days of the emperors, and we do not make an exact reckoning. But when the times have extended beyond the prescribed number of years of the promised Christ, no excuse can be put forward to deny that He who has come is the Christ, unless, which God forbid, the one who promised is said to have lied. For when the time of the promise has elapsed, and it is denied that the one who was promised has come, what else is charged against the promiser but falsehood? Yet that He who made the promise is truthful, all the signs teach which were foretold in Christ and are known to have been found in Christ. The Jews, however, while they are ashamed to change themselves, do not consider that there will be a judgment to come. For nothing is worse than for someone to deny that a thing is true when he understands that it is not a lie.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

IF THE LAW AND THE PROPHETS WERE UNTIL JOHN, HOW IS IT THAT THE SAVIOR SENDS THE LEPER TO THE PRIESTS TO HAVE OFFERINGS MADE FOR HIS CLEANSING (Matt. 8:4; Mark 1:44; Luke 5:14)? — This was done not because of the time, but for the condemnation of the Jews: so that when they did not understand that the summit of truth, belonging to a better time, had been established for the gain of their salvation, Truth might bend down instead to their accusation. For since they regarded the Savior as an enemy of the Law, because for the sake of mercy he wished to free them from the burden of the Law, just as had been foretold by the prophet Jeremiah, for he says among other things, “And I will give them a new covenant, not like the one I gave to their fathers” (Jer. 31:31–32), then the Savior, so that he might not appear, as they thought, to be an enemy when preaching new things, sent the man who had been cleansed from leprosy to the priests to offer gifts for his cleansing, as Moses had commanded (Lev. 14:2). And to show that this was to serve for their accusation, he said, “For a testimony to them,” so that this matter might be a witness against them in judgment, they who were saying that the Savior was an enemy of the Law. The apostle Paul followed this as well: for although he preached that circumcision was no longer necessary, he himself circumcised Timothy because of the scandal of the Jews (Acts 16:3); for he preferred to do something unnecessary rather than have an uproar stirred up by false brothers; and this in fact contributed to the Jews’ error. Enough was done for them for the moment, through which they might err forever.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 60: WHY THE SAVIOR SENT THE CLEANSED LEPER TO THE PRIESTS

From the prophets I will prove that the Old and New Covenants have one Lawgiver. And so, what does Jeremiah say? "I will give you a new covenant." Do you see Jeremiah's prophetic reference to a new covenant that shines forth brilliantly for so many years before Christ's coming? "I will give you a new covenant."
